docs.title: CVE-2026-111812 — Apache Traffic Server: origin_server_auth Signs Attacker-Chosen AWS Headers
docs.text: Educational content only. This writeup explains the vulnerability conceptually. Nothing here is a working exploit. Do not test against systems you do not own.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Field Value Severity CRITICAL — CVSS 3.1 10.0 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N) Product Apache Traffic Server Type Incorrect Authorization (CWE-863) Attack vector Network — unauthenticated

This CVE is one of three CVSS 10.0 flaws disclosed together in Apache Traffic Server's October 2026 security bulletin, alongside six sibling issues (CVE-2026-111814, CVE-2026-111815, CVE-2026-111811, CVE-2026-111809, CVE-2026-111805, CVE-2026-111808, CVE-2026-111810, CVE-2026-112381).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The origin_server_auth plugin signs requests forwarded to AWS backends using the proxy's own IAM credentials (AWS SigV4). It builds the signed payload from the request headers as received from the client, without distinguishing headers the proxy generated itself from headers supplied by the remote client. Any client can therefore submit attacker-chosen headers and have them stamped with the proxy's real cloud identity.

In short: a signature proves the request passed through the proxy, but the proxy never verified who wrote the headers. Signing is not the same as trusting the sender.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptual only — educational. The attack chain works like this:

  1. The attacker sends an HTTP request to the proxy carrying custom headers that mimic AWS-signed API request fields.
  2. The plugin treats the client-supplied headers as legitimate signing input and signs the whole set with the proxy's IAM credentials.
  3. The signed request is forwarded to the AWS backend, which validates the signature against the proxy's identity.
  4. The backend cannot distinguish the attacker's request from genuine proxy traffic, so the attacker operates with the proxy's cloud privileges.

No secret keys are stolen — the proxy is tricked into lending its identity.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update immediately to Apache Traffic Server 9.2.16, 10.1.5, or 10.2.1.
  • Until patched, disable the origin_server_auth plugin (and the experimental tsmemcache plugin, affected by CVE-2026-111811).
  • Audit cloud access logs for API calls signed by the proxy that the proxy never legitimately issued; rotate IAM credentials if forgery is suspected.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111813 — Apache Traffic Server: Unsigned ImageMagick Arguments Become Remote Shell
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 10.0 (v3.1) Product Apache Traffic Server — the high-performance caching reverse proxy Type Argument injection (CWE-88) — unauthenticated client controls ImageMagick convert arguments in the experimental magick plugin's default (unsigned) configuration Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker sends a crafted image URL → the magick plugin passes the query string into ImageMagick convert as command-line arguments → arbitrary OS command execution on the proxy

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The experimental magick plugin built a shell command by concatenating the request's query string into ImageMagick convert arguments. In the default configuration there was no signature or allowlist on those arguments, so attacker-controlled text reached a command line verbatim — a textbook argument-injection path to remote code execution.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo contrasts handle_vulnerable() (query string spliced straight into a command) with handle_fixed() (arguments must carry a valid HMAC signature before anything is executed).

The poc.py file next to this writeup demonstrates the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern as a safe, offline logic demo — no network, no shell, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Traffic Server 9.2.16, 10.1.5 or 10.2.1.
  • Workaround: disable the experimental magick plugin (and audit every other experimental plugin before enabling it).
  • Search access logs for unusual image URLs carrying extra convert arguments.
  • Never pass unsigned, client-controlled strings into shell commands.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111823 — Mage AI: OAuth Error Path Creates an Authenticated Session
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product mage-ai data pipeline orchestration Type Detection of Error Condition Without Action (CWE-390) Vector Unauthenticated, network → full authenticated session

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Mage OSS versions through 0.9.80. Fixed in the commit after 0.9.80 (upstream PR mage-ai/mage-ai#6204, change 76c4f46).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
In the OAuth callback handler, when the login flow encounters an unknown OAuth provider, the code detects the error condition — and then keeps going. Session creation is not aborted, so an unauthenticated request that merely triggers the error path ends up with a valid, authenticated session.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
if provider not in KNOWN_PROVIDERS:
    log("unknown oauth provider")   # error detected...
create_session(user)                 # ...but the flow continues anyway

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker starts the Mage OAuth login flow and steers the callback into the "unknown provider" error path.
  2. The error is logged, but the handler proceeds to session creation.
  3. The attacker holds a valid authenticated session — no credentials, no real identity provider involved.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock OAuth callback that detects an unknown provider and (in the vulnerable variant) still mints a session, versus the fixed variant that aborts. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

A public proof of concept for the real vulnerability has been observed in the wild; treat any internet-facing Mage instance as potentially probed.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Mage AI past 0.9.80 to the fixed commit immediately.
  • Rotate every credential stored in Mage (S3 keys, Snowflake, Salesforce tokens, etc.) — assume they were readable.
  • Audit active sessions for logins that bypassed OAuth providers.
  • Restrict Mage's network exposure; it should not be reachable from the open internet without additional access controls.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111830 — WP Mailster: One Fake Signup Hides a Live Script in Your Dashboard
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v3.1) Product WP Mailster — the WordPress newsletter / mailing-list plugin Type Stored cross-site scripting (CWE-79) — unsanitized signup data rendered in the admin panel Vector Attacker submits a newsletter signup carrying script markup → the value is stored raw in the subscriber list → when the site owner opens the admin panel the script executes in their session → session hijack, admin takeover

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: WP Mailster from n/a through 1.9.1.0. Fixed in 1.9.2.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A newsletter signup was stored without sanitization and later rendered as HTML inside the admin panel. Stored cross-site scripting turns a database field into a payload that fires in a privileged browser:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def add_subscriber(email):
    db.save(email)                     # BUG: stored raw
def admin_list():
    return "<li>%s</li>" % db.get()    # BUG: rendered as HTML

# Simplified fixed pattern
def add_subscriber_fixed(email):
    db.save(sanitize(email))           # neutralize on the way in
def admin_list_fixed():
    return "<li>%s</li>" % escape(db.get())  # encode on the way out
Treat every stored value as hostile text until it is encoded for its output context.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker submits a newsletter signup containing script markup.
  2. WP Mailster stores the value raw in the subscriber list.
  3. The site owner opens the subscriber list in the admin panel.
  4. The stored markup executes as live script in the admin's session — hijacking it, and with it the site.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: stored input is not safe input: the demo contrasts raw storage and rendering with sanitization plus output encoding. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: WP Mailster 1.9.2.0.
  • Hunt the subscriber list for suspicious entries and remove them.
  • Rotate admin credentials and revoke sessions — assume the admin browser was exposed.
  • Encode on output as a standing rule: sanitizing on input alone is not enough.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111832 & CVE-2026-111834 — Unrestricted File Upload → Web Shell → Server Takeover
docs.text: Field CVE-2026-111832 CVE-2026-111834 Severity Critical 10.0 (CVSS v3.1) Critical 9.9 (CVSS v3.1) Product WP Mailster (WordPress plugin) Mang Board WP (WordPress plugin) Type Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vector Network, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction (S:C) Network, low complexity, low privileges, no user interaction (S:C) Weakness CWE-434 CWE-434

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• WP Mailster: from n/a through 1.9.1.0 (update past 1.9.1.0)
  • Mang Board WP: from n/a through 2.4.4 (update past 2.4.4)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Both plugins expose public-facing upload features — subscriber attachments in the Mailster newsletter plugin and guest post image uploads in the Mang Board plugin — without properly validating the type or content of the uploaded file. The check (if any) inspects only the attacker-controlled file name/extension, so a web shell renamed to look harmless is stored in a web-accessible uploads directory. Mang Board's boards allow guest posts by default, so exploitation can be unauthenticated. This is the classic CWE-434 unrestricted-upload pattern: the application trusts metadata the attacker controls instead of verifying the file's real content.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptual attack flow (educational illustration only — no working payload):

  1. Attacker submits an upload form with a file carrying a dangerous extension disguised as an image (e.g. shell.php.jpg semantics where only the name is checked).
  2. The plugin stores the file inside the site's uploads folder, reachable via URL.
  3. Attacker requests the uploaded file's URL; the server executes it.
  4. The web shell now runs commands with the web server's privileges (www-data): reading wp-config.php, database credentials, dropping further malware.

See poc.py for a safe, offline demonstration of the validation logic difference between an unsafe name-based check and a safe allow-list + content validation.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Update WP Mailster past 1.9.1.0 and Mang Board WP past 2.4.4 immediately.
  2. Allow-list safe file extensions server-side; reject everything else by default.
  3. Validate file content (magic bytes / mime sniffing), never trust the file name alone.
  4. Store uploaded files outside the web root or with randomized names and no extension.
  5. Disable script execution in upload directories (php_flag engine off / server config).
  6. Use a WAF/virtual patch as a stopgap while you roll out the update.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111841 — FunnelKit Automations for WordPress: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) Product FunnelKit Automations for WordPress (wp-marketing-automations), through 3.8.5.2 Type Cross-Site Request Forgery (CWE-352) Vector Network, low complexity, no privileges required, user interaction required, scope unchanged

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• FunnelKit Automations for WordPress from n/a through 3.8.5.2.
  • Some plugin actions do not verify that a request genuinely originated from the site's own dashboard, so a request triggered from another site is executed with the victim administrator's session.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin performs state-changing actions without a per-action security token (nonce) check. Browsers attach the victim's session cookies to every request, even one triggered by a page on a different site. Without a token proving the request came from the site's own dashboard, the plugin cannot distinguish a legitimate administrator click from a forged request (CWE-352: cross-site request forgery).

// Simplified vulnerable pattern (conceptual)
// action handler without a nonce check
function handle_automation_action() {
    // no check that this request came from our own dashboard
    update_automation_rules($_REQUEST);
}

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain:

  1. The attacker builds a malicious page that silently fires requests against the victim site's automation endpoints.
  2. They lure a logged-in WordPress administrator to open the page, for example through a phishing email.
  3. The administrator's browser sends the requests with full admin cookies.
  4. The plugin executes the forged requests: automation rules are rewritten, customer emails redirected, and order data exposed.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely and offline: a request handler that executes any request (vulnerable) versus one that requires a valid per-session token (fixed). No site, no network, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update FunnelKit Automations past version 3.8.5.2 immediately.
  • Audit automation rules for changes you did not make, including redirected emails and altered workflows.
  • Log out of WordPress when you are done, and avoid clicking links in unexpected emails while logged in as an administrator.
  • Plugin authors should verify a nonce on every state-changing action.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111851 — Royal Elementor Addons: This Widget Runs Attacker Code
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.6 (v3.1) Product Royal Elementor Addons (by WProyal) — widgets and extensions for the Elementor page builder Type Code injection via unsafe reflection (CWE-470) — class name taken from the request and instantiated Vector Authenticated remote attacker sends a request naming an arbitrary class → the widget handler loads that class through reflection with no allowlist → attacker code executes on the server: backdoors, defacement, data theft

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Royal Elementor Addons from n/a through 1.7.1068. Fixed in 1.7.1069.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A widget handler took a class name straight from the request and loaded it via reflection — with no allowlist. Reflection turns a string into behavior; when the string is attacker-controlled, so is the behavior:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def render_widget(request):
    cls = load_class(request["widget"])   # BUG: any class, attacker's pick
    return cls().render()

# Simplified fixed pattern
ALLOWED = {"Heading", "Button", "Gallery"}
def render_widget_fixed(request):
    name = request["widget"]
    if name not in ALLOWED:               # fixed menu only
        raise ValueError("unknown widget")
    return load_class(name)().render()
Never build a class name from request data — map input to a fixed allowlist and reject everything else.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker, logged in with any account, names an arbitrary class in a widget request.
  2. The handler loads that class through reflection — no allowlist, no check.
  3. The attacker's chosen code runs on the server with the site's privileges.
  4. Backdoors, defaced pages, stolen data: the server obeys the attacker's class.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: reflection must only reach a fixed allowlist: the demo contrasts loading any named class with a strict menu of known-safe widgets. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Royal Elementor Addons 1.7.1069.
  • Scan for unknown admin accounts and strange files — assume the worst on exposed sites.
  • Review recently modified content for injected scripts or iframes.
  • Rotate credentials and secrets reachable from the site.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111852 — Blind SQL Injection in WPdreams Ajax Search Lite
docs.text: Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.3 (CVSS 3.1 / AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:L) Product WPdreams Ajax Search Lite (WordPress plugin, ajax-search-lite) Type Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command — SQL Injection (CWE-89), blind variant Vector Network, no privileges required, no user interaction

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Ajax Search Lite from n/a through 4.14.6. Fixed in 4.14.7 and later.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The plugin's search handler builds its database query by concatenating the visitor's search keyword directly into a raw SQL string instead of using a prepared statement. A quote character in the keyword breaks out of the intended string literal, and the remainder of the input is interpreted as SQL. Because this is the blind variant, the attacker gets no query output back — only a yes/no signal per request — but by asking thousands of boolean questions through the public search box they can exfiltrate the entire database bit by bit (usernames, password hashes, post content, etc.).

// conceptual illustration of the vulnerable pattern (simplified)
$sql = "SELECT * FROM posts WHERE title LIKE '%" . $search_keyword . "%'";
//     ^ attacker-controlled quote in $search_keyword breaks out of the string literal

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational, conceptual demo only — no working exploit. poc.py uses a local SQLite toy database to show the difference between the vulnerable pattern (string concatenation, where an injected quote alters the query logic) and the safe pattern (parameterized queries, where the input stays plain data).

Run it with: python3 poc.py

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Update Ajax Search Lite to 4.14.7 or later immediately (mass exploitation campaigns are expected for this class of bug).
  2. Enable WordPress plugin auto-updates so the window of exposure stays small.
  3. If you develop plugins: never interpolate user input into SQL — always use $wpdb->prepare() / parameterized queries so the query shape is locked.
  4. Until patched, a web application firewall rule blocking suspicious quotes in search parameters reduces exposure (defense in depth only — update is the fix).

docs.title: CVE-2026-111853 — Tektronix 3 Series MDO: SCPI Command Injection (+2 Path Traversals)
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 Product Tektronix 3 Series MDO oscilloscopes Type OS Command Injection (CWE-78); Path Traversal (CWE-22) Vector Network attacker → arbitrary OS command execution on the instrument

This writeup covers three CVEs published together for the same product:

CVE Issue CVE-2026-111853 High 8.8 — OS command injection in the FILESystem:MOUNT:DRIve SCPI command handler CVE-2026-111854 High 8.1 — path traversal in the SCPI FILESystem command interface (read/modify arbitrary files) CVE-2026-111855 High 7.5 — path traversal in the web management interface (read arbitrary files, unauthenticated)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Firmware before 1.21.1. Fixed in 1.21.1 (vendor advisory TEK-PSA-002-092026).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The SCPI FILESystem:MOUNT:DRIve handler concatenates user-supplied input into an operating-system command without neutralization. A "filename" can therefore smuggle shell metacharacters, and the instrument's OS executes them. The sibling flaws skip path validation, so ../ sequences escape the intended directory on both the SCPI interface and the web UI.

/* Simplified vulnerable pattern */
char cmd[256];
sprintf(cmd, "mount %s", user_input);  /* user_input = '"; id #' */
system(cmd);                           /* attacker's command runs */

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain for CVE-2026-111853 is:

  1. The attacker reaches the instrument over the network (SCPI remote control is a normal lab feature).
  2. They send a crafted FILESystem:MOUNT:DRIve command whose "drive" argument contains shell metacharacters.
  3. The handler builds an OS command from the raw input — the attacker's commands execute with the device's privileges.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock SCPI handler that interpolates raw input into a shell string versus a fixed one that validates the path and never shells out. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update the 3 Series MDO firmware to 1.21.1 immediately.
  • Segment lab instruments onto an isolated network; do not expose SCPI or the web UI to untrusted networks.
  • Disable remote SCPI if the lab does not use it.
  • Inspect the device for unexpected files or configuration changes.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111880 — FreeRDP: Rogue Server Attacks the Client (Heap OOB + Int Underflow)
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.6 Product FreeRDP open-source RDP client library Type Heap-based Buffer Overflow (CWE-787); Integer Underflow (CWE-191) Vector Malicious RDP server → memory corruption on the connecting client

This writeup covers two CVEs published together:

CVE Issue CVE-2026-111880 High 7.4 — heap out-of-bounds write in the server hash-callback NTLM path: a crafted AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE with a backward session-key offset defeats MIC validation CVE-2026-111881 High 7.6 — integer underflow in the WinPR BMP writer: a mismatched stride passes SIZE_MAX - 3 to Stream_Zero for sub-byte images, reachable via a malicious RDP clipboard peer returning a crafted 1-bpp BMP

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• CVE-2026-111880: FreeRDP 2.0.0 through 3.31.x. Fixed in 3.32.0.
  • CVE-2026-111881: FreeRDP 3.14.1 through 3.31.x. Fixed in 3.32.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Both flaws are unchecked arithmetic on attacker-influenced values. In the NTLM path, the MIC offset from the server is used to compute a write destination without verifying it stays inside the heap buffer — a backward offset writes before the buffer. In the BMP writer, the stride calculation for sub-byte images underflows, producing a gigantic length for a zero-fill operation.

/* Simplified vulnerable pattern */
// MIC offset from the server is never range-checked:
memcpy(buf + offset, key, len);   // offset can point backwards -> heap OOB

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The victim (or their automated tooling) connects to a malicious RDP server.
  2. During NTLM authentication the server sends a crafted AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE with a backward session-key offset; the client's hash-callback writes out of bounds. Alternatively the server returns a poisoned 1-bpp clipboard BMP that underflows the stride math.
  3. Client memory is corrupted — the classic precursor to code execution, with the roles reversed: the server exploits the client.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock message parser that applies an unchecked offset versus a fixed one that range-checks before writing. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update FreeRDP to 3.32.0 immediately.
  • Do not connect to untrusted RDP servers.
  • Disable clipboard redirection where it is not needed.
  • Audit in-house tools and thin clients that bundle FreeRDP.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111911 — phpMyFAQ: Eight Auth Flaws, Including WebAuthn Login Bypass
docs.text:
Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product phpmyfaq open-source FAQ software Type Improper Authentication (CWE-287) and related Vector Unauthenticated, network → account takeover (passkey registration without auth)

This writeup covers the batch of eight CVEs published together for phpMyFAQ, led by CVE-2026-111911:

CVE Issue CVE-2026-111911 Critical 9.8 — WebAuthn registration endpoints attach credentials to any account without authentication or challenge validation CVE-2026-111882 High 8.1 — SSO callbacks let IdP-authenticated users skip TOTP 2FA (Keycloak / Entra ID) CVE-2026-111884 High 8.3 — e-mail change does not require the current password → account takeover CVE-2026-111898 High 7.5 — Keycloak implicit account linking lets attackers take over local accounts CVE-2026-111908 High 8.3 — BOLA in PUT /api/v3.1/faq/update: no per-FAQ authorization check CVE-2026-111909 High 8.1 — deleteUser() API lets non-superadmins delete superadmin accounts CVE-2026-111907 High 7.1 — CSRF on POST /admin/api/update-database runs DB migrations CVE-2026-111901 High 7.5 — unauthenticated DoS via unbounded faqs/search API pagination

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: phpMyFAQ 4.0.0 through 4.1.8 (several also cover 3.2.0-alpha+ and the 4.2.0-alpha line). Fixed in 4.1.9 / 4.2.0-beta.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The headline flaw (CVE-2026-111911): the WebAuthn registration endpoints never require the caller to be authenticated and never validate the ceremony challenge. They accept a caller-supplied username, attach the submitted credential to that account, and that's it — a forged fmt=none attestation registers a working passkey for someone else's account. Login then proceeds with the attacker's passkey, bypassing password and TOTP.

The siblings share the same DNA: authentication steps that exist on paper but are skipped in code — password-change without the current password, attachment management without ownership checks, account linking on colliding usernames.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
function registerWebAuthn($username, $attestation) {
    // no session check, no challenge check
    $account = findUser($username);          // any account
    $account->addCredential($attestation);   // forged fmt=none accepted
}

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain for CVE-2026-111911 is:

  1. The attacker picks a victim username (e.g. the admin account).
  2. They submit a forged WebAuthn attestation to the registration endpoint — no login, no valid challenge.
  3. The server attaches the attacker's passkey to the victim account.
  4. The attacker logs in with the passkey: password skipped, TOTP skipped — full account takeover.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock credential-registration function that accepts an unattested binding versus a fixed one that requires an authenticated session and a valid challenge. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update phpMyFAQ to 4.1.9 (or 4.2.0-beta) immediately — it fixes all eight.
  • Force password resets for all users, especially administrators.
  • Audit admin accounts and review webauthn credential registrations for keys nobody recognizes — treat unknown credentials as hostile.
  • Check logs for forged attestation submissions and unusual SSO callbacks.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111915 — Yank Note: One Single-Pass Sanity Check Away From Reading Any File (Path Traversal)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.2 Product purocean/yn — Yank Note, versions before 3.93.1 Type Path Traversal (CWE-22) Vector Unauthenticated, network → arbitrary file read

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Yank Note before 3.93.1. Fixed in v3.93.1 (commit d3b0ad27), tracked in issue #543.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The /api/help endpoint is publicly allowlisted — no authentication required — and takes a path or doc parameter. Its sanitization did a single, non-recursive replacement of ../ segments. A payload of repeated ../../ segments collapses into valid traversal after the single pass, so the request walks out of the intended folder. Two stacked mistakes: an auth-free endpoint and a sanitizer that assumed one pass is enough.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern (sanitizer, one pass only)
const clean = userPath.replace('../', '');
// '../../' → '../' survives → resolves outside the base folder

// Fixed in v3.93.1: resolve then validate containment
const resolved = path.resolve(join(baseDir, userPath));
if (!resolved.startsWith(baseDir + path.sep)) {
  throw new Error('Invalid path'); // rejected
}

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain:

  1. The attacker sends an unauthenticated request to /api/help with a path/doc value packed with repeated ../../ segments.
  2. The one-pass sanitizer strips one layer; the remainder still contains traversal sequences and resolves outside the help folder.
  3. The server reads and returns the file — SSH private keys, database configs, the user's own notes.
  4. Stolen credentials open the door to further compromise of the host.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock file server that contrasts the vulnerable one-pass replacement with the fixed resolve-and-validate approach, fully offline against a synthetic mock filesystem — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Yank Note to v3.93.1 or later.
  • Do not expose the Yank Note local server to the network: bind to localhost, firewall the port, never run it on untrusted networks.
  • Rotate any credentials (SSH keys, API tokens, configs) that were readable while the flaw was exposed.
  • Audit local file access logs for suspicious /api/help requests.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111923 — Fleet: 150 Bytes Crash the MDM Server (Unauthenticated DoS)
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product fleet open-source device management (MDM) Type Uncontrolled Recursion (CWE-674); Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (CWE-409) Vector Unauthenticated, network → denial of service

This writeup covers two CVEs published together:

CVE Issue CVE-2026-111923 High 7.5 — unbounded recursion in Apple MDM enrollment plist parsing: a crafted ~150-byte binary plist crashes the server CVE-2026-111924 High 7.5 — denial of service via unbounded gzip decompression: small, highly compressed request bodies exhaust server memory

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• CVE-2026-111923: Fleet before 4.89.0. Fixed in 4.89.0.
  • CVE-2026-111924: Fleet before 4.83.0. Fixed in 4.83.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The MDM enrollment endpoint parses a binary property list recursively with no depth limit — a deeply nested 150-byte payload makes the parser recurse until the process stack is exhausted. Separately, request bodies with Content-Encoding: gzip are decompressed without a size cap, so a tiny upload expands into gigabytes of resident memory.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
func parsePlist(node *Node) {
    for _, child := range node.Children {
        parsePlist(child)   // no depth limit -> stack exhaustion
    }
}

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker — no login, no credentials — POSTs a ~150-byte crafted binary plist to the unauthenticated Apple MDM enrollment endpoint.
  2. The parser recurses without bound and the server process crashes. (Alternatively: a small gzip bomb balloons in memory until the host is exhausted.)
  3. The Fleet server is down: no policies, no device visibility, no remote wipe — the whole managed fleet goes unmanaged.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock plist parser that recurses without limits versus a fixed one with a depth cap, plus a bounded-decompression helper. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Fleet to 4.89.0 or later (covers both flaws).
  • Rate-limit the enrollment endpoint and put it behind a WAF/reverse proxy with request-size limits.
  • Monitor the Fleet process for crashes and restart loops.
  • Keep MDM highly available — it is the control plane you need most during an incident.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111927 — Coder: Lookalike Domains Pass the Workspace Proxy Check
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.7 Product coder cloud development environments Type Improper Hostname Validation (CWE-522 credential exposure pattern) Vector Network attacker registers lookalike domain → credential theft from developers

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
GetWorkspaceProxyByHostname validates proxy hostnames with a SIMILAR TO pattern that performs a prefix match instead of an exact match. Any domain that merely starts with a legitimate workspace hostname passes validation — so ws-42.attacker.com is accepted as if it were the real ws-42 proxy. Victims' browsers and tooling then send session tokens and credentials to the attacker's lookalike domain.

-- Simplified vulnerable pattern
SELECT * FROM workspace_proxies
WHERE host SIMILAR TO 'ws-42.%';   -- prefix match: ws-42.attacker.com passes

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker registers a domain that is a string prefix of a real workspace proxy hostname (not a real subdomain — just "starts with").
  2. Coder's validation waves it through as a legitimate proxy.
  3. Developers are routed (or phished) to the twin; their session tokens, API keys, and cloud credentials are harvested.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock hostname validator using a prefix match versus a fixed one requiring an exact, anchored match. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Coder to 2.35.4 (or the fixed release on your LTS line: 2.29.20, 2.33.12, 2.34.8).
  • Rotate all workspace tokens, API keys, and cloud credentials that passed through workspace proxies.
  • Watch DNS/certificate transparency for lookalike domains impersonating your workspace hostnames.
  • Treat hostname validation as identity: always exact, anchored, and boundary-aware.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111998 — Vanus: Hardcoded Admin Token and Open Receivers
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 Product Vanus serverless event streaming, versions 0.8.0–0.9.0 Type Use of Hard-coded Credentials (CWE-798); sibling flaws allow unauthenticated event publishing and tenant subscription hijacking Vector Network (gateway port reachable) → cluster admin

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Vanus 0.8.0 through 0.9.0. No patch is available yet — the issues are still open upstream.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A hardcoded admin token ships in the source code itself: the same fixed Bearer token in every install, publicly visible. A credential that never changes is just a password everyone shares. The gateway checks that a token is present — not that it belongs to someone — and on some endpoints it checks nothing at all. Three flaws, one pattern: authentication built as decoration instead of a wall.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
const adminToken = "<same-value-in-every-install>" // shipped in source
if r.Header.Get("Authorization") == "Bearer "+adminToken {
    grantClusterAdmin()  // never asks WHO the caller is
}
// fixed: random per-install secret, verified identity per request

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker reads the token from the public source — no guessing, no brute force.
  2. They connect to the gateway gRPC proxy port and send the hardcoded Bearer token. Vanus accepts it without question.
  3. As cluster admin they can create and delete namespaces, publish or read any event, manage users, tokens, and role bindings. A second flaw lets unauthenticated attackers publish events straight through the CloudEvents HTTP receiver, and a third lets any authenticated user hijack other tenants' subscriptions.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock gateway whose vulnerable auth accepts the well-known token from anyone, versus the fixed auth that requires a per-install secret and verifies identity. Fully offline, synthetic data — no real token, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Block all network access to the Vanus gateway ports right now — never expose them to the internet.
  • Audit every eventbus for forged CloudEvents.
  • Watch the upstream project for a release, and rotate every token the moment you upgrade.
  • Treat the deployment as compromised until proven otherwise.

docs.title: CVE-2026-111999 — Vanus: Missing Authentication Lets Anyone Publish to Any Eventbus
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product vanus-labs/vanus — event-driven serverless platform, versions 0.8.0 through 0.9.0 Type Missing authentication for critical function (CWE-306): the gateway CloudEvents HTTP receiver skips token authentication and authPublish checks Vector Network, no privileges, no user interaction → unauthenticated remote attackers publish forged events to any eventbus

This writeup covers two gateway auth CVEs published together against Vanus:

CVE Issue CVE-2026-111999 Missing authentication (CWE-306): the gateway CloudEvents HTTP receiver lets unauthenticated remote attackers publish events to any eventbus, bypassing token auth and authPublish checks. CVSS 7.5. CVE-2026-112000 Missing authorization (CWE-862): any authenticated user can call Subscribe, Ack and unregistered gateway methods without permission checks — hijack another tenant's subscription, read and acknowledge its events, starve the legitimate consumer, enumerate cluster users via ListUser. CVSS 7.6.

(Companion to CVE-2026-111998, the 9.8 default-admin-credentials hole in the same gateway — Vanus shipped three auth failures in one day.)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Vanus 0.8.0 through 0.9.0. Track the fix via vanus-labs/vanus#647 and upgrade past 0.9.0 once a patched release lands.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The gateway's CloudEvents HTTP receiver (/namespaces/{ns}/eventbus/{name}/events and the legacy /gateway/{name} paths) goes straight from parsing the request to storing the event — the token authentication and authPublish checks exist in the codebase but never run on these paths. Likewise, the gRPC proxy path accepts Subscribe/Ack calls from any authenticated identity without checking ownership of the subscription. Security code that never executes is the same as no security at all.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def handle_publish(req):
    # no checkToken(req), no checkPublish(user, eventbus)
    store_event(req.eventbus, req.event)      # stranger's event lands here
    forward_to_subscribers(req.eventbus)

# Simplified fixed pattern
def handle_publish(req):
    if not check_token(req): return reject()
    if not check_publish(req.user, req.eventbus): return reject()
    store_event(req.eventbus, req.event)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The target runs Vanus 0.8.0–0.9.0 with its gateway reachable on the network.
  2. The attacker crafts a CloudEvent and POSTs it to the gateway's event path for the victim's eventbus — no token, no login.
  3. The gateway stores the forged event and delivers it to the bus's real subscription sinks (billing, alerts, automation).
  4. With any low-privilege account (CVE-2026-112000), the attacker calls Subscribe with another tenant's subscription ID, reads its events, and Acks them so the legitimate consumer never sees them.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a receiver with the auth checks commented out versus one that validates token + publish permission before storing. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Video walkthrough
docs.text: Watch the explainer Short

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Vanus past 0.9.0 as soon as the upstream fix lands (follow issue #647).
  • Keep the gateway off the public internet — firewall the HTTP/gRPC gateway ports to trusted networks only.
  • Rotate all tokens and secrets; assume any token-bearing path was reachable.
  • Audit subscriptions for unknown consumers and watch for events you never sent.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112000 — Vanus: Missing Authorization Lets Any User Hijack Subscriptions
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.6 Product vanus-labs/vanus — event-driven serverless platform, versions 0.8.0 through 0.9.0 Type Missing authorization (CWE-862): gateway streaming RPCs (Subscribe, Ack, unregistered methods) skip permission checks Vector Network, low privileges, no user interaction → any authenticated user hijacks other tenants' subscriptions

Companion to CVE-2026-111999 (missing authentication — unauthenticated event publishing), covered in the same explainer video.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Vanus 0.8.0 through 0.9.0. Track the fix via vanus-labs/vanus#647 and upgrade past 0.9.0 once a patched release lands.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The gateway proxy accepts Subscribe, Ack and other streaming RPC calls from any authenticated identity and never verifies that the caller owns the subscription it names. An attacker passes another tenant's subscription ID to Subscribe and the gateway hands over that tenant's event stream; Acks from the attacker then advance the offset, so the legitimate consumer starves. ListUser is similarly unguarded, enabling user enumeration.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def subscribe(user, subscription_id):
    return attach(user, subscription_id)   # ownership never checked

# Simplified fixed pattern
def subscribe(user, subscription_id):
    if owner_of(subscription_id) != user:
        return reject("not your subscription")
    return attach(user, subscription_id)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker holds any low-privilege Vanus account.
  2. They call Subscribe with a victim tenant's subscription ID — no permission check runs.
  3. They read the victim's events and Ack them, advancing the offset past the legitimate consumer.
  4. They call ListUser to enumerate cluster users for follow-up attacks.

The accompanying poc.py (shared with the CVE-2026-111999 writeup) demonstrates the pattern safely: an ownership-blind Subscribe versus one that verifies the caller owns the subscription. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Video walkthrough
docs.text: Watch the explainer Short

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Vanus past 0.9.0 as soon as the upstream fix lands (follow issue #647).
  • Enforce tenant isolation at the gateway: every RPC must check caller-vs-resource ownership.
  • Audit subscription offsets for unexplained Ack jumps and unknown attached consumers.
  • Rotate credentials and restrict gateway network exposure in the meantime.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112001 — ProjectSend: Scoped API Token Can Reset Its Owner's Password
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.2 Product ProjectSend self-hosted file sharing Type Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key (CWE-639) Vector Low-privilege token holder, network → full account takeover of the token owner

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: ProjectSend before 2.7.0. Fixed in 2.7.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
In the users API, a token holder with manage_users and edit_users scopes can call PATCH /api/v1/users/{user} — and change the credentials of the token's own owner. The scopes guard which action is allowed, but nobody checks whose account is being changed. The ability check asks "can this token manage users" but never asks "is this token allowed to touch THIS user". Authorization was written for the action, not the target.

// Simplified vulnerable pattern
// PATCH /api/v1/users/{user}
if ($token->can('manage_users') && $token->can('edit_users')) {
    update_user($user_id, $new_password, $twofa = null); // whose account?
}
// fixed: deny when $user_id === $token->owner_id unless a separate
// 'manage_own_account_recovery' scope is present

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker already holds a low-privilege scoped token (limited API access, nothing dramatic).
  2. They send PATCH /api/v1/users/{user} naming the token's owner, set a brand-new password, and clear two-factor authentication in the same call.
  3. They open the login page and sign in — with the owner's full role and permissions. Passwords, two-factor settings, and role boundaries are all gone.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock users API whose vulnerable PATCH honors any target the scopes allow, versus the fixed one that refuses self-targeting. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

One limited token becomes the keys to the whole installation.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update to ProjectSend 2.7.0 immediately.
  • Force a password reset for every staff account and re-enforce two-factor authentication.
  • Revoke and reissue all API tokens.
  • Audit the user change log for password or 2FA changes you did not make.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112005 — WhoDB: DuckDB Query Editor Allows Arbitrary File Access
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.7 Product WhoDB database dashboard Type Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') (CWE-22) Vector Network (dashboard reachable) → arbitrary file read/write on the host

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: WhoDB before 0.135.0. Fixed in 0.135.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The query editor passes user SQL straight to DuckDB — including its filesystem functions. DuckDB is an analytics engine with a full filesystem toolkit (read_text, read_blob, COPY ... TO, ATTACH), and WhoDB hands it raw user SQL with no path allow-list. A query language meant for tables was given the keys to the filesystem, and the editor never asked where the path points.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
result = duckdb.sql(user_query)   # read_text('/etc/passwd') sails through
# fixed: reject filesystem functions, confine DuckDB file access to an
# allow-listed directory, keep the dashboard off the public internet

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker logs in to a DuckDB file — no credentials needed — and types filesystem calls into the query editor.
  2. First they steal session.key, the secret that signs sessions. Then the stored database credentials.
  3. With COPY ... TO, they overwrite files on the host. Every step is just SQL.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock query gate whose vulnerable variant passes everything to the "engine", versus the fixed gate that rejects filesystem functions and out-of-scope paths. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no real DuckDB, no network calls.

The database dashboard becomes an unauthenticated file server for whoever knows the DuckDB tricks: session keys and stored credentials exfiltrated, config files rewritten, a foothold for deeper compromise.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update to WhoDB 0.135.0 immediately.
  • Rotate session.key right away, and change every database credential stored in WhoDB — assume they were stolen.
  • Keep WhoDB off the public internet and restrict who can reach the dashboard.
  • Treat embedded query engines as filesystem access until proven sandboxed.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112015 — Omnigent: Sub-Agent Working Directory Escapes the Sandbox
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product Omnigent AI agent runner Type Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') (CWE-22) Vector Malicious bundle upload → arbitrary file read/write on the host as the runner user

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Omnigent before 0.14.0. Fixed in 0.14.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Workspace paths are supposed to stay inside the root — but when a nested sub-agent sets os_env.cwd, the root-only validation in bundles.py is bypassed. An absolute path or a parent-traversing one like ../../.. sails right through, and the agent runs outside its sandbox. The workspace boundary was enforced by string checks on the top-level config, but nested sub-agents write their own working directory, and nobody canonicalized the final path before comparing it to the root.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
cwd = sub_agent.get("os_env", {}).get("cwd", root)
workdir = os.path.join(root, cwd)      # "../../.." escapes silently
# fixed:
resolved = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(root, cwd))
if not resolved.startswith(os.path.realpath(root) + os.sep):
    raise ValueError("working directory escapes the workspace")

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker uploads a bundle whose sub-agent sets os_env.cwd to an absolute path or a traversal sequence.
  2. Omnigent accepts it. The agent now reads and writes host files as the runner user — configs, secrets, SSH keys — while everyone still believes it is locked in its little workspace.
  3. One ../ at a time, the agent walks out the front door.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock workspace resolver whose vulnerable variant joins paths blindly, versus the fixed one that canonicalizes and enforces containment. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no filesystem access, no network calls.

The platform that runs untrusted code by design hands attackers the very filesystem it promised to protect.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update to Omnigent 0.14.0 immediately.
  • Audit every bundle you have ever run for suspicious os_env.cwd values.
  • Run agents as a least-privilege user from now on.
  • Treat uploaded bundles like untrusted code — because they are.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112018 — cgltf: Heap Out-of-Bounds Write via Sparse Accessor Indices
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.0 Product cgltf glTF 3D model parser Type Out-of-bounds Write (CWE-787) Vector Malicious 3D model file → memory corruption (denial of service, possible code execution)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: cgltf through 1.15. No patch is available yet — defend at the call site and watch the repository for a fixed release.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Heap out-of-bounds write in cgltf_accessor_unpack_floats(): sparse accessors carry their own indices, and the function never validates them before writing. The parser treats attacker-controlled numbers as trusted offsets — indices from the file are used as write positions before anyone checks they fit the buffer. Validation exists (cgltf_validate()), but unpacking without calling it first is the loaded gun.

/* Simplified vulnerable pattern */
for (i = 0; i < sparse_count; ++i) {
    out[indices[i]] = values[i];   /* indices never validated */
}
/* fixed: */
for (i = 0; i < sparse_count; ++i) {
    if (indices[i] >= count) return ERROR;  /* bounds-check first */
    out[indices[i]] = values[i];
}

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker crafts a GLB with huge sparse indices and gets the target app to open it — an uploaded avatar, a shared asset, a preview thumbnail.
  2. cgltf_accessor_unpack_floats() writes where the indices say, past the output buffer into heap memory.
  3. Crash at best, code execution at worst — especially when the app skips cgltf_validate().

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely in Python: a mock unpack routine whose vulnerable variant applies indices unchecked (flagging the out-of-bounds write), versus the fixed variant that bounds-checks every index. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no real memory corruption, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Always call cgltf_validate() before unpacking accessors; reject any model that fails validation.
  • Parse untrusted models in a sandboxed worker process.
  • Pin the dependency and watch the repository for a fixed release.
  • Treat 3D model files as untrusted input, like images and fonts.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112021 — snac2: Heap Buffer Overflow in JSON Lexer Crashes the Server
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product snac2 fediverse (ActivityPub) server Type Heap-based Buffer Overflow (CWE-122) Vector Unauthenticated, single POST → remote denial of service

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: snac2 before 2.93. Fixed in 2.93.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Heap-based buffer overflow in _xs_json_load_lexer(): when the JSON contains a \u0000 escape, the lexer mishandles the embedded null and overflows heap allocations while copying the string. Worse, it happens on unauthenticated input — the handler parses the body before verifying the signature, so a malformed message reaches the fragile lexer with zero authentication. Parse-before-auth plus a lexer that trusts escape sequences means every anonymous sender gets a shot at the heap.

/* Simplified vulnerable pattern */
parse(body);            /* \u0000 escape mishandled in the lexer */
verify_signature(body); /* ...only afterwards */
/* fixed: verify the signature FIRST, then parse;
   plus hardened escape handling in the lexer */

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. The attacker sends a single crafted application/activity+json POST to activitypub_post_handler() containing the \u0000 escape. No account, no signature, nothing to forge.
  2. The lexer overflows while parsing, corrupting heap memory — and the server crashes.
  3. One request, unauthenticated, remote. Every message can be replayed at will, so the instance can be kept down indefinitely.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock inbox handler whose vulnerable variant parses before verifying (flagging the crash), versus the fixed variant that verifies the signature first and hardens escape handling. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no real overflow, no network calls.

Federation stays open by design — which makes a pre-auth crash bug the worst kind to have.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update to snac2 2.93 immediately.
  • If you cannot update right away, put the instance behind a reverse proxy with request size and rate limits to slow the attack.
  • Monitor for crash loops and run the process under supervision so it restarts.
  • Never parse untrusted input before authenticating it.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112082 — SGLang: Unauthenticated DoS via the Expert-Distribution Recording Endpoint
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product sgl-project/sglang up to 0.5.19 — Scheduler.expert_distribution_handle (python/sglang/srt/eplb/expert_distribution.py) Type Improper input handling leading to denial of service (no CWE assigned yet) Vector Network, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction → one crafted request crashes the inference server; exploit is public; fix PR still pending

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • SGLang <= 0.5.19. Upstream fix: PR #42098 (awaiting acceptance — no released patch yet).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The expert-distribution recording endpoint (expert_distribution_handle) processes attacker-influenced fields without sufficient validation. A single remote, unauthenticated request carrying a manipulated payload drives the scheduler into a crash — taking down the inference server and every model it serves. The exploit is publicly available while the official fix is still an unmerged pull request.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def expert_distribution_handle(request):
    record = parse(request.payload)   # no validation
    scheduler.apply(record.weights)   # crash on malformed data

# Simplified fixed pattern
def expert_distribution_handle(request):
    record = parse(request.payload)
    if not valid_distribution(record):
        return 400
    scheduler.apply(record.weights)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker reaches the SGLang server's recording endpoint over the network — no login needed.
  2. They send one request with a manipulated expert-distribution payload.
  3. The scheduler crashes → denial of service for all inference traffic on that server.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: an unvalidated handler versus a validating one, against a synthetic offline scheduler. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Firewall the debug/admin ports now — do not expose SGLang's recording endpoints to untrusted networks.
  • Track PR #42098 and upgrade as soon as a fixed release ships.
  • Front the inference tier with authentication / a reverse proxy plus request-size limits.
  • Monitor for crashes correlated with requests to the recording endpoint.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112085 — webpack-dev-server: WebSocket Proxy Bypass Let Attacker Pages Into Your Backend
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.2 (v3.1) Product webpack-dev-server — the webpack development server used by millions of frontend developers Type Missing origin validation (CWE-346) / improper limitation of a pathname — non-HMR WebSocket upgrade requests forwarded to proxy targets without Host/Origin checks Vector A developer visits a malicious web page while the dev server is running → the page opens a cross-origin WebSocket through the dev server → the request is forwarded to the proxied backend without allowedHosts validation → attacker reads and writes the backend, even when bound to loopback

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: webpack-dev-server before 5.2.7 and 6.0.0. Fixed in 5.2.7 and 6.1.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
When a proxy entry forwards WebSockets, the server forwarded non-HMR WebSocket upgrade requests to the proxy target without validating the Host or Origin headers — the allowedHosts protection was never consulted for those requests. A proxy match was treated as authorization:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def handle_upgrade(request, proxy_entry):
    if proxy_entry.forwards_websockets:
        forward_to_target(request)          # BUG: no Host/Origin check
    elif is_hmr_socket(request):
        check_allowed_hosts(request)        # only this path was guarded

# Simplified fixed pattern
def handle_upgrade_fixed(request, proxy_entry):
    check_host_and_origin(request)          # validate FIRST, always
    if proxy_entry.forwards_websockets:
        forward_to_target(request)

An attacker page in the developer's browser could open a WebSocket to ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/..., ride the proxy entry, and reach the backend behind it — read and write — even though the server was bound to loopback.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Developer runs webpack-dev-server with a proxy entry that forwards WebSockets.
  2. Developer visits an attacker-controlled web page (phishing link, ad, compromised site).
  3. The page opens a cross-origin WebSocket to the local dev server.
  4. The dev server forwards the upgrade to the proxy target — no Origin/Host validation, allowedHosts not consulted.
  5. The attacker now reads and writes the proxied backend through that socket.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a local request router contrast — one path forwarding a WebSocket upgrade with no origin check (vulnerable), one rejecting cross-origin upgrades (fixed). Offline, no network, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: webpack-dev-server 5.2.7 or 6.1.0 or later.
  • Workaround: omit WebSocket forwarding from proxy entries that do not need it; scope each proxy entry to the specific paths it must serve.
  • Review backend access logs for unexpected activity during the exposure window.
  • Keep dev servers behind firewall rules and avoid exposing them to networks you do not trust.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112145 — speaches: One Model Name Away From Hijacking Code Loading (No Patch)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.3 Product speaches-ai/speaches — open-source self-hosted speech-to-text API (OpenAI audio API compatible), up to 0.9.0-rc.3 Type Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code (CWE-470) Vector Remote, unauthenticated → attacker-influenced code loading

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • speaches up to 0.9.0-rc.3. The project was informed early through issue #679 but has not responded — there is no patch yet. The exploit has been publicly disclosed.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
PyannoteDiarizationModelManager._load_fn in src/speaches/executors/pyannote_diarization.py takes the client-controlled model argument and uses it to select and load classes or code — remotely, with no validation. A model name is treated as a code path, so the remote attacker gains influence over what the server loads and executes.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def _load_fn(self, model: str):          # 'model' is attacker-controlled
    cls = resolve_class(model)            # resolves attacker input to code
    return cls(...)                       # attacker-chosen class instantiated

# Fixed pattern: strict allowlist, never resolve raw input
ALLOWED = {"pyannote/speaker-diarization": DiarizationModel, ...}
def _load_fn(self, model: str):
    if model not in ALLOWED:
        raise ValueError("Unknown model")
    return ALLOWED[model](...)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain:

  1. The attacker sends a request to the audio API with a crafted model parameter pointing at an attacker-chosen class or module.
  2. _load_fn resolves the externally-controlled input into a class and instantiates it — attacker-influenced code now runs inside the server.
  3. The public PoC demonstrates remote code-path manipulation: the doorway to data theft, service takeover, and full host compromise.
  4. No patch exists — every up-to-0.9.0-rc.3 deployment is exposed.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock model loader that contrasts the vulnerable raw-input resolution with a fixed strict-allowlist loader, fully offline with synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
There is no patch, so the fix is isolation until the project responds:

  • Restrict network access to the speaches API: bind to localhost, firewall the port, put it behind an authenticated reverse proxy.
  • Disable the diarization component (pyannote) until a fixed release ships — remove or block the vulnerable loader path.
  • Run with least privilege: strict egress rules, read-only filesystem where possible, container isolation.
  • Monitor for suspicious model values in API logs; rotate any credentials and audit the host if exposure is suspected.
  • Track issue #679 and the upstream repo for a fix; upgrade immediately when one is released.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112146 — D-Link EAGLE PRO AI routers: hard-coded MQTT broker credentials
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 3.1 7.4 Product D-Link E15, M32, R15, R32 (EAGLE PRO AI mesh routers) Type Hard-coded credentials — CWE-259 / CWE-798 Attack vector Remote (network), low attack complexity, low privileges required

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: D-Link EAGLE PRO AI mesh line models E15, M32, R15 and R32 with firmware whose /etc/emDaemon/passwd (MQTT Broker component) carries the factory-baked credential. Check D-Link's support page for your hardware revision and install the latest firmware as updates ship.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The MQTT broker inside the router authenticates with a credential stored in /etc/emDaemon/passwd. That credential is hard-coded into the firmware image, so every unit of every affected model shares the exact same password. Anyone who recovers the credential from one firmware dump can authenticate to the MQTT broker of any deployed router. The NVD record notes the exploit is now public.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptual attack chain (educational only — no working exploit):

  1. Firmware extraction. The attacker downloads the router firmware from D-Link's support site and unpacks the image offline.
  2. Credential recovery. Inside the filesystem image, the file /etc/emDaemon/passwd is found carrying the same credential that ships on every unit.
  3. Reuse across the fleet. Because the secret never varies per device, that one credential authenticates to the MQTT broker of any E15, M32, R15 or R32 reachable on the network.
  4. Broker access. With broker access the attacker can observe mesh node chatter (status, configuration) and inject messages into the control plane — the vulnerable pattern below versus the fixed pattern:
# VULNERABLE pattern: one secret baked into every firmware image
CREDENTIAL = load_from("/etc/emDaemon/passwd")   # identical on every unit

# FIXED pattern: a unique secret generated per device at first boot
CREDENTIAL = load_from("/etc/emDaemon/passwd")    # generated once, per device

This writeup deliberately does not reproduce the public exploit. Do not test against devices you do not own; only ever test in controlled environments.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update firmware: check D-Link's official support page for your exact model and hardware revision; install security updates the moment one ships.
  • Isolate the IoT network: place routers and IoT devices on a separate VLAN/SSID from personal devices.
  • Disable remote management: keep the admin interface and the MQTT broker off the WAN; restrict management to trusted local systems.
  • Watch for oddities: failed authentication attempts, unexpected config changes, or routers dropping off the mesh.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112177 — Ghostscript (RHEL 8): Lost Rebase Guard Reopens -dSAFER Sandbox Escape
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L) Product Ghostscript as shipped with Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 (rebase from 9.25 to 9.27) — the PostScript/PDF interpreter behind printing pipelines, document thumbnails, and upload converters Type Incorrect Privilege Assignment (CWE-648) Vector Remote — a specially crafted PostScript file processed by Ghostscript bypasses -dSAFER restrictions and can access files outside the permitted paths or execute commands with the permissions of the Ghostscript process

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Ghostscript 9.27 as packaged for RHEL 8. The correction for CVE-2019-14869 was present in 9.25 but was omitted during the 9.25 → 9.27 rebase, leaving privileged .forceput operations in the .charkeys procedure insufficiently protected.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
In PostScript, .forceput is a privileged write operation — normally unreachable from untrusted document content. The .charkeys font-rendering procedure reaches it, but an older guard (shipped as the fix for CVE-2019-14869) restricted it. During Red Hat's 9.25 → 9.27 rebase, that guard was dropped. A crafted document can now drive .charkeys into an unguarded .forceput, bypassing the -dSAFER sandbox: the interpreter trusts itself, and the attacker controls the interpreter.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def charkeys(document):
    forceput(document.char_data)   # privileged write — NO guard after the rebase

# Simplified fixed pattern
def charkeys_fixed(document):
    if not safer_mode_ok():        # guard restored (upstream commit 4859047)
        raise SandboxViolation("untrusted input cannot reach forceput")
    forceput(document.char_data)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker crafts a PostScript file that exercises the .charkeys procedure.
  2. The file is dropped into any pipeline that runs Ghostscript on RHEL 8 — a print queue, a PDF thumbnailer, an upload converter.
  3. Parsing reaches the unguarded .forceput; -dSAFER restrictions are bypassed.
  4. The attacker reads files outside the permitted paths or executes commands with the permissions of the Ghostscript process.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a sandbox model where an unguarded privileged write is reachable from crafted input, versus a model where the restored guard blocks it. Purely synthetic, offline, no PostScript, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: apply the Red Hat advisory updating the RHEL 8 ghostscript package to the revision carrying the backported fix.
  • Containers: rebuild from an updated base image; the package revision from your distro's package manager — not gs --version — is the reliable indicator.
  • Workaround: until patched, restrict or refuse untrusted PostScript/PDF processing and consider isolating the Ghostscript service.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112212 — GitLab: OAuth/OIDC Login Flows Redirected via Poisoned Discovery Cache
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.1) Product GitLab CE/EE — OAuth/OIDC login flows using cached discovery documents Type Improper trust of user-supplied values when building endpoint URLs (CWE-444) Vector Unauthenticated attacker poisons a shared cache's OAuth/OIDC discovery document → endpoint URLs point at an attacker-controlled server → victims' login flows are redirected there

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: All versions from 18.3 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1. Fixed in 19.3.6, 19.4.3, 19.5.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
GitLab cached OAuth/OIDC provider discovery documents in a shared cache to avoid refetching them. When constructing the cached response, endpoint URLs were built from user-supplied values without proper validation. An attacker could therefore plant a discovery document whose authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, etc. pointed at their own server — and every user whose login flow read that cached document would be silently redirected to the attacker's infrastructure:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def cache_discovery(provider, user_hint):
    doc = fetch_discovery(provider)
    doc["authorization_endpoint"] = build_url(user_hint)  # BUG: untrusted input
    shared_cache.store(provider, doc)                     # poisoned for everyone

# Simplified fixed pattern
def cache_discovery_fixed(provider):
    doc = fetch_discovery(provider)
    for endpoint in doc.endpoints:
        assert_trusted_origin(endpoint, provider)  # validate before caching
    shared_cache.store(provider, doc)

Cached security metadata must be validated, not just stored.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker triggers discovery-document caching with a crafted request carrying attacker-influenced values.
  2. The poisoned document — with login/token endpoints rewritten to the attacker's host — lands in the shared cache.
  3. A victim starts an OAuth/OIDC login; GitLab reads the cached (poisoned) document.
  4. The victim's browser is redirected to the attacker's server mid-login, exposing authorization codes/tokens.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: building endpoint URLs from untrusted input vs. allow-listed provider origins. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade: 19.3.6 / 19.4.3 / 19.5.1.
  • Flush OIDC discovery caches after upgrading; treat cached documents as untrusted until then.
  • Pin and allow-list identity-provider origins; alert on discovery documents pointing elsewhere.
  • Rotate OAuth application secrets if logins traversed the affected window.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112241 — SureCart: Forged Identity Claims Walk Straight Into Your Store
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) Product SureCart (by Brainstorm Force) — the WordPress e-commerce / checkout plugin Type Authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290) — identity claim trusted without verification Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker forges an identity claim → SureCart accepts it without verification → attacker receives a logged-in session, potentially with administrator privileges → store orders, customer records, and settings exposed

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: SureCart from n/a through 4.9.5. Fixed in 4.9.6.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
SureCart's login handling accepted an identity claim — essentially "I am user X" — without verifying it came from a trusted source. Authentication must answer two questions: who are you, and can you prove it. The affected code answered the first and skipped the second:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def login(claim):
    user = find_user(claim.user_id)      # BUG: claim never verified
    return start_session(user)           # logged in, no proof required

# Simplified fixed pattern
def login_fixed(claim):
    if not verify_signature(claim):      # proof checked first
        return reject()
    return start_session(find_user(claim.user_id))
A claim is not a credential. Anything accepted as proof of identity has to be cryptographically verified — a forged token must fail, never log in.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker crafts an identity claim naming a privileged account.
  2. Attacker submits the forged claim to SureCart with no password and no prior account.
  3. The plugin trusts the claim and starts a logged-in session.
  4. The attacker now browses and acts as that user — reading orders and customer data, changing store settings, and potentially reaching full admin control.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: an identity claim is only as good as its verification: the demo contrasts trusting a raw claim with verifying its signature first. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: SureCart 4.9.6 or later.
  • Audit admin accounts for ones you did not create; force password resets.
  • Review order, customer, and settings changes made during the exposure window.
  • Revoke all active sessions so forged logins are cut off.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112242 — Profile Builder: One Signup Made Attackers Admin
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 (v3.1) Product Profile Builder (by Cozmoslabs) — the WordPress user-registration / membership plugin Type Incorrect privilege assignment (CWE-266) — role value taken from the signup request Vector Low-privilege remote attacker registers an account and slips an administrator role into the signup request → plugin assigns the requested role without an authorization check → attacker becomes a full site administrator

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Profile Builder from n/a through 4.0.4. Fixed in 4.0.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The registration flow trusted a role value arriving in the signup request and assigned it to the new account. Roles are a server-side decision — the server must choose them; the request may only ask:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def register(request):
    role = request.get("role", "subscriber")  # BUG: client-chosen
    return create_user(request.email, role)  # admin for the asking

# Simplified fixed pattern
def register_fixed(request):
    role = "subscriber"                      # server decides, always
    return create_user(request.email, role)
Never let the browser make a server-side decision. Privilege must flow from policy, not from the request.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker opens the site's registration form as an ordinary visitor.
  2. Attacker adds a role parameter claiming administrator to the signup request.
  3. Profile Builder assigns the requested role without any authorization check.
  4. The attacker logs in as a full administrator — plugins, users, data, everything.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: roles are the server's decision, never the request's: the demo contrasts a client-chosen role with a server-assigned one. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Profile Builder 4.0.5.
  • Audit every user account for ones you did not create or that hold unexpected roles.
  • Force password resets for all privileged accounts.
  • Review what changed while the flaw was live: new plugins, users, or content.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112257 - GIMP: Stack-based Buffer Overflow
docs.text: Field Value Severity High - CVSS 7.8 Product GIMP (PSD plug-in) Type Stack-based Buffer Overflow (CWE-121) Vector Opening or previewing a crafted PSD file

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: GIMP builds shipping the vulnerable PSD thumbnail loader (see Red Hat CVE page).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The PSD thumbnail resource loader performed a BGR-to-RGB channel swap with a fixed 3-byte stride without verifying that the JPEG thumbnail was actually RGB. A crafted grayscale PSD thumbnail caused a heap out-of-bounds read and write in the plug-in process.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain is:

  1. Victim browses to or opens a crafted PSD file.
  2. The thumbnail loader assumes a 3-byte RGB layout on a grayscale thumbnail.
  3. Heap out-of-bounds read and write corrupt plug-in memory.
  4. Crash, with potential for arbitrary code execution.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable mock versus the fixed pattern. Fully offline, synthetic data - no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update GIMP to the patched release for your distribution. Do not open untrusted PSD/XCF files, disable automatic thumbnail generation for untrusted directories, and treat every downloaded image as potentially hostile until parsers are patched.

docs.title: CVE-2026-112263 — Television: A Filename That Runs Shell Commands (OS Command Injection)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.5 Product alexpasmantier/television — Rust fuzzy-finder TUI, 0.15.0 through 0.15.9 Type OS Command Injection (CWE-78) Vector Local, user-assisted → arbitrary command execution as the victim user

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Television 0.15.0 through 0.15.9. Fixed by upstream commits 32695ccc and d7d46abb.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
format_command in television/utils/command.rs builds shell command lines by substituting selected entries into a template and wrapping the values in single quotes — but it never escapes single quotes inside the values. Actions wired in cable/unix/files.toml (including the default edit action) pass filenames through this path. A filename containing an apostrophe terminates the quoted string early, and the shell interprets the remainder of the filename as shell syntax:

# what the template produces for a hostile filename
edit 'notes'; malicious_command;''     # <-- two commands, not one argument

The attacker's command executes with the privileges of the user running television.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker plants a file with a crafted name containing an apostrophe — e.g. inside a repository the victim is likely to browse, or anywhere the victim points television at.
  2. The victim opens the folder in television and triggers an action on the file — even the default edit action.
  3. format_command substitutes the hostile name into the shell string without escaping the quote; the quote breaks the quoting, and the injected command executes as the victim.
  4. From there: data theft, persistence, lateral movement — all from opening a directory.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: naive single-quote wrapping of a synthetic hostile filename versus properly escaped quoting, and the safest fix — skipping the shell entirely and passing an argv array. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no subprocess calls on untrusted input.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade television to a release past 0.15.9 (fixes in commits 32695ccc and d7d46abb).
  • Avoid building shell strings from untrusted input: spawn processes with an argv array instead of going through a shell.
  • When quoting is unavoidable, escape every embedded quote, never assume wrapping alone is sufficient.
  • Treat filenames as untrusted input: directory listings are attacker input in every tool that acts on them.
