docs.title: DrayTek Vigor2960: Command Injection Trio in the CGI Interface (CVE-2026-113389, CVE-2026-113390, CVE-2026-113391)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product DrayTek Vigor2960 (firmware 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218) firewall/VPN router Type Improper neutralization of special elements used in a command (CWE-74) — OS command injection in the CGI handler Vector Authenticated remote attacker crafts a request to /cgi-bin/mainfunction.cgi where the sectiontype argument (set_table function) is glued into a shell command → root command execution. Two sibling flaws, CVE-2026-113390 and CVE-2026-113391, inject through other CGI functions.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Vigor2960 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218. Fixed in 1.5.1.7. Note: the vendor marks the 2960 end of support — plan a replacement.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
In mainfunction.cgi, three functions paste request arguments straight into shell command strings with no sanitizing. set_table takes the sectiontype argument; sub_182B0 (jsonstatus) takes usefile/usescript /option; uploadlangs takes the upload filename. A ; or $() in the value becomes a second command:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def set_table(sectiontype):
    os.system("set_table.sh " + sectiontype)   # attacker: "x; id > /tmp/p"

# Simplified fixed pattern
ALLOWED = {"lan", "wan", "vpn"}
def set_table_fixed(sectiontype):
    if sectiontype not in ALLOWED:
        raise ValueError("rejected")
    subprocess.run(["set_table.sh", sectiontype], shell=False)
All three exploits are public. Any valid login is enough.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker logs in with any valid account and crafts a request to /cgi-bin/mainfunction.cgi with a shell metacharacter hidden in sectiontype (CVE-2026-113389), usefile/usescript/option (CVE-2026-113390), or the upload filename (CVE-2026-113391).
  2. The CGI handler glues the value into a shell command and executes it as root.
  3. The attacker owns the VPN gateway: reads internal traffic, pivots into the LAN, harvests VPN credentials.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Request parameters are data, never shell syntax: allowlist values and pass them as argument lists. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:

  • Restrict admin UI access to trusted networks; monitor CGI logs for metacharacters.

docs.title: DrayTek Vigor2960: OS Command Injection via jsonstatus Arguments (covered in the DrayTek trio video)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product DrayTek Vigor2960 (firmware 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218) firewall/VPN router Type OS command injection (CWE-77) in the CGI jsonstatus handler Vector Authenticated remote attacker manipulates usefile/usescript/option arguments of the sub_182B0 function in /cgi-bin/mainfunction.cgi → command injection → root execution and file clobbering

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Vigor2960 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218. Fixed in 1.5.1.7 (device is end of support).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The sub_182B0 function behind the jsonstatus CGI endpoint interpolates the usefile, usescript, and option arguments into shell commands and file paths. Beyond command execution, crafted values also clobber arbitrary files. The fix is identical to its siblings: never build shell strings from request input, and never let filenames leave their intended directory:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def jsonstatus(usefile):
    os.system("status " + usefile + " > /tmp/out")  # injection + clobber

# Simplified fixed pattern
def jsonstatus_fixed(usefile):
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+", usefile):
        raise ValueError("rejected")
    subprocess.run(["status", usefile], shell=False, stdout=open("/tmp/out","w"))
Covered in the same explainer video as CVE-2026-113389 and CVE-2026-113391; the runnable vulnerable/fixed demo lives in the CVE-2026-113389 folder.

docs.text:

  2. The CGI handler executes them as root — and file-writing variants clobber device files.
  3. Full gateway compromise, same as the sibling CVEs.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Constrain every request value to a safe charset and execute commands without a shell. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: DrayTek Vigor2960: Command Injection via the Upload Filename (covered in the DrayTek trio video)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product DrayTek Vigor2960 (firmware 1.5.1.6 Revision 8218) firewall/VPN router Type Improper neutralization of special elements used in a command (CWE-74) — OS command injection in the upload endpoint Vector Authenticated remote attacker uploads through uploadlangs in /cgi-bin/mainfunction.cgi with a crafted filename → filename interpolated into a shell command → root command execution

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The uploadlangs upload endpoint takes the uploaded file's name and interpolates it into a shell command — filenames are attacker input, and this one becomes syntax:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def uploadlangs(filename, data):
    save(data, "/tmp/" + filename)
    os.system("process_lang /tmp/" + filename)   # filename becomes shell

# Simplified fixed pattern
def uploadlangs_fixed(filename, data):
    name = os.path.basename(filename)
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+\.[a-z]+", name):
        raise ValueError("rejected")
    path = os.path.join("/tmp/langs", name)
    save(data, path)
    subprocess.run(["process_lang", path], shell=False)
Covered in the same explainer video as CVE-2026-113389 and CVE-2026-113390; the runnable vulnerable/fixed demo lives in the CVE-2026-113389 folder.

docs.title: Argo CD: Jsonnet Imports Escape the Repo and Leak Cluster Secrets (covered in the Argo CD triple-flaw video)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product Argo CD 0.9.0 – 3.6.0-rc2 (GitOps continuous delivery for Kubernetes) Type Path traversal (CWE-22) — Jsonnet importer not confined to repository root Vector Attacker commits a .jsonnet file using absolute paths / .. traversal / symlinks in import/importstr/importbin → repo-server reads any readable file (service-account tokens, /proc/self/environ, private keys) → contents returned to caller via a ConfigMap; importstr on /dev/zero exhausts memory

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Argo CD 0.9.0 through 3.6.0-rc2. Fixed in 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4, 3.6.0-rc2. Directory Applications evaluate every .jsonnet file in the application directory.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The repo-server evaluates .jsonnet files with an importer that never confines import, importstr, or importbin to the repository root. Absolute paths, parent-directory traversal, and repository symlinks open any file the repo-server can read — projected service-account tokens, mounted private keys, repository credentials, /proc/self/environ. Generated Secrets are redacted, but placing the imported contents in a ConfigMap returns the data to the caller; importstr on /dev/zero exhausts repo-server memory:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def import_file(path):
    return open(path).read()          # any path the process can read

# Simplified fixed pattern
def import_file_fixed(path):
    resolved = resolve(REPO_ROOT, path)
    if not inside(REPO_ROOT, resolved):
        raise ValueError("import escapes repository root")
    return open(resolved).read()
The same repo-server delivery story as CVE-2026-113709 and CVE-2026-113708 — one explainer video covers all three; the vulnerable/fixed poc.py pattern lives in the CVE-2026-113709 folder.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker commits a .jsonnet file with absolute-path or .. imports, or uploads it via POST /api/v1/applications/manifestsWithFiles (only Application get permission on a directory Application needed).
  2. The repo-server evaluates it and reads cluster secrets into the rendered output.
  3. Placing the content in a ConfigMap returns it to the caller; importstr on a non-terminating device can exhaust memory.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: File access must be confined: every import resolves inside the intended root, or it is rejected. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Argo CD to 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4 or newer.
  • Disable built-in tools you do not use (tool detection docs); restrict Application get.
  • Rotate any secrets the repo-server could read.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113678 — Froxlor: Symlink Trick Hands Your Customers Root
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) / 9.4 (v4.0) Product Froxlor — open-source web hosting control panel (manages shared-hosting accounts, domains, traffic statistics) Type Symlink following (CWE-59) — privilege escalation Vector Authenticated hosting customer replaces their own stats directory with a symlink; a root-run cron follows it and chown -Rs arbitrary host directories to the attacker → root

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Froxlor before 2.3.15.
  • Fixed in Froxlor 2.3.15.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
After regenerating per-customer traffic statistics with goaccess, Statistics::makeChownWithNewStats recursively changes ownership of the stats directory tree — running as root from a cron job. The customer owns their stats directory, so they can delete it and plant a symlink to any host path. The chown follows the symlink, handing root-owned directories to the attacker:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def make_chown_with_new_stats(stats_dir, customer):
    run_as_root(["chown", "-R", f"{customer}:{customer}", stats_dir])
    # stats_dir is a symlink -> /etc -> attacker now owns /etc (as root)

# Simplified fixed pattern (2.3.15)
def make_chown_with_new_stats_fixed(stats_dir, customer):
    if not is_safe_dir(stats_dir):          # no symlinks, canonical path checked
        raise ValueError("refusing to chown through a symlink")
    run_as_root(["chown", "-R", f"{customer}:{customer}", stats_dir])

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker is a legitimate (low-privilege) hosting customer.
  2. They remove their goaccess stats directory and replace it with a symlink pointing at a root-owned host directory (e.g. /etc or /).
  3. The root-run traffic cron fires and chown -Rs through the symlink.
  4. The attacker now owns root files — they edit sudoers/configs and escalate to full root on the shared host.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: how a symlink check with os.path.realpath distinguishes a plain directory from a symlink swap, and why ownership operations must validate the resolved path — all synthetic, offline, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Froxlor to 2.3.15 or later immediately.
  • Harden the hosting stack: never let privileged crons walk user-writable paths, prefer chown -h semantics or directory-fd-based traversal, and monitor for symlink swaps in customer directories.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113682 — networknt light-4j: An Empty Password Is a Valid Login
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.1 (v4.0) Product networknt light-4j — lightweight Java microservices framework (basic-auth middleware) Type Authentication bypass (CWE-287) — empty-password LDAP bind accepted as success Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker sends a Basic Authorization header with a known username and an empty password → LDAP/AD bind succeeds → logged in as the delegated user

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• light-4j 2.1.5 through before 2.4.0.
  • Fixed in light-4j 2.4.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
BasicAuthHandler builds an LDAP bind from the supplied username and password. LDAP servers treat a bind with an empty password as an unauthenticated (anonymous) bind — but the handler reads "bind completed without error" as "authentication succeeded", so a blank password logs you in as anyone whose username you know:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def basic_auth(username, password):
    conn.ldap_bind(username, password)     # empty password -> anonymous bind, no error
    return "authenticated"                 # BUG: bind success != login success

# Simplified fixed pattern (2.4.0)
def basic_auth_fixed(username, password):
    if not password:
        raise ValueError("REFUSED: empty password")
    if not conn.ldap_bind_authenticated(username, password):
        raise PermissionError("invalid credentials")
    return "authenticated"

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker knows (or guesses) a valid username — many are predictable service accounts.
  2. They send a Basic Authorization header: username:<empty>.
  3. The LDAP bind with an empty password completes without an error, and the handler accepts it as a successful authentication.
  4. The attacker is now logged in as the LDAP/AD-delegated user — no password required.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock LDAP bind that models the empty-password flaw versus a fixed version that rejects blank passwords — pure Python functions, no network, no real directory, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: light-4j to 2.4.0 or later immediately.
  • If you cannot upgrade yet, enforce non-empty passwords at the handler level and verify that binds return an authenticated (not anonymous) result; audit auth logs for empty-password login attempts.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113703 — SuggestArr: One Header Makes You Localhost
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.3 (v3.1) Product SuggestArr — media request manager for the *arr stack (Sonarr/Radarr family tooling) Type Authentication bypass via IP spoofing (CWE-290) — client-controlled X-Forwarded-For trusted as the source address Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker sends X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1 → enforce_authentication() in local_bypass mode treats the request as local → full access without credentials

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• SuggestArr before 3.0.0.
  • Fixed in SuggestArr 3.0.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The app enables ProxyFix(x_for=1) in api_service/app.py, so request.remote_addr is derived from the client-controlled X-Forwarded-For header. Then enforce_authentication() in api_service/auth/middleware.py trusts remote_addr to decide "local" — and local_bypass mode skips authentication for local requests. Spoof the header, become localhost:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
app.wsgi_app = ProxyFix(app.wsgi_app, x_for=1)   # X-Forwarded-For -> remote_addr

def enforce_authentication(request):             # middleware.py
    if request.remote_addr in ("127.0.0.1", "::1") and LOCAL_BYPASS:
        return "authenticated as local"          # BUG: header is attacker-controlled

# Simplified fixed pattern (3.0.0)
def enforce_authentication_fixed(request):
    if not trust_proxy_headers(request):         # only honor XFF from known proxies
        request.remote_addr = request.peer_ip    # real socket address, unspoofable
    if request.remote_addr in ("127.0.0.1", "::1") and LOCAL_BYPASS:
        return "authenticated as local"
    return require_login(request)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker sends any API request with the header X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1.
  2. ProxyFix rewrites request.remote_addr to 127.0.0.1.
  3. enforce_authentication() sees a "local" address and, in local_bypass mode, skips login entirely.
  4. Full unauthenticated access to the request manager — media libraries, API keys, settings.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a mock request pipeline showing how an untrusted X-Forwarded-For header becomes remote_addr and passes a local check, versus a fixed version that only honors the header from trusted proxies — pure Python, no network, no real server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: SuggestArr to 3.0.0 or later immediately.
  • Disable local_bypass mode unless the instance is truly localhost-only; only trust X-Forwarded-For when it comes from your own reverse proxy, and require authentication on every API route.

docs.title: Argo CD: Git Ref Becomes --upload-pack Command in repo-server (covered in the Argo CD triple-flaw video)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product Argo CD 2.7.0 – 3.6.0-rc2 (GitOps continuous delivery for Kubernetes) Type Argument injection (CWE-88) — git ref passed without end-of-options separator Vector Low-privileged attacker commits a Kustomization whose remote URL carries a leading-dash ref/version query value → Kustomize hands it to git fetch → parsed as --upload-pack → command execution inside argocd-repo-server

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Kustomize passes ref/version query values from remote resource, base, or component URLs to git fetch without an end-of-options separator. A value starting with - is parsed by git as an option — so --upload-pack=<cmd> executes an arbitrary command inside argocd-repo-server when the remote uses a local transport like file:// (egress filtering does not stop it):

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def fetch(remote_url, ref):                     # ref = "-u 'cmd'" from repo
    run(["git", "fetch", remote_url, ref])       # git reads it as an OPTION

# Simplified fixed pattern
def fetch_fixed(remote_url, ref):
    run(["git", "fetch", remote_url, "--", ref])  # "--" ends option parsing
The same repo-server delivery story as CVE-2026-113709 and CVE-2026-113672 — one explainer video covers all three; the vulnerable/fixed poc.py pattern lives in the CVE-2026-113709 folder.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker commits a Kustomization whose remote URL carries a leading-dash ref/version value, or uploads it via POST /api/v1/applications/manifestsWithFiles (only Application get permission needed).
  2. The repo-server runs git fetch with the value — git parses it as --upload-pack and executes the attacker's command.
  3. The command runs as the repo-server user; output comes back through manifest-generation errors.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Separate options from untrusted arguments: an explicit end-of-options separator stops flag parsing cold. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Argo CD to 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4 or newer.
  • Restrict who can commit to built repos and who holds Application get; enable NetworkPolicies around the repo-server.
  • Rotate repository credentials.

docs.title: Argo CD: Repo-Controlled Helm Config Path Runs Commands in repo-server (CVE-2026-113709, CVE-2026-113708, CVE-2026-113672)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product Argo CD 2.1.0 – 3.6.0-rc2 (GitOps continuous delivery for Kubernetes) Type Inclusion of functionality from untrusted control sphere (CWE-829) — Helm plugin auto-load from repo-controlled configHome Vector Low-privileged attacker commits a crafted Kustomization (or uploads files via POST /api/v1/applications/manifestsWithFiles with only Application get) → repo-server runs a Helm downloader plugin from a repository-controlled path → command execution as repo-server, repository credentials readable

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Argo CD 2.1.0 through 3.6.0-rc2. Fixed in 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4, 3.6.0-rc2. Only deployments with --enable-helm for kustomize builds are affected.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
When --enable-helm is on for Kustomize builds, Argo CD passes helmGlobals.configHome straight through to Helm. Helm automatically loads a downloader plugin from <configHome>/.data/plugins and executes its program inside argocd-repo-server whenever a helmCharts repo URL uses the plugin's protocol. The attacker controls configHome — so the plugin is theirs:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def build_with_kustomize(kustomization):            # attacker commits this
    config_home = kustomization["helmGlobals"]["configHome"]  # repo-controlled
    plugin_dir = config_home + "/.data/plugins"
    for plugin in list_dir(plugin_dir):            # no verification
        run(plugin.executable)                     # runs as repo-server!

# Simplified fixed pattern
def build_with_kustomize_fixed(kustomization):
    config_home = SERVER_PINNED_CONFIG_HOME        # never repo-controlled
    plugin_dir = config_home + "/.data/plugins"
    for plugin in list_dir(plugin_dir):
        if not plugin.is_operator_approved():
            continue
        run(plugin.executable)
Covered together in the explainer video: CVE-2026-113708 (git --upload-pack command injection via a leading-dash ref with no end-of-options separator) and CVE-2026-113672 (Jsonnet import/importstr not confined to the repository root, leaking service-account tokens and /proc/self/environ into ConfigMaps).

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker commits a Kustomization with helmGlobals.configHome pointing at their own tree, including a fake Helm downloader plugin (CVE-2026-113709) — or a leading-dash ref value in a remote URL (CVE-2026-113708), or a .jsonnet file with an absolute-path import (CVE-2026-113672).
  2. Any Application build picks the files up — or the attacker uploads them through POST /api/v1/applications/manifestsWithFiles, which needs only Application get permission.
  3. The repo-server executes the payload as its own user and reads repository credentials and other process-accessible data.
  4. Secrets harvested → manifest cache poisoned → auto-sync spreads the attack across managed clusters.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Manifest builders must treat repository content as untrusted data: pin tool config server-side, separate options from arguments, and jail file access to the repo. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Argo CD to 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4 or newer.
  • Restrict who can commit to built repos and who holds even Application get — the upload path needs only that.
  • Enable the shipped NetworkPolicies around the repo-server and rotate repository credentials.
  • Pin Kustomize/Helm versions; disable --enable-helm if you do not need it.

docs.title: D-Link DHP-W610AV: Crafted HNAP Login Request Empties the Admin Password
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) Product D-Link DHP-W610AV PowerLine Wi-Fi extender (firmware 1.02EUb03) Type Empty-password configuration write (CWE-258) Vector Remote unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted request to the HNAP login handler → admin password in config file becomes empty

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: D-Link DHP-W610AV firmware 1.02EUb03. Fixed in the latest D-Link firmware release — apply it as soon as available.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The HNAP login handler (login_prepare_hnap) passes an attacker-manipulated Password argument into the device configuration writer without validation. Instead of rejecting the malformed value, the device stores an empty password in etc/defnodes/defaultvalue.xml — the admin account survives, but its credential becomes nothing:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def login_prepare_hnap(password_arg):
    cfg = load_config()
    cfg["admin_password"] = password_arg   # no validation at all
    save_config(cfg)                      # attacker-controlled "" is stored

# Simplified fixed pattern
def login_prepare_hnap_fixed(password_arg):
    if not is_valid_login_value(password_arg):
        raise ValueError("malformed login value rejected")
    # never write empty credentials; only the device itself rotates the stored hash

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker sends a single crafted request to the HNAP login handler with a manipulated Password field.
  2. The handler writes an empty password into the device configuration file.
  3. Attacker opens the admin panel and logs in as admin with a blank password.
  4. From there: reroute traffic, flash rogue firmware, pivot into the home network.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Input that reaches a credential store must be validated; a malformed value must never overwrite a real credential. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: install the latest D-Link firmware for the DHP-W610AV.
  • Re-set a strong admin password and verify the configuration actually holds it.
  • Disable remote administration and never expose the HNAP login page to the internet.

docs.title: Tenda AC19: Stack Overflow in the Firewall Settings Page Gives a Remote Root Shell
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 10.0 (v3.1) Product Tenda AC19 (firmware 16.03.10.07) home router Type Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-119) in the httpd web management service Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker sends a request to /goform/SetFirewallCfg with an oversized firewallEn argument → stack buffer overflow in formSetFirewallCfg → control of execution, root shell

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Tenda AC19 firmware 16.03.10.07. A public exploit is already circulating; check the vendor site for a fixed firmware.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The httpd web management service handles firewall configuration in formSetFirewallCfg. The firewallEn argument is copied into a fixed-size stack buffer with no length validation. One oversized request overwrites the saved return address and redirects execution:

/* Simplified vulnerable pattern */
void formSetFirewallCfg(request_t *req) {
    char buf[64];
    strcpy(buf, req->param("firewallEn"));   /* attacker controls length! */
    apply_firewall(buf);
}

/* Simplified fixed pattern */
void formSetFirewallCfg_fixed(request_t *req) {
    char buf[64];
    const char *val = req->param("firewallEn");
    if (strlen(val) >= sizeof(buf)) return;  /* reject before copying */
    strcpy(buf, val);
    apply_firewall(buf);
}
No login, no click — the endpoint is reachable remotely and the exploit is public.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker sends one HTTP request to /goform/SetFirewallCfg with a firewallEn value far longer than the stack buffer.
  2. The unchecked copy overflows the buffer and overwrites the return address.
  3. Execution jumps to attacker code — a root shell on the home gateway.
  4. From there: sniff LAN traffic, hijack DNS, plant malware on devices behind the router.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Untrusted network input is never copied into a fixed buffer without measuring it first. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: install the fixed Tenda firmware as soon as it is available.
  • Disable remote administration and never expose the router web panel to the internet.
  • Change the default admin password; monitor for unusual requests to /goform/ endpoints.

docs.title: CVE-2026-113779 — pfSense REST API privilege escalation
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH 8.8 (CVSS 3.1: AV:N / AC:L / PR:L / UI:N / S:U / C:H / I:H / A:H) Product pfSense-pkg-RESTAPI (unofficial REST/GraphQL API for pfSense CE and pfSense Plus) Vulnerability type Privilege escalation (improper privilege management / overly-broad permission) Attack vector Network — an authenticated low-privilege account (e.g. held by help-desk staff) calls the HA settings-sync endpoint and rewrites the REST API's own configuration secrets, elevating itself to full administrator (page-all).

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• pfSense-pkg-RESTAPI before 2.9.0
  • Fixed in 2.9.0 (GitHub release pfrest/pfSense-pkg-RESTAPI v2.9.0)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The settings-sync privilege was designed for a limited job: replicate configuration to the high-availability peer. However, that same privilege also granted write access to the REST API package's own configuration secrets. Since API secrets control authentication and authorization inside the API, a holder of the sync privilege could modify them to escalate their own account to full administrator. One permission was secretly doing two jobs — and the weaker one opened the door to the stronger one.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Conceptually (no working exploit is provided):

  1. An attacker holds a legitimate low-privilege account with only the settings-sync permission.
  2. They authenticate to the pfSense REST API normally — no password guessing involved.
  3. They call the HA settings-sync endpoint, which they are allowed to use.
  4. The sync path permits modification of the REST API's stored configuration secrets.
  5. They rewrite the secrets so their own account resolves as a full administrator.
  6. On the next request the account has page-all privileges: full control of the firewall — rules, VPN accounts, packet captures, anything an admin can do.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update the REST API package to 2.9.0 or later. From that version, access to the HA settings-sync endpoint strictly requires full administrative privileges.
  • Audit every account that held the old sync privilege and check for unauthorized changes made before the update.
  • Rotate the REST API configuration secrets after patching.
  • Follow the principle of least privilege: sync-only duties should never imply API configuration access.

docs.title: FreeRDP: Heap Overflow via the Server-Side rdpsnd Audio Channel
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 (v3.1) Product FreeRDP before 3.32.1 (open-source RDP client/server engine) Type Heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) — integer wraparound in audio channel Vector Low-privileged malicious RDP client sends two crafted SNDC_FORMATS PDUs → unbounded heap write during server audio playback → potential code execution

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: FreeRDP before 3.32.1. Fixed in 3.32.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
In rdpsnd_server_select_format(), the server computes DVI_ADPCM block-alignment arithmetic that can wrap around before validation runs. The check sees a small, innocent-looking size while the allocation and the audio write use the true, huge size — an unbounded heap write:

/* Simplified vulnerable pattern */
uint32_t calc = nChannels * nBlockAlign;   /* wraps on 32-bit math */
if (calc < LIMIT)                          /* check runs on wrapped value */
    write_audio(buffer, calc);             /* ...but the write overflows */

/* Simplified fixed pattern */
if (nChannels > UINT32_MAX / nBlockAlign)
    return ERROR;                          /* validate operands first */
uint32_t calc = nChannels * nBlockAlign;    /* now safe */

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker connects to a FreeRDP-based server as an ordinary RDP client.
  2. They send two SNDC_FORMATS PDUs with nBlockAlign too small for nChannels.
  3. The integer wraparound defeats the size check.
  4. Server-side audio playback performs an unbounded heap write — heap corruption, possible code execution.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Validate arithmetic operands before the math — never trust a size computed after a wraparound. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: FreeRDP to 3.32.1 or later (client and server builds).
  • Until patched, restrict which clients can reach RDP servers and monitor for unusual audio-format negotiation traffic.

docs.title: vLLM: Remote Code Execution via Client-Supplied Multimodal Processor Revision
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.1 (v3.1) Product vLLM 0.7.3 – 0.31.0 (LLM/vision model serving engine) Type Code injection (CWE-94) — client-chosen processor code revision Vector Unauthenticated attacker controlling a revision in the served model repo sends a multimodal request to /tokenize with mm_processor_kwargs.code_revision set → server imports hostile processor code with trust_remote_code → arbitrary Python in the API process

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: vLLM 0.7.3 through 0.30.x. Fixed in 0.31.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
vLLM forwarded the request-supplied mm_processor_kwargs.code_revision into the Transformers model loader. With trust_remote_code enabled, the server imports whichever revision of the model's dynamic processor code the client names — and the attacker controls a revision in the repository:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def load_processor(request):
    revision = request.mm_kwargs.get("code_revision")  # attacker-controlled
    return AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model, revision=revision,
                                         trust_remote_code=True)

# Simplified fixed pattern
PINNED_REVISIONS = {"model-a": "abc123"}                # server-side allowlist
def load_processor_fixed(request):
    revision = PINNED_REVISIONS[model]                  # client can't choose
    return AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model, revision=revision,
                                         trust_remote_code=True)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker publishes a malicious processor revision in the served model repository.
  2. They send a multimodal request to the unauthenticated /tokenize endpoint naming that revision.
  3. The server imports the hostile revision with trust_remote_code enabled.
  4. Attacker Python executes inside the vLLM API process: weights, keys, and the GPU fleet are exposed.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Never let client input select trusted code: pin revisions server-side. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: vLLM to 0.31.0 or later.
  • Pin model processor revisions server-side; never take the revision from the request.
  • Restrict trust_remote_code to models you fully control; audit tokenize logs for suspicious revision names.

docs.title: SvelteKit: Path Traversal in the Vite Preview Server Leaks Source and Secrets
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.1) Product @sveltejs/kit 2.10.0 – 3.0.0 (SvelteKit web framework) — Windows Type Path traversal (CWE-22) in the vite preview server Vector Unauthenticated attacker reaching the preview server (network or tunnel) sends crafted requests → paths escape the prerendered output directory → source code, configs, and credentials disclosed

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: @sveltejs/kit 2.10.0 through 3.0.0 (exclusive) on Windows. Fixed in 3.0.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The vite preview server joined untrusted URL input into filesystem paths without confining the result to the output directory. Crafted requests escape the prerendered folder on Windows:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def serve_preview(path_param):
    file = output_dir / path_param      # attacker-controlled
    return send_file(file)              # escapes to anywhere

# Simplified fixed pattern
def serve_preview_fixed(path_param):
    file = (output_dir / path_param).resolve()
    if output_dir.resolve() not in file.parents:
        return 404                      # refuse anything outside output_dir
    return send_file(file)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker reaches a SvelteKit preview server — directly or through a tunnel.
  2. They send crafted requests with traversal sequences.
  3. The server resolves the path outside the project and returns the file.
  4. Source code, .env files, and credentials are disclosed — no login required.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Confine every served path to its intended directory; reject anything that resolves outside it. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: @sveltejs/kit to 3.0.0 or later.
  • Never expose the preview server to the network or internet; bind it to localhost.
  • Rotate any credentials that may have been readable through the preview server.

docs.title: Trigger.dev: CSRF in CLI Auth Flow Steals Personal Access Tokens
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 (v3.1) Product Trigger.dev before 4.5.2 (developer agent/background-job platform) Type Cross-site request forgery (CWE-352) in CLI authorization-code flow Vector Attacker mints an unauthenticated auth code → lures a logged-in user to /account/authorization-code/<code> → page mints a PAT with no consent → attacker retrieves the victim's token from an unauthenticated endpoint → account takeover

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Trigger.dev before 4.5.2. Fixed in 4.5.2.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Loading /account/authorization-code/<code> minted a Personal Access Token instantly — a credential-issuing, state-changing action on a plain GET request with no consent screen and no CSRF protection:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def authorization_code_page(code):
    user = current_session_user()      # victim's logged-in session
    token = mint_pat(user)             # BUG: no consent, no CSRF check
    return token

# Simplified fixed pattern
def authorization_code_page_fixed(code, csrf, consent):
    require_valid_csrf(csrf)
    if not consent:
        return render_consent_screen() # explicit user approval required
    return mint_pat(current_session_user())

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker generates an unauthenticated authorization code.
  2. They lure a logged-in Trigger.dev user to the crafted authorization URL.
  3. Loading the URL mints a PAT tied to the victim's session — no consent asked.
  4. Attacker retrieves the token from an unauthenticated endpoint → full account takeover.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Credential issuance is a state-changing action: it needs an explicit consent step and CSRF protection. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Trigger.dev to 4.5.2 or later.
  • Rotate any personal access tokens that may have been minted unexpectedly.
  • Review audit logs for unexpected token creation; treat stray authorization links with suspicion.

docs.title: Dulwich: DOS Drive-Letter Paths Escape the Worktree on Windows
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 (v3.1) Product Dulwich before 1.2.9 (pure-Python Git library) — Windows Type Path traversal (CWE-22) via DOS drive-letter prefixes Vector User clones a malicious repo on Windows → tree entry named C: bypasses NTFS validation → checkout writes files outside the worktree → arbitrary file write → code execution

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Dulwich before 1.2.9 (Windows). Fixed in 1.2.9.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Dulwich validated tree path elements against Unix-style traversal but never considered DOS drive letters — a Windows-only path form. A tree entry named C: slips past the checks, and checkout writes outside the working tree:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def checkout_path(worktree, entry):
    if ".." in entry.split("/"):       # only guards Unix traversal
        raise ValueError("traversal")
    return worktree / entry            # "C:" sails through on Windows

# Simplified fixed pattern
def checkout_path_fixed(worktree, entry):
    if ".." in entry.split("/") or is_drive_letter(entry):
        raise ValueError("traversal / drive prefix")
    dest = (worktree / entry).resolve()
    if worktree.resolve() not in dest.parents:
        raise ValueError("escapes worktree")
    return dest

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker crafts a repository with a tree entry named C:.
  2. Victim clones it with Dulwich on Windows.
  3. During checkout, the path validation is bypassed and the file escapes the project folder.
  4. Attacker drops executables into system/startup paths → remote code execution.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Path validation must account for platform-specific syntax — including DOS drive letters on Windows. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Dulwich to 1.2.9 or later.
  • Do not clone untrusted repositories with older versions.
  • Audit working trees for unexpected files.

docs.title: HKUDS Vibe-Trading: Missing Authentication Gives Strangers a Root Shell
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) Product HKUDS Vibe-Trading 0.1.0 – 0.1.7 (AI trading agent, FastAPI) Type Missing authentication (CWE-306) — fail-open auth gate Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker posts to /sessions endpoints → BashTool executes root shell commands; files uploadable; session data and partial API keys readable

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: HKUDS Vibe-Trading 0.1.0 through 0.1.6. Fixed in 0.1.7.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The require_auth() gate protects the whole FastAPI surface — but when the API_AUTH_KEY environment variable is unset, the function returns early instead of denying access. No key configured means no check performed:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def require_auth(request):
    key = os.environ.get("API_AUTH_KEY")
    if not key:
        return True            # BUG: fail-open, everyone is "authorized"
    return request.key == key

# Simplified fixed pattern
def require_auth_fixed(request):
    key = os.environ.get("API_AUTH_KEY")
    if not key:
        return False           # fail-closed: missing credential denies access
    return request.key == key

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker finds a Vibe-Trading server running without an API key configured.
  2. They POST a message to /sessions/{id}/messages — no key, no login.
  3. The agent's BashTool executes the message as a root shell command.
  4. They upload .py/.sh files via /upload, read session histories, and harvest partial API keys.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Security gates must fail closed: a missing credential denies access, never skips the check. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: Vibe-Trading to 0.1.7 or later.
  • Always configure a strong API_AUTH_KEY; never run the server with auth effectively disabled.
  • Audit session histories and uploaded files for anything you did not put there; rotate exposed API keys.

docs.title: uv: Malicious Wheels Write Outside the Scripts Directory via Entry Points
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.8 (v3.1) Product uv before 0.11.15 (fast Python package installer) Type Path traversal (CWE-22) via wheel entry-point names Vector User installs a malicious wheel → crafted console_scripts/gui_scripts entry-point names escape the scripts directory → executables land in PATH directories → binaries shadowed/overwritten → code execution

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: uv before 0.11.15. Fixed in 0.11.15.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Entry-point names from a wheel are package metadata — attacker input — but uv joined them into filesystem paths without sanitization. A name like ../../bin/python traverses out of the scripts directory:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def install_entry_point(name):
    path = scripts_dir / name          # name is attacker-controlled
    write_executable(path, payload)    # lands anywhere on disk

# Simplified fixed pattern
def install_entry_point_fixed(name):
    if not is_safe_entry_name(name):   # reject separators, "..", absolutes
        raise ValueError("unsafe entry-point name")
    path = scripts_dir / name
    assert path.is_relative_to(scripts_dir)
    write_executable(path, payload)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker publishes a wheel with a poisoned console_scripts entry-point name.
  2. Victim runs uv pip install on the malicious package.
  3. uv writes an executable into a directory on the victim's PATH.
  4. The real binary is shadowed or overwritten — the next invocation runs attacker code.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: Package metadata is attacker input: sanitize entry-point names and confine every write to the target directory. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: uv to 0.11.15 or later.
  • Audit your scripts and PATH directories for files you did not install.
  • Pin and audit dependencies; install only from sources you trust.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114111 — sharp: Crafted Images Become Remote Code Execution via Bundled Decoders
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.9 (v4.0) Product sharp — the high-performance Node.js image processing library Type Use-after-free / memory corruption (CWE-416) — sharp before 0.35.5 bundles a librsvg with a memory vulnerability; a crafted SVG can lead to code execution on glibc-based Linux (sibling issue CVE-2026-114112 covers libheif/AVIF in sharp before 0.35.4) Vector Attacker uploads a crafted SVG/AVIF through any upload form → sharp decodes it with the vulnerable bundled library → memory corruption → arbitrary code execution on the server

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: sharp before 0.35.5 (librsvg path) and before 0.35.4 (libheif/AVIF path). Fixed in 0.35.5 and later.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Image decoding is complex, memory-unsafe code processing fully untrusted input. sharp bundles its decoders, so a memory bug in librsvg/libheif becomes a server-side RCE wherever user uploads are decoded — and the application developer never touched those libraries directly.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo contrasts decode_vulnerable() (no version/input gate) with decode_fixed() (minimum safe version enforced, untrusted input quarantined).

The poc.py file next to this writeup demonstrates the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern as a safe, offline logic demo — no network, no shell, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: sharp 0.35.5 or newer (npm update sharp).
  • Validate and constrain uploads (type, size, dimensions) before decoding.
  • Sandbox image processing (separate worker, seccomp, containers) so a decoder bug cannot reach the app.
  • Track bundled native dependencies — they age independently of your package version.

docs.title: D365 F&O MCP Server: Unauthenticated AI Agent Access (CVE-2026-114123)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 Product D365 F&O MCP Server (Model Context Protocol server for Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations X++ code/metadata), prior to 1.11.0 Type Missing authentication for critical function (CWE-306) + insecure default initialization (CWE-1188) Vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U — remote, unauthenticated: a blank optional API key in the official Azure one-click deploy leaves the App Service's /mcp endpoint open to the internet with no auth

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• All versions prior to 1.11.0, when deployed via the official Azure one-click template (infrastructure/azuredeploy.json, infrastructure/main.bicep) with the optional apiKey parameter left blank.
  • Fixed in the 1.11.0 release: https://github.com/dynamics365ninja/d365fo-mcp-server/releases/tag/v1.11.0
  • Deployments with a configured API key, effective upstream authentication, or network restrictions blocking attacker access are not affected.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Three harmless-looking defaults stacked into a public data exposure:

  1. The Azure template defaults the apiKey parameter to an empty string, and the parameter is optional — deployers are never forced to set a secret.
  2. The auth middleware (src/middleware/apiKeyAuth.ts) treats an unset or empty API_KEY as "no authentication configured" and passes requests straight through.
  3. The HTTP listener (src/index.ts) binds to 0.0.0.0 by default — every interface, including the public one the App Service exposes.

The deploy-time MCP_SERVER_MODE=read-only setting does not help: it limits writes, not anonymous reads. So a public App Service served unauthenticated tools/call JSON-RPC requests to read/search tools (search, get_object_info, batch_get_info, extension_info, security_info, find_references, find_event_handlers), leaking indexed proprietary X++ source snippets, business logic, extension/event-handler wiring, security-role and privilege structure, and labels from PackagesLocalDirectory.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational-only)
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern: empty secret => no authentication at all
def api_key_auth(request, api_key):
    if not api_key:                      # blank template default
        return "pass_through"            # auth SKIPPED for everyone
    return "valid" if request.key == api_key else "rejected"

# Simplified fixed pattern: fail closed on an empty secret
def api_key_auth_fixed(request, api_key):
    if not api_key:
        raise RuntimeError("API_KEY is required: refuse to start")  # fail closed
    return "valid" if request.key == api_key else "rejected"

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates this fail-open vs fail-closed logic with synthetic, offline objects — it performs no network calls, deploys nothing, and cannot be used against real systems.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: D365 F&O MCP Server to 1.11.0 or later, where the one-click template forces a real API key.
  • Set a strong, non-empty API key at deploy time; rotate any key that was ever exposed.
  • Bind the listener to localhost or your private network; add Azure network restrictions or upstream authentication in front of the App Service.
  • Review Azure activity logs for anonymous /mcp traffic; assume indexed code/metadata that anonymous readers could reach is exposed.
  • Never deploy AI-agent infrastructure on template defaults alone.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114135 + CVE-2026-114140 — Jupyter Double Trouble
docs.text:
Two high-severity flaws in the Jupyter ecosystem published October 2026: an authorization bypass in Jupyter Server's gateway mode, and a path traversal in nbconvert's notebook export pipeline.

Severity Product Type Attack vector HIGH — CVSS 8.8 (CVSS:3.1 AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) Jupyter Server 2.0.0–2.6.0 Missing authorization (CWE-862) Network, low-privileged authenticated user HIGH — CVSS 8.8 (CVSS:4.0 AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:A/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:H/SI:H/SA:H) nbconvert 5.4.0–7.17.2 Path traversal (CWE-22) Local, victim converts a malicious notebook

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Jupyter Server: 2.0.0 through 2.6.0 (fixed in 2.6.0 for the default gateway configuration; deployments that manually register the deprecated jupyter_server.gateway.handlers module stay vulnerable in 2.6.0+)
  • nbconvert: 5.4.0 through 7.17.2 (fixed in 7.17.2)

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
CVE-2026-114135: Enabling the gateway URL replaces the normal kernel websocket handler with WebSocketChannelsHandler. The replacement handler authenticates the user but never consults the configured Authorizer for the execute action on the kernels resource. Authentication passes, the permission check never happens, and a restricted user gets kernel execution.

CVE-2026-114140: ExtractOutputPreprocessor joins the attacker-controlled cell-output metadata filename onto output_files_dir without confining the result to the intended directory. Converting a malicious notebook with the markdown, LaTeX, reStructuredText, or AsciiDoc exporter writes attacker-controlled output data to arbitrary paths the victim can reach.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. Conceptual demonstration of the flaw pattern — not a working exploit.

See poc.py: an inert, offline demo showing (1) how a handler can authenticate yet skip authorization (the CVE-2026-114135 pattern) and (2) how an unsanitized filename join enables path traversal in an export pipeline (the CVE-2026-114140 pattern). Nothing here touches a network or a real server.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Jupyter Server to 2.6.1+ (and remove any manual registration of the deprecated gateway handlers module).
  • Update nbconvert to 7.17.2+.
  • On shared multi-user servers, audit recent kernel activity for restricted accounts executing unexpected code.
  • Never run jupyter nbconvert on notebooks from untrusted sources; convert in an isolated environment if you must.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114136 / CVE-2026-114138 / CVE-2026-114137 — Django REST framework 3.18.2 security release
docs.text: Django REST framework published security release 3.18.2 on October 21, 2026, fixing three vulnerabilities at once. All three are remotely triggerable and all three share a theme: the framework trusted client-controlled input where it should not have.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Severity Product Type Attack vector HIGH (CVSS 7.5) Django REST framework < 3.18.2 Improper input validation leading to memory exhaustion (CWE-409/CWE-770) — decompression bomb via charset codec Network, no auth — any endpoint accepting a JSON body HIGH (CVSS 7.5) Django REST framework < 3.18.2 Uncontrolled resource consumption / CPU exhaustion (CWE-400/CWE-407) — unbounded Accept header parsing Network, no auth — any reachable endpoint HIGH (CVSS 7.4) Django REST framework 3.12.0–3.18.1 Incorrect authorization / credential revocation failure (CWE-390/CWE-613) — token delete matches no row Network, no auth (the revocation caller is the victim: believed-dead tokens stay live)

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• CVE-2026-114136: DRF 3.6.4 through 3.18.1 (fixed in 3.18.2)
  • CVE-2026-114138: DRF prior to 3.18.2
  • CVE-2026-114137: DRF 3.12.0 through 3.18.1 (fixed in 3.18.2)

Django REST framework 3.18.2 (and 3.18.3, which reverts an unrelated regression from 3.18.2) are safe.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
CVE-2026-114136 — charset-driven decompression bomb. JSONParser.parse in rest_framework/parsers.py took the charset value from the client-supplied Content-Type header and passed it to codecs.getreader(). That function accepts any codec, including byte-transform codecs such as bz2_codec — not only text encodings. A remote unauthenticated client could therefore send a compressed JSON body; Django enforced DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE against the wire bytes only, and the parser then expanded the compressed stream in memory. A few kilobytes on the wire became gigabytes per worker. The default parser set was sufficient, so every reachable JSON endpoint was affected.

CVE-2026-114138 — Accept-header CPU exhaustion. DefaultContentNegotiation.get_accept_list in rest_framework/negotiation.py accepted an unbounded number and aggregate size of Accept tokens, while select_renderer repeatedly ran media-type parsing for each attacker-controlled token, every renderer, and forced 406 renegotiation. A client could send thousands of distinct media types with large quoted parameter values and many semicolons, forcing Django's parameter parser and DRF's repeated parsing into disproportionate CPU work — pinning synchronous workers until the service stopped responding.

CVE-2026-114137 — revocation that revokes nothing. TokenProxy.delete() in rest_framework/authtoken/models.py issued the deletion using the proxy's user-id primary key, while the concrete Token rows are identified by the token-string primary key. Django's query therefore matched no row and reported zero deletions without raising an error. Any code path revoking credentials through a TokenProxy instance believed revocation succeeded while the token stayed live and kept authenticating. Because DRF tokens do not expire automatically, such ghost tokens could remain valid indefinitely. (DRF's own TokenAdmin.delete_model had a workaround and was not affected.)

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational-only. The demo below illustrates the pattern behind each flaw on synthetic data. It is not a working exploit and cannot be pointed at a real server.

See poc.py. It demonstrates:

  1. How a charset value that is a compression codec rather than a text encoding can inflate a small byte buffer when expanded by a naive parser (memory bomb pattern, CVE-2026-114136).
  2. How repeated parsing of many oversized Accept tokens multiplies CPU cost per request (CPU exhaustion pattern, CVE-2026-114138).
  3. How deleting a credential by the wrong primary key matches zero rows while reporting success — leaving the credential live (revocation failure pattern, CVE-2026-114137).

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Update to Django REST framework 3.18.2 or later immediately (pip install -U djangorestframework) and pin it in requirements.txt.
  2. Audit the authtoken table. If any operational script or integration revoked tokens via TokenProxy, verify those tokens are actually gone — the revocation may have been a silent no-op.
  3. Review worker timeouts and memory limits (gunicorn/uvicorn) so a single request cannot exhaust a worker before DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE-style guards kick in; consider a reverse-proxy request-size/time cap.
  4. Subscribe to DRF security announcements (the project's release notes and GitHub security advisories) — this release contained three advisories at once.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114139 — Sentry JavaScript SDK middleware bypass
docs.text:
Educational write-up only. The demo below is a conceptual illustration of the failure pattern. It is not a working exploit, and it contains no exploit code. Never test against systems you don't own.

Severity Product Type Attack vector CRITICAL (CVSS 4.0: 9.1) @sentry/nextjs (Sentry JavaScript SDK) Protection mechanism failure (middleware bypass / missing authorization) Network — unauthenticated

CVSS vector: CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• @sentry/nextjs from 9.36.0 up to, but not including, 9.47.2
  • Fixed in 9.47.2, 10.75.2, and 11.0.0-rc.1

Exploitation also requires all of: a configured tunnelRoute, a webpack build, an application route that collides with (or a root dynamic segment resolving under) the tunnel path, and middleware being the only authorization control.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The Sentry webpack integration for @sentry/nextjs marks every request path under the configured tunnel route as middleware-exempt, so application middleware (auth checks) never runs for those paths. However, the tunnel rewrite itself only serves the exact tunnel path — and only with valid tunnel query parameters.

That mismatch is the bug: the exemption is broad (everything under the tunnel path), while the rewrite is narrow (exactly the tunnel path). Any application route that collides with the tunnel path, or any root dynamic segment resolving beneath it, loses its middleware authorization entirely. An unauthenticated request can reach that route without middleware authorization.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
poc.py in this folder demonstrates the pattern — not the vulnerability — using a toy router:

  1. A broad "skip" rule exempts middleware for every path sharing a prefix with the tunnel route.
  2. A narrow "serve" rule only answers the exact tunnel path.
  3. A request to a colliding app route matches rule 1, misses rule 2, and reaches the protected handler with no auth check.

Read it to build intuition about why broad exemption lists are dangerous — broad match, narrow service. That's the whole failure in miniature.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Update immediately to @sentry/nextjs 9.47.2 (or 10.75.2 / 11.0.0-rc.1 on those tracks).
  2. Re-test middleware coverage on every protected route after upgrading — confirm auth middleware actually executes.
  3. Never rely on middleware as your only authorization layer. Put authorization checks in the route handlers too (defense in depth).
  4. Audit for routes that share a path prefix with your tunnel route.

docs.title: toml-node security update — 4 CVEs fixed in v5.0.1
docs.text:
Product: toml-node (TOML parser for Node.js and the browser) Fix: upgrade to 5.0.1 (patch release addressing all four issues) Disclosure: 2026-10-21 (NVD)

Severity Product Type Attack vector HIGH — CVE-2026-114142 (CVSS 8.8) toml-node < 5.0.1 Prototype pollution Network, no privileges, no user interaction HIGH — CVE-2026-114141 (CVSS 8.7) toml-node < 5.0.1 Algorithmic complexity (quadratic rescan) Network, no privileges, no user interaction HIGH — CVE-2026-114143 (CVSS 8.7) toml-node < 5.0.1 Algorithmic complexity (quadratic slice/join) Network, no privileges, no user interaction MEDIUM — CVE-2026-114144 (CVSS 7.5) toml-node < 5.0.1 Uncontrolled resource consumption (BigInt) Network, no privileges, no user interaction

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• All toml-node versions prior to 5.0.1 are affected by all four CVEs.
  • Version 5.0.1 contains the fixes.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
CVE-2026-114142 (prototype pollution). During toml.parse(), quoted dotted key paths that are visually distinct can produce the same internal bookkeeping string in lib/compiler.js. That collision lets the table-array compiler clear another key's safety guard. The assign() path then descends through an unowned Date value without the owned-container check and reaches the prototype chain, writing attacker-controlled properties onto Object.prototype. Every object created elsewhere in the process inherits them.

CVE-2026-114141 (event-loop block). The table-array compiler rescans the full assignedPaths/valueAssignments bookkeeping sets for every [[table-array]] header and never prunes distinct paths — a document with many headers does quadratic synchronous work and stalls the Node.js event loop.

CVE-2026-114143 (quadratic path slicing). Long dotted keys, table headers, array-of-tables headers, and inline-table keys are repeatedly sliced and rejoined in assign(), deepRef(), and setNestedKey(). Quadratic work can block the event loop for seconds; long enough paths exhaust memory and kill the process. The maxDepth option does not limit key-segment count, so it does not mitigate this.

CVE-2026-114144 (BigInt CPU burn). Unbounded hex/octal/binary/decimal digit sequences go through BigInt() before the 64-bit range check in reduceInteger() runs, so one huge integer literal burns super-linear CPU synchronously on the event loop.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. The demo below is a conceptual illustration of the vulnerability pattern — it does not ship a working exploit and does not target any real system. Its goal is to show why key-path bookkeeping collisions are dangerous and how the fix pattern stops them.

See poc.py: a safe simulation of the flawed assignment pattern (descending an unchecked key path until it reaches a shared prototype record) side by side with the fixed pattern (blocked magic segments, owned-container checks), plus a note on the three denial-of-service siblings.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Upgrade toml-node to 5.0.1 — one release fixes all four CVEs.
  2. Audit past exposure: if your app parsed untrusted TOML with an affected version, review configs and state for injected properties (for example unexpected keys on parsed objects or global behavior changes).
  3. Defense in depth: never parse untrusted input with lax parsers; pin dependencies in lockfiles; run parsers of untrusted documents with timeouts / worker isolation where feasible.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114145 — GitPython submodule path leads to hook planting and remote code execution
docs.text:
Severity Product Type Attack vector HIGH (CVSS 7.5) GitPython (< 3.2.1) Incorrect behavior order (CWE-696) Network — untrusted submodule path

GitPython's create_submodule() clones into the requested destination before checking that the destination is a legal one. An attacker who can influence the submodule path (for example pointing it at .git/hooks) gets the library to write attacker-controlled files into Git's hook directory, then a later Git operation executes the planted post-checkout hook.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• GitPython < 3.2.1
  • In the 3.1.x line the destination check (_validate_repo_path()) does not exist at all, so the operation succeeds silently.
  • In 3.2.0 the check raises ValueError — but only after the clone has already written to disk, and it does not remove the planted files.

Fixed in 3.2.1 (commit 97eadb8, PR #2264, release tag 3.2.1).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The validation order is inverted: the clone operation runs first and the destination validation runs after it. A rejected destination still leaves everything the clone wrote behind, so an attacker-controlled path like .git/hooks results in executable hook files being persisted. Git hooks (such as post-checkout) run with the privileges of whoever executes the next Git operation.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. This is a conceptual illustration of the vulnerable pattern — not a working exploit. Do not use it against systems you do not own.

# Conceptual flow of the vulnerable versions (< 3.2.1):

attacker_path = ".git/hooks"          # attacker-influenced submodule path
dest_is_empty   = True                # e.g. default sample hooks absent

make_submodule(path=attacker_path)
    -> clone_repo(attacker_path)      # 1. clone runs FIRST, files land in .git/hooks
    -> validate(attacker_path)        # 2. check runs AFTER -> ValueError raised
    -> planted files are NOT removed  # 3. hook survives on disk

# later, on the victim machine:
git checkout main                     # triggers post-checkout hook
                                      # -> attacker's executable runs

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the order-of-operations flaw using harmless local files — it shows that a write-then-validate sequence leaves residue, without performing any real attack.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
1. Update GitPython to 3.2.1 or later — the fix validates the destination path before any cloning happens.
  2. Never pass attacker-influenced paths to create_submodule() or any Git operation without your own allowlist validation first.
  3. Audit .git/hooks/ directories in repositories your tooling has handled for unexpected executables.
  4. Pin GitPython>=3.2.1 in your requirements files.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114196 — Paytium PHP Object Injection
docs.text:
Educational only. This writeup explains the vulnerability pattern for defensive learning. Test only in controlled environments you own.

Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.8 (CVSS 3.1) Product Paytium WordPress plugin (Mollie payment forms and donations) Type Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) Vector Network: unauthenticated attacker Fixed in 5.0.6

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Paytium through 5.0.5.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The plugin deserializes data supplied by an unauthenticated visitor without validating it first. A crafted serialized object can trigger a gadget chain in the PHP code, turning an ordinary form submission into remote code execution on the server.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Conceptual illustration: poc.py models unserializing attacker-controlled input (vulnerable) versus accepting only a strict, validated data format (fixed). The demo uses plain dictionaries, not real PHP serialization.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Paytium to 5.0.6 or later.
  • Never unserialize data that comes from visitors; prefer JSON with strict schema validation.
  • Put a firewall rule in front of payment forms and audit payment records for tampering.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114268 — Tenda BE3L Pro: Wi-Fi Setting Buffer Overflow Gives Remote Attackers a Router Shell
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product Tenda BE3L Pro home router (firmware 16.03.60.62) Type Buffer overflow (CWE-119/CWE-120) — the formWifiBasicSet handler in /goform/WifiBasicSet copies the security_5g parameter without a length check; a public exploit exists Vector Remote attacker (low-privileged) sends an oversized security_5g value to the router's settings endpoint → stack/heap buffer overflow → control-flow hijack → shell on the router

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Tenda BE3L Pro firmware 16.03.60.62. Update to the vendor's latest firmware release.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Classic embedded-firmware bug: a request parameter is copied into a fixed-size buffer with no bounds check. Because the settings page is reachable over the network, any long input becomes a weapon — and with a published exploit, the window between disclosure and mass scanning is effectively zero.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The demo contrasts set_wifi_vulnerable() (unchecked copy) with set_wifi_fixed() (length validated before copying).

The poc.py file next to this writeup demonstrates the vulnerable pattern versus the fixed pattern as a safe, offline logic demo — no network, no shell, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now to the latest Tenda firmware for the BE3L Pro.
  • Disable remote/WAN administration on the router.
  • Change the default admin password and reboot to verify the running version.
  • Segment IoT devices so a compromised router cannot pivot freely.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114382 / CVE-2026-114383 — TOTOLINK EX200: Unauthenticated Remote Stack Buffer Overflow (10.0)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 10.0 (both CVEs) Product TOTOLINK EX200 router, firmware 5.2.3c.7200 — home Wi-Fi router Type Stack-based Buffer Overflow (CWE-119) in the cstecgi.cgi settings handlers — no authentication required Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker → oversized Comment / macAddress field → stack overflow → remote code execution; public exploit released

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• TOTOLINK EX200 5.2.3c.7200.
  • CVE-2026-114382: setStaticDhcpConfig handler (component lan.so) — the Comment argument overflows a stack buffer.
  • CVE-2026-114383: setWiFiAclAddConfig handler (component wireless.so) — the macAddress argument overflows a stack buffer.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The router's web interface (/cgi-bin/cstecgi.cgi) copies attacker-controlled settings fields into fixed-size stack buffers with no length check. Same classic C mistake in two handlers:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def set_static_dhcp_config(comment):
    buf = bytearray(64)                    # fixed-size stack buffer
    buf[:len(comment)] = comment           # NO length check!
    # oversized comment -> stack smashed -> execution hijacked

# Simplified fixed pattern
def set_static_dhcp_config_fixed(comment):
    buf = bytearray(64)
    if len(comment) >= len(buf):
        raise ValueError("input too long") # bounds enforced
    buf[:len(comment)] = comment

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The attack chain, conceptually:

  1. Attacker (anywhere on the internet, if the admin page is exposed) sends a settings request with an oversized Comment (CVE-2026-114382) or macAddress (CVE-2026-114383) field.
  2. The CGI handler copies it into the stack buffer without checking length.
  3. The stack overflows; the return address is overwritten; execution jumps to attacker-controlled data.
  4. Remote code execution on the router — traffic sniffing, LAN pivoting, or botnet recruitment. A public exploit is already circulating.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a fixed-size buffer copy with no length check (overflow detected) versus one with bounds enforcement — all synthetic, offline, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update the firmware to a fixed TOTOLINK release.
  • Never expose the router admin interface to the internet — bind it to LAN only, change default credentials.
  • Segment IoT / smart-home gear from your main network so a compromised router can't pivot freely.

docs.title: hMailServer: Broken Admin Authorization Trio (CVE-2026-114489, CVE-2026-114476, CVE-2026-114490)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.1 (CVE-2026-114489), 7.8 (CVE-2026-114490), 7.5 (CVE-2026-114476) Product Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0–6.3.6 (114489), 6.3.4–6.3.6 (114476, 114490); fixed in 6.3.7 Type Missing authorization (CWE-862) and incorrect authorization (CWE-863) in the REST and COM admin APIs Vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:H — a remote, already-authenticated user with a domain-scoped credential (domain admin, scoped API key, or narrowed admin role) escapes the scope and gains whole-server administrative authority

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• CVE-2026-114489: 6.0.0 through 6.3.6 (REST and COM admin APIs)
  • CVE-2026-114476: 6.3.4 through 6.3.6 (REST DELETE /api/v1/role-assignments/{address})
  • CVE-2026-114490: 6.3.4 through 6.3.6 (COM admin API)
  • Fixed in the 6.3.7 release: https://gitlab.com/hmailserver/hmailserver/-/releases/v6.3.7

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Three variations of the same design failure: authorization was checked once, on the wrong state, or never at all.

  • Missing gate (114489): the REST/COM handlers that rename domains, create domain aliases, rewrite mail rules (bind-to-address, send-using-route, script-function actions) and set relay hosts never re-checked the caller's domain scope. Over COM the domain-alias save performed no authorization check at all, the domain rename required only a domain administrator, and rule saves only required ownership of the rule. A credential confined to named domains could therefore divert other tenants' mail to an attacker address, reach the server's own addresses, a route's stored credentials, or a function in the event script.
  • Snapshot check (114476): a role "narrows" an account whose admin level is server-administrator. The DELETE role-assignment route checked what the account held at the time, not what it would hold afterwards. A scoped credential could strip that narrowing role, snapping the account back to server-admin authority — a password the attacker set earlier then opened the server.
  • Ignored scope list (114490): the COM API's server-administrator check read the administer_server permission as whole-server regardless of the domain list on the grant. A credential meant to be confined to named domains signed in via the Control Panel (or a server-side script) as the server administrator of every domain: reading every domain's mail, renaming domains, mapping aliases, writing settings and secrets, and creating further server admins.
# Simplified vulnerable pattern (CVE-2026-114476): check the *current* state
def delete_role_assignment(caller, account, role):
    if caller.can_manage(account.current_role()):   # checks what it HOLDS now
        account.remove_role(role)                   # ...not what it holds AFTER
        return "removed"

# Simplified fixed pattern: re-evaluate the *resulting* state
def delete_role_assignment_fixed(caller, account, role):
    resulting = account.role_after_removing(role)
    if caller.can_manage(resulting):                # checks what it WILL hold
        account.remove_role(role)
        return "removed"
    raise PermissionError("removal would exceed caller's scope")

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker holds a domain-scoped credential on a multi-tenant hMailServer: a domain-admin account or an API key issued for customer-a.com.
  2. Via REST they call DELETE /api/v1/role-assignments/{address} against a scoped account in their domains that carries a narrowing role (CVE-2026-114476). The pre-removal check passes; afterwards the account is server administrator — and the attacker signs in with the password they set earlier.
  3. Via REST or COM they now (or directly, via CVE-2026-114489 / CVE-2026-114490) create a domain alias for another tenant's domain name, rewrite a rule's delivery action to the server's own addresses or event script, or set a relay host on the server's own network.
  4. Other tenants' mail diverts to the attacker, or the attacker's scripts execute at delivery time; new server-admin accounts are minted to keep access.

The accompanying poc.py models the pattern safely in offline Python: a scope check against pre-change state (vulnerable) versus a check re-evaluated against the post-change state (fixed). No network, no real hMailServer, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update now: hMailServer to 6.3.7 or later, where every handler re-checks the caller's domain scope and scoped grants stay scoped.
  • Audit every domain-scoped API key and custom role ever issued — assume one may have escalated. Re-check role assignments for stripped roles.
  • Rotate all admin credentials and secrets; review domain aliases and rule actions for attacker-added entries (aliases to unfamiliar names, rules delivering to external addresses or script functions).
  • Until patched, treat any tenant-scoped admin account as fully privileged.

docs.title: CVE-2026-114509 — Laravel TokenGuard: Authentication Bypass via Crafted Non-String Credential
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.2 Product Laravel 12 (before 12.68.0) and Laravel 13 (before 13.29.0) — the PHP web framework behind millions of apps Type Improper Authentication (CWE-287) in the token-based API guard Vector Unauthenticated remote attacker → sends crafted non-string credential → guard's DB lookup matches an unintended user → full account takeover

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Laravel 12.x before 12.68.0 and 13.x before 13.29.0, when TokenGuard is configured as a standard token-based API guard, on MySQL/MariaDB configurations with loose type comparison.
  • Fixed in 12.68.0 and 13.29.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
TokenGuard takes the credential straight from the request and passes it to the user lookup without verifying it is actually a string. Under MySQL/MariaDB, a crafted non-string value is compared loosely against the stored token column, so the query can match an unintended user record instead of failing authentication:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def authenticate(request):
    credential = request.credential          # attacker-controlled, ANY type
    user = db.query("WHERE api_token = ?", credential)  # no type check!
    # MySQL loose comparison: non-string credential matches the wrong row
    return login_as(user) if user else reject()

# Simplified fixed pattern
def authenticate_fixed(request):
    credential = request.credential
    if not isinstance(credential, str):
        return reject()                      # guard rejects non-strings
    user = db.query_strict("WHERE api_token = ?", credential)
    return login_as(user) if user else reject()

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The attack chain, conceptually:

  1. Attacker picks any route protected by TokenGuard — no valid token needed.
  2. Attacker submits a crafted non-string credential value in place of the token.
  3. TokenGuard forwards it to the lookup without type validation.
  4. MySQL/MariaDB loosely compares it against stored tokens and matches an unintended existing user.
  5. Attacker is authenticated as that user — account takeover.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a lookup model where a raw credential of any type is compared loosely (matching the wrong record) versus one where non-string credentials are rejected and comparison is strict — all synthetic, offline, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Laravel 12.68.0 / 13.29.0 — the guard now rejects crafted non-string credentials.
  • Audit authentication logs for sessions with no corresponding token issuance — the bypass leaves logins that never had a real token.
  • Validate credential types strictly anywhere you do custom token checks; never let a database do loose type juggling on authentication input.
