docs.title: CVE-2026-115506 — libexpat: Billion-Laughs Guard Fires Too Late (CPU Exhaustion)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.5 (v3.x) / 8.7 (CVSS 4.0) Product libexpat — the XML parser embedded in Python, browsers, and countless applications Type XML entity expansion ("billion laughs"), CWE-776 — amplification guard detects the attack too late Vector Remote attacker supplies a moderately sized XML document with nested entity expansions → the parser expands it exponentially → accountingDiffTolerated() in xmlparse.c notices the amplification only after the expansion → tens of seconds of CPU burned per parse → denial of service, no authentication needed

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: libexpat through 2.9.0, including copies bundled inside Python distributions and other applications. Fixed in releases after 2.9.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
libexpat ships a defense against billion-laughs attacks: it accounts for entity amplification and aborts runaway expansion. The accounting, however, runs after the expensive expansion work instead of before it. A dozen lines of XML — each entity level repeating the previous one tenfold — turns kilobytes of input into gigabytes of text, and the guard's verdict arrives only after tens of seconds of CPU have already burned. A guard that runs after the expansion is a guard that doesn't protect.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def parse(entities):
    text = expand_all(entities)          # KB -> GB, CPU burns here
    if amplification_too_high(text):    # checked AFTER the damage
        abort()

# Simplified fixed pattern
def parse_fixed(entities):
    if would_amplify_too_much(entities):  # budget checked BEFORE
        abort()
    text = expand_all(entities)

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker defines one tiny entity, then an entity repeating it 10x, then another repeating that 10x — a few kilobytes total.
  2. The XML document reaches any app parsing untrusted XML with libexpat.
  3. The parser dutifully expands every nesting level: KB → MB → GB.
  4. The amplification guard fires only after the expansion — tens of seconds of CPU per parse.
  5. Repeated in a loop, legitimate traffic starves: cheap, effective DoS.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: it computes the expansion math of nested entities synthetically and shows a before-vs-after budget check. No real XML bomb, no parser, offline only.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade libexpat past 2.9.0 — and audit bundled copies (Python, apps, vendored trees), which are easy to miss.
  • Cap entity expansion for untrusted XML (depth and total expansion limits).
  • Set parse timeouts so one document cannot pin a worker.
  • Validate XML from untrusted sources before parsing.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115546 — Okta Access Gateway: Forged SAML via Unvalidated Authentication Source
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.1 (v3.1) Product Okta Access Gateway (OAG) — the bridge that brings Okta single sign-on to on-premises applications Type Improper authentication (CWE-287) — authentication source never validated during sign-on Vector Authenticated user with an active session modifies the authentication source parameter mid-sign-on → gateway trusts it without validation → gateway issues a SAML assertion granting access to the Admin Console

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Okta Access Gateway versions before 2026.10.2 and before 2026.44.0. Fixed in 2026.10.2 and 2026.44.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
During sign-on, OAG accepts a user-selected authentication source parameter — and never verifies it. A signed-in user can alter that parameter mid-session; the gateway takes it at face value and mints a SAML assertion for it:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def sign_on(request):
    auth_source = request.params["auth_source"]   # attacker-controlled
    return issue_saml(assertion_for(auth_source))  # BUG: never validated

# Simplified fixed pattern
def sign_on_fixed(request, session):
    auth_source = request.params["auth_source"]
    if auth_source != session.registered_auth_source:
        return deny("authentication source mismatch")  # trust, verified
    return issue_saml(assertion_for(auth_source))
Security assertions must be bound to a verified session context — never to a client-supplied hint.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker signs in to OAG normally and holds an active session.
  2. Attacker modifies the auth_source parameter in a sign-on request.
  3. The gateway issues a SAML assertion based on the tampered source — no check performed.
  4. The forged assertion grants access to the Admin Console.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: an authentication decision must be bound to the verified session: the demo contrasts trusting a client-supplied parameter with comparing it against the registered source. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Okta Access Gateway 2026.10.2 / 2026.44.0.
  • Audit Admin Console sign-ins for logins you cannot explain — assume assertions may have been forged.
  • Rotate service credentials and session tokens issued during the exposure window.
  • Restrict which identities can reach the Admin Console at the network layer.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115547 — Okta Access Gateway: Command Execution via Admin Console Configuration
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.1 (v3.1) Product Okta Access Gateway (OAG) Admin Console — configuration interface of the SSO bridge Type Improper input validation (CWE-20) — crafted configuration values executed as OS commands Vector Authenticated administrator saves a specially formatted configuration value in the Admin Console → OAG processes it without validation → value interpreted as an operating system command → runs in the context of the OAG service account

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Okta Access Gateway versions before 2026.10.2 and before 2026.44.0. Fixed in 2026.10.2 and 2026.44.0.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The Admin Console accepts configuration values and the gateway processes them without validating their shape. A specially formatted value is interpreted as an operating system command by the OAG service account:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def save_config(value):
    parsed = parse_config(value)       # no validation of shape
    return run_as_service(parsed)      # BUG: value reaches the shell

# Simplified fixed pattern
def save_config_fixed(value):
    if not is_allowed_config(value):   # strict allow-list validation
        return reject("invalid configuration value")
    return run_as_service(safe_render(value))
Configuration data must be validated against a strict schema — and never interpreted as code.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Attacker holds an authenticated administrator session (reachable directly, or via the forged SAML from CVE-2026-115546).
  2. Attacker saves a crafted configuration value in the Admin Console.
  3. OAG processes the value without input validation.
  4. The value executes as an OS command with the OAG service account's privileges.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: configuration input must be validated before interpretation: the demo contrasts passing a raw value to the shell with allow-listing it first. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade now: Okta Access Gateway 2026.10.2 / 2026.44.0.
  • Audit Admin Console access logs for logins and config changes you cannot explain.
  • Rotate service account credentials — assume command execution is possible until patched.
  • Limit who can reach the admin interface to a small, monitored set of identities.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115570 — Electron: Compromised eMudhra Intermediates Not Blocked, Enabling TLS Impersonation
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.4 (v3.1) Product Electron — before 42.11.16, 43.8.1, 44.9.1, 45.0.0-beta.6 Type Improper check for certificate revocation (CWE-299) Vector Attacker holds a certificate issued through a compromised eMudhra intermediate and can intercept network traffic → Electron's Chromium networking, Node.js tls, Node.js https and Node.js fetch do not block those intermediates → the attacker impersonates any TLS server to the affected application (VS Code, Discord, Slack, and every other Electron app) → credentials, tokens and traffic readable and modifiable

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Electron before 42.11.16 (42.x line), before 43.8.1 (43.x), before 44.9.1 (44.x), and before 45.0.0-beta.6 (45.x beta). Fixed in those releases (PRs 55127–55130, commits adding the eMudhra intermediates to the blocked list).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When a certificate authority's intermediate is compromised, every certificate it issued becomes untrustworthy — browsers and runtimes respond by blocklisting the intermediate. Electron missed that step: the compromised eMudhra intermediates were never added to its blocked-certificate list across four of its networking stacks (Chromium, Node tls, Node https, Node fetch). Certificate validation is only as strong as its revocation data; a validator that never learns which intermediates died will happily trust certificates from them.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# VULNERABLE - trust chain checked, blocklist never consulted
def verify(chain):
    return all(cert.signature_valid for cert in chain)

# FIXED - reject any chain rooted in a compromised intermediate
BLOCKED_INTERMEDIATES = {"<eMudhra intermediate fingerprint>", ...}

def verify(chain):
    if any(c.fingerprint in BLOCKED_INTERMEDIATES for c in chain):
        return False
    return all(cert.signature_valid for cert in chain)

The demo poc.py models chain verification with and without a blocklist using synthetic certificate objects — no real TLS, no network.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update Electron to 42.11.16, 43.8.1, 44.9.1, 45.0.0-beta.6 or later (and any Electron app you ship or use — check with its vendor). Until updated, avoid untrusted networks for sensitive work in Electron apps, and treat any certificate warnings as hostile.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115572 — pypdf: Crafted PDFs Cause CPU Exhaustion via Malformed Cross-References (3 CVEs)
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v4.0) Product pypdf — prior to 6.21.2 (pure-Python PDF library) Type Uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400) / excessive iteration (CWE-834) — CPU exhaustion Vector Attacker crafts a tiny PDF whose cross-reference table declares an impossible entry count, or that repeatedly references the same nonexistent indirect object → the parser trusts the declared numbers → each access triggers repeated full-file recovery scans → minutes of CPU burned per file → parsing workers exhausted, upload queues stall

Covers CVE-2026-115572 (repeated references to nonexistent indirect objects trigger repeated full-file recovery, 7.1), CVE-2026-115580 (xref entry count exceeds what the file can contain, 7.1), and CVE-2026-115585 (incomplete remediation of malformed xref entries still reloads the PDF stream per recovery attempt, 7.1).

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: pypdf prior to 6.21.2. Fixed in 6.21.2, which fails fast on impossible cross-reference data instead of looping recovery.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The parser treated the file's own metadata as authoritative. The declared index size was never sanity-checked against the actual file, and references to missing objects triggered expensive full-file recovery scans instead of a fast error. A tiny input could therefore demand an unbounded amount of work. Parsers must validate structural claims against reality before spending resources - reject impossible counts, budget recovery attempts, and cap total parse time.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# VULNERABLE - declared count trusted, recovery loops forever
def open_pdf(xref):
    for entry in range(xref.declared_count):   # <-- tiny file claims 99999
        recover_object(entry)                  # <-- full-file scan each time

# FIXED - sanity-check the claim against the file first
def open_pdf(xref, real_file_size):
    if xref.declared_count * ENTRY_SIZE > real_file_size:
        raise ValueError("impossible xref size")
    for entry in range(min(xref.declared_count, HARD_CAP)):
        recover_object(entry)

The demo poc.py below models trusted-claim looping vs validated claims on synthetic numbers - no PDFs, no pypdf involved.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade pypdf to 6.21.2 or newer. Parse user-supplied PDFs with a hard timeout inside an isolated worker process, and reject files whose declared index size dwarfs their actual size.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115586 — virtualenv: Command Injection via Unescaped Prompt in bash activate
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v4.0) Product virtualenv — 21.14.9 through 21.14.13 Type Improper neutralization of special elements used in a command (CWE-78) — OS command injection Vector Attacker ships a project whose folder name (or --prompt value) contains command substitution → victim creates a venv inside it and runs bin/activate → the value is copied into the shell prompt variable with no escaping → re-enabling promptvars, set -o posix, or spawning an interactive child bash expands the substitution → the hidden command executes with the victim's privileges

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: virtualenv 21.14.9 through 21.14.13. Fixed in 21.14.13, which escapes the prompt value.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The activate script treated user-influenced data as shell syntax instead of plain text. The prompt value was stored raw into the prompt variable, deferring interpretation to the shell, which happily expanded command substitution at a later moment. The injection window spans activation and any later shell expansion - quoting or escaping the value at storage time closes it completely.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# VULNERABLE - prompt value copied raw into the prompt variable
VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT="my$(whoami)"      # attacker-controlled name
PS1="($VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT) $PS1"      # expands later: whoami runs

# FIXED (21.14.13) - prompt value escaped before storage
VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT='my$(whoami)'      # treated as literal text

The demo poc.py below models raw-vs-escaped prompt storage on synthetic strings - nothing is executed, no shell is spawned.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade virtualenv to 21.14.13 or newer. Treat unusual folder names in downloaded projects as suspicious, inspect activate scripts you did not write yourself, and pass explicit, simple --prompt values when creating environments.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115608 — SQL Injection in Crocoblock JetEngine for WordPress
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 3.1 score 8.5 Product Crocoblock JetEngine (WordPress plugin) Type SQL Injection (CWE-89) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:L Affected versions JetEngine up to and including 3.9.0 Fixed version 3.9.0.1 or later Reported by Ayukiab (via Patchstack) Published 2026-10-26

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: JetEngine versions from n/a through 3.9.0 are vulnerable. Version 3.9.0.1 patches the flaw.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: A value supplied by a logged-in, low-privilege user is joined directly into a database query instead of being sent as bound data. The database cannot distinguish the fixed query from attacker-supplied text, so crafted input is executed as part of the SQL command. The query runs with the site database privileges, and its scope changes to the wider database context, which is why a low-privilege account can read data it should never see.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. poc.py in this folder simulates the pattern locally with an in-memory database: a vulnerable query built by string concatenation returns rows for a crafted filter value, while the fixed version binds the same value as data and returns only the legitimate match. It never targets a real WordPress site.

Run it with:

python3 poc.py

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update JetEngine to 3.9.0.1 or later immediately — this is the fix.
  • Use prepared statements / parameterized queries for every database query that touches user input.
  • Give the WordPress database user only the permissions the site actually needs.
  • Keep a tested backup, and review accounts holding low-privilege roles on the site.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115723 — Snap7 Out-of-Bounds Write via Unvalidated BSend Length
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 7.4 Product Snap7 S7 PLC library, through 1.4.3 Vulnerability type Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) Attack vector Network — malicious active partner in a BSend/BRecv block transfer

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Snap7 through 1.4.3. Used in SCADA drivers, HMIs and industrial gateways that talk to Siemens S7 controllers.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: During a block transfer, the active partner declares the total message length first (up to 65535 bytes) and the passive partner's receive routine trusts that declared value without checking it against the real receive buffer. When the declared length is larger than what actually arrives — and larger than the destination buffer — the copy writes past the end of the buffer, corrupting memory of the industrial process.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational-only conceptual walkthrough — no working exploit.

  1. The passive partner (SCADA gateway) accepts a connection from a configured peer address and starts a BRecv block transfer.
  2. The attacker declares a huge total length (e.g. 65535) in the transfer header.
  3. The attacker then sends only a short fragment of actual data.
  4. The receive routine copies declared_length bytes into the fixed-size buffer, writing past its end.
  5. Result: heap/stack memory corruption → SCADA driver crash, frozen HMI screens, or corrupted gateway state.

Illustrative vulnerable vs fixed pattern (simplified, educational):

// VULNERABLE: declared length used without validation
void brecv(const uint8_t* wire, uint16_t declared, uint8_t* buffer, size_t bufsize) {
    memcpy(buffer, wire, declared); // overflow if declared > bufsize
}

// FIXED: clamp the declared length to the real buffer
void brecv(const uint8_t* wire, uint16_t declared, uint8_t* buffer, size_t bufsize) {
    if (declared > bufsize) return; // reject impossible lengths
    memcpy(buffer, wire, declared);
}

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Snap7 past version 1.4.3.
  • Validate every declared length against the real buffer size before copying (clamp, never trust the header).
  • Allowlist peer addresses; segment industrial networks so a compromised peer cannot reach the core.
  • Only ever test in controlled environments.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115726 — Poisoned .aider.conf.yml executes OS commands (Aider AI coding CLI)
docs.text: Field Value CVE CVE-2026-115726 Severity HIGH — CVSS 7.8 Product Aider AI coding CLI, through 0.86.2 Vulnerability type CWE-78 — OS Command Injection (attacker-controlled config values passed to the shell) Attack vector Local — victim clones a repo containing a malicious config and runs Aider inside it

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Aider AI coding CLI through 0.86.2. Upgrade past 0.86.2 immediately.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Aider auto-loads the repository's .aider.conf.yml config file with no trust prompt, no consent dialog, no warning. Several config values (notably the notifications setting and the editor setting) are then passed to subprocess with shell=True, so attacker-controlled strings from a cloned repository are executed as OS commands with the victim's privileges. Execution is triggered after model replies or when the /editor command is used. A plain text config file becomes a command-execution primitive: data is treated as code, with no validation and no user consent.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational only)
docs.text:
No working exploit is provided. The attack chain:

  1. The attacker commits a poisoned .aider.conf.yml into a public repository.
  2. The victim clones the repo and runs aider inside it.
  3. Aider silently loads the config — no warning, no prompt.
  4. The victim sends a prompt; when the model replies, Aider executes the attacker-controlled value through the shell.
  5. The command runs as the victim's user, on the victim's machine.

What a suspicious setting looks like (redacted, non-functional — shown for recognition only):

# DO NOT RUN — redacted example for recognition only
notifications-command: "[REDACTED — attacker-controlled shell command]"
editor: "[REDACTED — attacker-controlled shell command]"

A legitimate config typically leaves these unset or points them at well-known local helper programs.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade Aider past 0.86.2 immediately.
  • Never run Aider inside an untrusted directory without reviewing .aider.conf.yml first.
  • Treat every config file in a cloned repo as untrusted input — read it before the tool does.
  • Prefer running Aider in directories you control; isolate coding-assistant runs in containers or sandboxes when exploring unfamiliar repos.
  • Watch for unexpected subprocess activity right after model replies.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115727 — Remote Code Execution via Flask Debug Mode in AgenticSeek llm_server
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 8.1 Product AgenticSeek llm_server (before commit 409840c) Vulnerability type CWE-489: Active Debug Code Attack vector Remote, network — no user interaction required

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: AgenticSeek before commit 409840c. The fix shipped in PR #558.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: llm_server/app.py hardcoded Flask debug mode (debug=True) while binding the server to all interfaces (0.0.0.0). In production this exposed the interactive Werkzeug debugger console to the whole network. The debugger's PIN is derivable from machine facts, so any attacker who could reach the server port could unlock the console and run arbitrary Python code — and therefore operating system commands — with llm_server privileges. This is the classic CWE-489 pattern: development scaffolding shipped into a production build.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual, educational)
docs.text:
Attack chain:

  1. Attacker scans for the exposed llm_server port.
  2. An error page reveals the Werkzeug debugger console.
  3. The debugger PIN is derived from machine facts, unlocking the console.
  4. The console runs Python code with server privileges → full RCE.

Illustrative vulnerable vs fixed Flask config (not a working exploit):

# VULNERABLE (what CVE-2026-115727 fixed):
app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True)   # debugger on the network

# FIXED:
app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=5000, debug=False)  # no debugger, localhost only

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update AgenticSeek past commit 409840c immediately.
  • Never run Flask/Werkzeug debug mode in production.
  • Never bind a debug-enabled server to 0.0.0.0; localhost only.
  • Put the LLM server behind authentication and a firewall.
  • Rotate any secrets that may have been exposed while debug mode was on.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115775 — Twisted: Unauthenticated Memory Exhaustion in XMPP, IRC and Telnet Handlers (3 CVEs)
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.7 (v4.0) Product Twisted — prior to 26.10.0rc1 (Python event-based networking framework) Type Uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400/CWE-770) — pre-authentication memory exhaustion Vector Attacker opens a single TCP connection → never authenticates → sends bytes without line feeds (IRC), an unclosed stream element (XMPP), or subnegotiation bytes without a terminator (telnet) → the handler buffers everything with no byte, element-count, or time limit → process memory exhausted → server process dies, taking every hosted service down

Covers CVE-2026-115775 (XMPP ExpatElementStream unbounded stanza buffering, 8.7), CVE-2026-115776 (IRC dataReceived unlimited per-connection line buffer, 7.5), and CVE-2026-115778 (telnet subnegotiation buffer with no maximum length, 7.5). All three are pre-authentication, same fix release.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Twisted prior to 26.10.0rc1. Fixed in 26.10.0rc1, which enforces byte and element limits on pre-authentication parsing.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Three protocol handlers crossed a trust boundary: they appended attacker-controlled bytes to per-connection buffers without any size limit, and the parsing happened before authentication. A single slow connection could therefore inflate server memory indefinitely. Resource consumption must be bounded before identity is established - a byte cap, an element cap, or a parse timeout breaks the attack for all three handlers.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# VULNERABLE - buffer grows with attacker input, no cap
buffer = b""
def data_received(chunk):
    global buffer
    buffer += chunk            # <-- one slow connection = dead server

# FIXED (26.10.0rc1 style) - hard cap enforced before auth
MAX_PREAUTH = 65536
buffer = b""
def data_received(chunk):
    global buffer
    buffer += chunk
    if len(buffer) > MAX_PREAUTH:
        raise ConnectionError("pre-auth buffer limit exceeded")

The demo poc.py below models unbounded vs capped buffering on synthetic bytes - no sockets, no Twisted, no network involved.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade Twisted to 26.10.0rc1 or newer. As defense in depth, put pre-authentication services behind connection and rate limits, and monitor per-connection memory usage so a single peer can never starve the process.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115806 — Prime Mover backup plugin: unauthenticated PHP object injection via comments
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) Product Prime Mover – Backup and Migration for WordPress (before 2.2.2) Type PHP Object Injection (CWE-502) — deserialization of untrusted input Vector Attacker posts a comment containing a crafted base64-encoded serialized object → value sleeps in wp_comments.comment_content → admin runs a Prime Mover export/restore → migration search-and-replace base64-decodes it and calls unserialize() with no allowed-classes restriction → bundled Freemius gadget chain (FS_Clone_Manager::__set → FS_Option_Manager::set_option → store() → update_option()) rewrites site options → full takeover

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Prime Mover – Backup and Migration 2.2.1 and earlier. Fixed in 2.2.2 (released 19 Oct 2026).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: During migration search-and-replace, the plugin decodes stored values and passes them to PHP's unserialize() without restricting which classes may be rebuilt. unserialize() is inherently dangerous: any serialized object it receives is reconstructed, and its magic methods (__wakeup, __destruct, __set, ...) execute on the way in. Here the attacker never touches the plugin directly — the payload is planted as an ordinary blog comment. When an admin later triggers an export or restore, the plugin wakes up the attacker's object itself. Worse, the gadget chain the payload needs is already bundled inside the plugin's own Freemius library, so no other plugin or theme has to be installed.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified — an allowlist of classes would have neutralized it:

# VULNERABLE - the stored comment value decides which classes come alive
def migrate_value(stored_b64):
    raw = base64.b64decode(stored_b64)
    return unserialize(raw)  # <-- no allowed_classes: attacker objects revive

# FIXED - only plain data containers may be rebuilt
def migrate_value(stored_b64):
    raw = base64.b64decode(stored_b64)
    return unserialize(raw, allowed_classes=["stdClass"])  # <-- gadget chain dead

The demo poc.py models a deserializer that either revives arbitrary classes or restricts them to an allowlist — purely synthetic, offline objects. No real product, no network, no exploit.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Prime Mover to 2.2.2 immediately — do not run any migration search-and-replace until updated.
  • Search wp_comments.comment_content for suspicious base64 blobs that were never displayed as readable text.
  • Review the administrator list and recently modified site options for signs of takeover.
  • As a general rule, never call unserialize() on data that crossed a trust boundary; prefer JSON and an explicit class allowlist.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115807 — User Profile Builder: Author users grant themselves Editor accounts
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.1 (v3.1) Product User Profile Builder – Beautiful User Registration Forms, User Profiles & User Role Editor (before 4.0.4) Type Privilege Escalation (CWE-269) — missing authorization on role attribute Vector Authenticated attacker with Author access edits the Gutenberg Register block's attacker-controlled Assigned Role attribute → value flows directly into the [wppb-register] shortcode without server-side authorization → the role guard only downgrades roles carrying manage_options or remove_users → Editor (and any role lacking those capabilities) is accepted → new privileged account created

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: User Profile Builder 4.0.3 and earlier. Fixed in 4.0.4.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The Register block takes a role attribute from the client and hands it straight to the registration shortcode. Server-side, the guard was written to prevent Administrator accounts from being created — it downgrades roles that carry the heaviest capabilities (manage_options, remove_users). But Editor needs neither of those, so the guard waves it through. The flaw is trusting a privilege decision to client-controlled input and checking "is this the top role?" instead of "is this role on the server-side allowlist?".

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# VULNERABLE - client-supplied role passes through a too-narrow guard
def register_vulnerable(requested_role):
    if has_cap(requested_role, "manage_options") or has_cap(requested_role, "remove_users"):
        requested_role = "subscriber"  # guard only catches admin-ish roles
    return create_account(role=requested_role)  # <-- editor slips through

# FIXED - server-side allowlist of roles a signup may receive
ALLOWED_SIGNUP_ROLES = {"subscriber", "customer"}

def register_fixed(requested_role):
    role = requested_role if requested_role in ALLOWED_SIGNUP_ROLES else "subscriber"
    return create_account(role=role)  # <-- editor downgraded, denied

The demo poc.py models the role guard against an attacker-chosen role — purely synthetic, offline objects. No real product, no network, no exploit.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update User Profile Builder to 4.0.4 immediately.
  • Audit every user account — especially Editors — created through registration forms.
  • Force password resets on suspicious accounts and review recent post/page modifications.
  • As a general rule, never accept a privilege level from client input; validate roles against a server-side allowlist.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115812 — AWS Multi Model Server: Path Traversal in Model Archives Leads to Remote Code Execution
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) Product Amazon Web Services Multi Model Server (MMS) — all versions through 1.1.11 Type Relative path traversal (CWE-23) — archive extraction without path validation Vector Attacker crafts a model archive (.mar) whose entry names contain ../ sequences → the server extracts the archive and writes files outside the intended model directory → arbitrary file write as the serving user → remote code execution

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: All released versions of Multi Model Server, 1.1.11 and earlier. There is no patched version: MMS is end of life, its repository is archived, and AWS will never fix this.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The archive extractor trusted the file names inside the model package. A path like ../../startup.py was joined to the extraction directory and written verbatim, so a "model" became a file-drop anywhere the service account could write. Anything that turns a data file into a write primitive is one step from code execution - model servers run the extracted code by design.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

import os

# VULNERABLE - archive entry names used verbatim
entry = "../../payload.py"                      # inside the attacker's .mar
dest = os.path.join(model_dir, entry)           # escapes model_dir!
open(dest, "w").write(malicious_code)

# FIXED - reject entries that escape the target directory
target = os.path.realpath(os.path.join(model_dir, entry))
if not target.startswith(os.path.realpath(model_dir) + os.sep):
    raise ValueError("archive entry escapes extraction directory")

The demo poc.py below models the traversal check with synthetic paths - no archives are extracted and nothing is written to disk.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: There is no patch. Stop running Multi Model Server entirely and migrate to a supported serving solution (e.g., Amazon SageMaker or TorchServe). Audit every .mar archive you ever downloaded or served, rotate credentials on hosts that ran MMS, and treat archived model packages as untrusted input going forward.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115863 — ConnMan: Forged DHCPv6 Reply Smashes the Stack via Oversized Domain List
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.6 (v3.1) Product ConnMan (Linux connection manager) — through 2.0 Type Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121) — DHCPv6 domain-list parsing Vector On-link attacker sends a forged DHCPv6 REPLY carrying a DOMAIN_LIST option (option 24) of 1025+ non-zero bytes → get_domains() in gdhcp/client.c copies a fixed 1025 bytes into a 1026-byte stack buffer with no length check → the DNS label walk then reads and writes past the buffer end in attacker-chosen strides → crash or code execution in a privileged network daemon, no authentication required

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: ConnMan through 2.0. Fixed upstream in commit bb06c47 (DHCPv6 domain-list parsing fix in gdhcp/client.c); take your distribution's security update.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The parser trusted the wire. It copied a fixed-size chunk of attacker-controlled option data onto the stack regardless of the option's real length, then walked the result with an unbounded loop. Network parsers must treat every length field as hostile: validate before copying, and never let attacker bytes dictate how far a loop runs.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

/* VULNERABLE - fixed copy, unbounded walk */
char dns_name[1026];
memcpy(dns_name, option_data, 1025);   /* option can be longer! */
for (c = dns_name; *c; c += jump + 1)  /* walks past the end */
    *c = '.';

/* FIXED - bound the copy and the walk */
size_t n = min(option_len, sizeof(dns_name) - 1);
memcpy(dns_name, option_data, n);
dns_name[n] = '\0';

The demo poc.py below models the length check with synthetic byte strings - no packets are crafted or sent.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Apply the upstream fix (commit bb06c47) or install your distribution's ConnMan security update. On untrusted networks, this is remotely triggerable by anyone on the link - patch promptly, and monitor for unexpected ConnMan crashes.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115893 — Wasmtime: a Giant Jump Table Escapes the Sandbox (9.9)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product Wasmtime (WebAssembly runtime) — before 36.0.19, 48.0.7, and 49.0.4 Type Incorrect branch target in compiled code (compiler bug) — sandbox escape Vector On aarch64, the Cranelift backend can miscompile a Wasm br_table instruction with more than about 256,000 targets, producing an incorrect conditional branch target. The branch can jump to arbitrary other code at a user-controlled offset, letting a user-controlled Wasm module escape the sandbox on aarch64 engines using the default Cranelift backend.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Wasmtime before 36.0.19, 48.0.7, and 49.0.4 (per release line). Fixed in 36.0.19, 48.0.7, and 49.0.4.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The compiler handling of very large jump tables produced a wrong branch destination. Because compiled code is trusted completely by the processor, a single wrong target breaks the sandbox boundary that the whole runtime depends on.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# VULNERABLE - jump table target computed without bounds handling
# target = table[index]            # index beyond verified range
# FIXED - bound-check every jump-table index before branching
# target = table[index] if index < len(table) else trap()

The demo poc.py below contrasts an unchecked table lookup with a bounds-checked one on synthetic data.

The demo poc.py below illustrates the vulnerable pattern against the fixed pattern with purely synthetic, offline objects — no real product, no network, no exploit.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Update Wasmtime to 36.0.19, 48.0.7, or 49.0.4 for your release line, and stop running untrusted modules on older builds — especially on aarch64 hosts.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115929 — MongoDB Compass trusts compromised eMudhra intermediate CA keys
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.6 (v4.0) Product MongoDB Compass (before 1.53.1) Type Improper certificate validation (CWE-295) — bundled TLS trust store retains compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs Vector Attacker presents a forged certificate signed by a leaked eMudhra intermediate key → Compass's bundled Electron trust store still trusts it → TLS session established → credentials and queries intercepted

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: MongoDB Compass prior to 1.53.1. Issue is resolved by updating to Compass 1.53.1, which includes Electron 44.9.1 with an updated root certificate store.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: MongoDB Compass relies on Electron, which ships its own TLS root certificate store instead of using the operating system's. That bundled store still carried the eMudhra intermediate CA certificates, whose private keys were compromised — the keys turned out to be tiny integers (one was literally the number 4), so they could be derived from the public certificates. Because the stale store kept trusting those intermediates, Compass would accept attacker-minted certificates for any host without warning. Browsers and OS vendors distrusted these certificates within days; the stale copy inside Compass's bundled store never got the memo.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# VULNERABLE - trust store keeps trusting compromised intermediates
COMPROMISED_ISSUERS = {"eMudhra DV TLS CA - G3B", "eMudhra EM Sign CA"}

def validate_chain(chain, trust_store):
    for cert in chain:
        if cert.issuer in COMPROMISED_ISSUERS and cert.issuer in trust_store:
            return True  # <-- trusts the compromised intermediate anyway
    return False

# FIXED - explicitly distrust the compromised intermediates
BLOCKED_ISSUERS = {"eMudhra DV TLS CA - G3B", "eMudhra EM Sign CA"}

def validate_chain(chain, trust_store):
    for cert in chain:
        if cert.issuer in BLOCKED_ISSUERS:
            return False  # <-- distrusted, connection fails closed
    return any(c.issuer in trust_store for c in chain)

The demo poc.py below models a TLS trust store that either keeps or drops compromised intermediate issuers — purely synthetic, offline objects. No real product, no network, no exploit.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade MongoDB Compass to 1.53.1 (ships Electron 44.9.1 with a cleaned root certificate store). Audit other Electron-based desktop apps for the same stale-store pattern and refresh them. Keep the operating system's root CA store updated and enable revocation checking (CRL/OCSP) where available. For high-risk environments, verify clients against the known-compromised SPKI hashes.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115931 — Postiz: Unrestricted Provider Function Dispatch Lets a Signup Read Any Server File (and Kill the Backend)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.9 (v3.1) Product Postiz (postiz-app) — before 2.25.1 Type Use of externally controlled input to select code (CWE-470) + external control of file name (CWE-73) — unrestricted provider-function dispatch Vector A signed-in user asks the backend to run a function for one of their connected channels; the backend never restricted which functions could be named, so internal helpers were reachable from the web interface. One helper reads a file from the server's disk using the channel's stored token as the path; another makes the backend process exit. Self-registration is open by default, so no existing account or interaction with another user is needed

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Postiz before 2.25.1. Fixed upstream in commit 9383f5be (release v2.25.1) — upgrade to 2.25.1 or later.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: The channel API treated the requested function name as an open choice instead of a strict allow-list. Two missing checks chained into total compromise: (1) any function name could be invoked, including internal helpers never meant to be reachable from the web, and (2) the file-reading helper trusted channel data (the stored token) as a file path. Because self-registration is open by default, the "privileged user" was just a brand-new stranger who signed up seconds earlier.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
The vulnerable pattern, simplified:

# VULNERABLE - the request names any function, no allow-list
def run_provider_function(name, channel):
    fn = getattr(provider_helpers, name)   # 'read_file', 'shutdown'... anything!
    return fn(channel)                     # channel.token is attacker-chosen

# FIXED - only approved functions are invocable
ALLOWED = {"schedule_post", "refresh_token"}

def run_provider_function(name, channel):
    if name not in ALLOWED:
        raise PermissionError("function not allowed")
    fn = getattr(provider_helpers, name)
    token = validate_token(channel.token)  # tokens are never treated as paths
    return fn(channel, token)

The demo poc.py below models the allow-list check with synthetic inputs — no real server is contacted and nothing here can be aimed at real systems.

Educational material only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text: Upgrade to Postiz 2.25.1 or later, where the dispatch is restricted. If you ran a vulnerable version, rotate every secret the environment held — the session signing key, the database address/credentials, and all connected-service tokens — and close open self-registration if you do not need it public.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115932 — Postiz Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read
docs.text:
Educational only. This writeup explains the vulnerability pattern for defensive learning. Test only in controlled environments you own.

Field Value Severity CRITICAL 9.6 (CVSS 3.1) Product Postiz social media scheduling app (postiz-app) Type Path traversal / improper limitation of a pathname (CWE-22, CWE-74) Vector Network: registered user (self-registration open by default) Fixed in 2.25.3

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Postiz before 2.25.3.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: When a post is published, Postiz treats a media path that is not a web address as a file on the server disk, but never checks that the file lies inside the upload directory. A registered user can store a crafted media path, get it past the checks, and have the publishing worker read an arbitrary file and send it as an attachment to a Discord server the user controls. Two further routes expose the same unconfined reads (one reveals file existence and can exhaust backend memory). Self-registration is open by default, so no existing account is needed.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text: Conceptual illustration: poc.py models resolving a user-supplied media path without a boundary check (vulnerable) versus confining every resolved path to the uploads directory (fixed). Only local demo paths are used.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Postiz to 2.25.3.
  • Close open self-registration if you do not need it.
  • Rotate every secret that may have leaked and audit Discord attachments sent by the publishing worker.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115933 — Postiz Forged Signed Tokens Allow Full Account and Organization Takeover
docs.text:
Postiz signs its session, invitation, and password reset tokens with one shared secret and without any marker of what a token is for. A route that refreshes the credentials of a browser-extension channel signs data taken from the request itself and stores the result where the requesting user can read it back. A self-registered user can therefore obtain a validly signed token containing any claims they choose, which the application accepts as a session, as an organization invitation with a chosen role, as a password reset, or as an enterprise provisioning token.

Field Value Severity CRITICAL (CVSS 3.1: 9.9) Product Postiz (gitroomhq/postiz-app) Type Authentication Bypass by Spoofing / Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Attributes (CWE-290, CWE-345, CWE-915) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H Affected versions 2.15.0 through 2.25.2 Fixed in 2.25.3

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Postiz versions 2.15.0 and later, fixed in 2.25.3. Self-registration is open unless DISABLE_REGISTRATION=true is set, so on a default instance the attacker only needs to create an ordinary account. The instance must be able to reach the Skool provider endpoint used by the extension channel flow.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The token system confuses "signed" with "meant for this purpose":

  1. One secret for every token type. Session tokens, organization invitations, password resets, and enterprise provisioning tokens are all signed with the same secret.
  2. No token-type marker. Nothing inside a token records what kind of token it is, so a token minted through one route is structurally identical to a token any other route would mint.
  3. A signing oracle in the extension flow. The browser-extension channel credential refresh route signs data taken from the request body and stores the signed result where the requesting user can read it back — so any registered user can ask the server to sign claims of their choosing.
  4. Claims accepted at face value. Downstream endpoints trust the claims inside a validly signed token, so a forged token is indistinguishable from a genuine one — and forged tokens do not expire.

Demonstrated end to end: a second self-registered user became super administrator of another user's organization (the organization id is exposed by shared post preview links) and read its API key. A second, narrower team-invitation route signs extra fields from the request body the same way.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the logic of the flaw, not an exploit against a real server. The included poc.py simulates token signing with plain data structures:

  • Vulnerable flow: one shared secret signs bare claims with no type marker, and verification accepts any validly signed token for any purpose — so a token minted as a "channel refresh" is accepted as a super-admin organization invitation.
  • Fixed flow: each token type is signed with a purpose-bound claim, and verification rejects a token presented for a different purpose than the one it was minted for.

Run it locally:

python3 poc.py

Disclaimer: for education and defense only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Postiz to 2.25.3 or later as soon as possible.
  • If you do not use channels that rely on the Postiz browser extension, block POST /integrations/extension-refresh at your reverse proxy. This removes the main signing route (the team-invitation route remains, so this is a workaround, not a fix).
  • Set DISABLE_REGISTRATION=true if you do not need public sign-ups. The attacker needs an ordinary account, so closing self-registration limits exposure — it does not close the issue.
  • Rotate secrets (especially the token signing secret) and audit organization memberships and roles for members you do not recognize; forged tokens cannot be told apart from genuine ones, so assume any pre-patch token may be compromised.
  • As a defense-in-depth rule: bind every signed token to exactly one purpose, verify that purpose on every use, and use separate keys or key scopes per token type.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115948 — Blind SQL Injection in Media Library Assistant for WordPress
docs.text: Field Value Severity HIGH — CVSS 3.1 score 8.5 Product Media Library Assistant (WordPress plugin, David Lingren) Type Blind SQL Injection (CWE-89) Vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:L Affected versions Media Library Assistant up to and including 3.42 Fixed version 3.43 or later Reported by Khanh Nguyen (via Patchstack) Published 2026-10-26

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Media Library Assistant versions from n/a through 3.42 are vulnerable. Version 3.43 patches the flaw.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: A value supplied by a logged-in, low-privilege user reaches a database query without proper handling. The stolen data is never printed directly — instead, the attacker asks the database yes-or-no questions through crafted filter values and reads the answers from small differences in the response (result present vs. absent). Repeating those questions rebuilds hidden values character by character. Blind does not mean harmless; it only means slower.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only. poc.py in this folder simulates the pattern locally with an in-memory database: a vulnerable builder lets a crafted condition change the result, leaking one bit of truth per request, while the fixed version binds the same value as data so the crafted condition is treated as a plain search term and leaks nothing. It never targets a real WordPress site.

Run it with:

python3 poc.py

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Media Library Assistant to 3.43 or later immediately — this is the fix.
  • Use prepared statements / parameterized queries for every database query that touches user input.
  • Review low-privilege accounts on the site, and keep a tested backup.
  • Treat any response difference driven by user input as a potential information channel.

docs.title: CVE-2026-115995 — Unitree Go2 Chat Volume Value Allows Remote OS Command Injection
docs.text:
The Unitree Go2 robot dog's AI chat feature (chat_go) passes the volume value from a request straight into a system shell command without sanitizing it. A remote attacker can send a volume value that is not a number at all, but a number followed by a shell separator and a second command of their choosing. The robot builds the shell command, runs it, and the attacker's command executes alongside the volume change — arbitrary command execution on a machine with cameras, microphones, and legs.

Field Value Severity CRITICAL (CVSS: 9.6) Product Unitree Robotics Unitree Go2 Type OS Command Injection (CWE-78) Vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:H/SI:H/SA:H Affected versions 1.1.11.0 through 1.1.11.4 Fixed in 1.1.11.5

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: Unitree Go2 firmware versions 1.1.11.0, 1.1.11.1, 1.1.11.2, 1.1.11.3, and 1.1.11.4, in the chat_go component (gpt_thread.py, set_volume handler). Fixed in version 1.1.11.5. The vendor confirmed the report early against its internal ticket #474. The attack can be launched remotely; no privileges are required, only passive user interaction (the victim's chat feature must be reachable).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The volume handler confuses "a value" with "a command":

  1. User input glued into shell text. The handler builds a shell command by concatenating the incoming volume value into a command string instead of passing it as a separate argument.
  2. No validation, no sanitizing. Nothing checks that the value is actually a number, and nothing strips shell metacharacters such as ;, &&, or | before the string reaches the shell.
  3. The shell cannot tell data from commands. A separator character inside the value simply starts a second command, and the shell runs both happily — the volume change and the attacker's command.
  4. A moving, sensing target. The compromised process runs on a robot with cameras, microphones, speakers, and locomotion, so command execution means surveillance, movement, and persistence, not just data theft.

docs.title: Proof of concept
docs.text:
Educational only — this demonstrates the logic of the flaw, not an exploit against a real robot. The included poc.py simulates command building with plain data structures:

  • Vulnerable flow: a volume value is concatenated into a shell command string with no validation, so a value containing a shell separator produces two commands — and both "run".
  • Fixed flow: the value is parsed as a number first, and the command is executed without a shell, with the value passed as a separate argument — so a crafted value is rejected or treated as harmless data.

Run it locally:

python3 poc.py

Disclaimer: for education and defense only. Do not use against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update your Go2 to firmware 1.1.11.5 or later as soon as possible — that release closes this hole.
  • Isolate the robot on its own network segment, away from your main devices and anything sensitive.
  • If you do not use the remote chat feature, turn it off to remove the reachable handler.
  • Check the robot for unknown processes or accounts that could indicate persistence from an earlier compromise.
  • As a defense-in-depth rule: never build shell commands by concatenating user input — parse numeric input as a number, and run commands without a shell, passing arguments separately.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116000 — PrivateGPT: One Crafted Link Turns Your Private AI Into a Network Probe (SSRF)
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.3 Product zylon-ai/private-gpt — PrivateGPT 1.0.0 / 1.0.1 Type Server-Side Request Forgery (CWE-918) Vector Unauthenticated, network → the server fetches attacker-chosen URLs

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• PrivateGPT 1.0.0 and 1.0.1. The vulnerable code is load_file_from_uri in private_gpt/server/ingest/uri_loader.py, the URI Artifact Loader used when PrivateGPT ingests documents from a URL.
  • No official patch is known yet — the vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond. A public exploit is available.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The URI loader takes a URL supplied by the user and fetches it without checking where that URL actually points (CWE-918: the server retrieves the contents of a URL but does not sufficiently ensure the request goes to the expected destination). Because the fetch happens from the server, an attacker-chosen address inside the private network — an internal service, or a cloud metadata endpoint — is perfectly reachable from the server's side of the firewall.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern (private_gpt/server/ingest/uri_loader.py)
def load_file_from_uri(value):
    response = fetch(value)   # BUG: value never validated
    return ingest(response)   # server-side fetch, attacker-chosen target

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain:

  1. The attacker, with no login, hands PrivateGPT's ingest endpoint a crafted URL pointing at an internal address (for example a cloud metadata endpoint that hands out temporary credentials).
  2. The server fetches that URL itself and ingests the response.
  3. The attacker reads the ingested content back through PrivateGPT's normal question-answering flow — the server did the probing for them.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a loader that fetches any URL versus one that allowlists hosts and blocks private and link-local ranges, driven by synthetic offline requests. Fully offline — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Disable URL ingestion if you do not need it — ingest local files only.
  • Allowlist the hosts PrivateGPT may fetch; deny everything else.
  • Block private, loopback, and link-local ranges (including cloud metadata addresses) at the loader and at the egress proxy.
  • Do not expose PrivateGPT to the internet; bind it to localhost or an internal network and require authentication in front of it.
  • Update PrivateGPT the moment a fixed release lands, and watch the release notes for versions after 1.0.1.
  • Rotate any cloud credentials that a metadata endpoint could have exposed during the exposure window.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116006 — ruoyi-vue-pro: The SMS Code Is Always 9999, So Anyone Can Log In As Admin
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.3 (NVD); the reporting researcher scores it 9.1 Critical on confidentiality/integrity impact Product YunaiV/ruoyi-vue-pro (Yudao) — up to 2026.09 Type Improper Authentication (CWE-287); also reported as hard-coded/predictable credential (CWE-798) and insecure default initialization (CWE-1188) Vector Unauthenticated, network → SMS login with a constant code → full account takeover

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• ruoyi-vue-pro up to 2026.09, branches master, master-jdk17, and master-jdk25. Verified on master-jdk17 and re-verified against upstream on 2026-10-21.
  • No fix is available as of 2026-10-21. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond. A public proof of concept exists.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
The shipped base configuration pins the SMS verification-code range to a single value, left that way for testing convenience:

# yudao-server/src/main/resources/application.yaml
sms-code:
  begin-code: 9999  # testing convenience
  end-code: 9999    # testing convenience

The code generator draws an integer from [begin-code, end-code) and formats it as four digits — so with both ends at 9999, every code the system can ever produce is 9999. Worse, this block lives in the base configuration, not a test profile, and no shipped profile overrides it, so any deployment keeps it unless the operator explicitly changes both keys. The SMS-login endpoint is open to anonymous requests by design, and the login path (scene=21) has no CAPTCHA hook at all. The built-in admin account's phone number is published in the shipped SQL seed data.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain:

  1. The attacker, with no login and no CAPTCHA, asks the server for a login code for a victim's phone number (POST /admin-api/system/auth/send-sms-code, scene=21).
  2. The attacker logs in with the code 9999 — the only code the system can produce (POST /admin-api/system/auth/sms-login).
  3. The server returns a full access token for that account, including the built-in super administrator: control over users, roles, permissions, tenant data, and file storage. No password, no CAPTCHA, and no real text message are ever needed.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a code generator with a pinned range versus one drawing from a wide random range, plus a login check, driven by synthetic offline data. Fully offline — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Set a wide random code range (for example 100000–999999) in the base configuration — never ship a constant verification code as a default.
  • Keep any test-only override in a test-only profile that production cannot load by accident.
  • Refuse to start (or log a loud warning) when begin-code == end-code outside a test profile.
  • Add a CAPTCHA / risk-control hook to the SMS-login path (scene=21 currently has none).
  • Disable SMS login for privileged accounts such as admin, or require an explicit confirmation for SMS login of admin accounts.
  • Force all sessions to re-login and audit recent logins for accounts you do not recognize — assume tokens may already have been issued.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116117 — Halo CMS: Path Traversal in the Theme View Resolver
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.3 Product Halo CMS (open source, Java/Spring Boot) — up to 2.27.0-beta.1 Type Path traversal (CWE-22) Vector Remote, low complexity — a crafted template value in a page request escapes the theme directory and reaches files elsewhere on the server; exploit published

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: • Halo up to 2.27.0-beta.1. No fixed release was listed in the NVD record at the time of writing (record status: Deferred, October 26, 2026) — move off the beta and watch for the Halo security fix.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Halo's theme view resolver turns a template name into a file path so it can render the page, but it never verifies that the resolved path stays inside the theme folder. A template value containing directory-climbing segments is joined to the theme directory as-is, and the resulting path walks out of the theme directory. The resolver treats a file path as if it were harmless text — and a path in disguise obeys no folder boundary.

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
view_path = theme_dir + template_name   # template_name is attacker-controlled
open(view_path)                          # ".." segments walk out of theme_dir

# Simplified fixed pattern
candidate = resolve(theme_dir, template_name)
assert candidate.is_inside(theme_dir)    # reject anything that escapes
allowlist(template_name)                 # only known theme templates resolve

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. The attacker requests a page with a crafted template value containing directory-climbing segments.
  2. The theme view resolver builds a path from that value without a containment check.
  3. The resolved path lands outside the theme folder, and the server opens a file the theme was never meant to expose.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a vulnerable resolver versus a fixed resolver, against purely synthetic offline directories created by the script itself. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network, no system changes.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Move off 2.27.0-beta.1 in production: do not run the vulnerable beta publicly; upgrade to a fixed Halo release as soon as one ships.
  • Allowlist template names: only resolve template names your themes actually ship — reject anything else outright.
  • Canonicalize and verify: resolve the final path and confirm it stays inside the theme directory before opening it; never trust a string-prefix check alone.
  • Hunt: audit theme and access logs for template values containing .. or path separators.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116233 — Oray Pugongying X5 Pro: A DHCP Lease Time Smuggles a Newline into Dnsmasq (CRLF Injection)
docs.text: Field Value Severity Critical — CVSS 9.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) Product Oray Pugongying X5 Pro 7.6.1 Type CRLF Injection (CWE-74, CWE-93) Vector Network, low complexity, high privileges required, no user interaction, scope changed

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Oray Pugongying X5 Pro firmware 7.6.1.
  • The vulnerable component is Dnsmasq: the rent_time (DHCP lease time) argument is written into a configuration file without neutralizing carriage-return / line-feed characters.
  • No vendor patch has been announced; the vendor was contacted before disclosure and did not respond.
  • This flaw is one of a cluster disclosed the same day against the same firmware: CVE-2026-116231 (Ser2net), CVE-2026-116232 (SNMP), CVE-2026-116234 (IPsec), CVE-2026-116235 (L2TP), and CVE-2026-116236 (PPPoE plugin upload).

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
User-controlled text is interpolated into a configuration file, but carriage returns (\r) and line feeds (\n) are never stripped or escaped. In a config file, a line break separates one directive from the next, so an attacker-controlled newline does not stay inside one value: it starts a brand new directive that the device then obeys as if an administrator wrote it (CWE-74: improper neutralization of special elements in output used by a downstream component, CWE-93: improper neutralization of CRLF sequences).

# Simplified vulnerable pattern (conceptual)
# lease-time value written straight into the dnsmasq config
rent_time = ATTACKER_VALUE
# attacker sends: "3600\n<new directive>"
# the config now contains a second, attacker-chosen line

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
The attack chain:

  1. The attacker holds a high-privilege account able to reach the device's DHCP/Dnsmasq configuration.
  2. They submit a lease time containing a hidden newline plus a crafted directive.
  3. Dnsmasq's configuration writer stores the value verbatim, and the hidden newline splits it into two lines.
  4. When the service reloads, the injected directive executes with the service's privileges, leading to root code execution.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely and offline: a config writer that interpolates raw input (vulnerable) versus one that strips line breaks and validates the value as a number (fixed). No device, no network, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Restrict management access to trusted networks only — do not expose the device's services to the internet.
  • Disable Dnsmasq's remote configurability where possible, and disable any services you do not use.
  • Watch configuration files for unexpected changes and audit device logs.
  • Check for a firmware update regularly, and replace the device if you cannot isolate it, since no patch has been announced.

docs.title: CVE-2026-116236 — Oray Pugongying X5 Pro: Unrestricted Plugin Upload via PPPoE Settings Leads to Root Code Execution
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.2 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) Product Oray Pugongying X5 Pro 7.6.1 Type Unrestricted Upload / Improper Access Control (CWE-284, CWE-434) Vector Network, low complexity, high privileges required, no user interaction, scope unchanged

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• Oray Pugongying X5 Pro firmware 7.6.1.
  • The vulnerable component is the PPPoE WAN setting handler: the plugin_init function writes the pppd_options argument into /tmp/upload_files without restricting what may be uploaded.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:

Because the daemon later loads those plugin options, an attacker-controlled file becomes attacker-controlled code (CWE-284: improper access control, CWE-434: unrestricted upload of a file with a dangerous type).

# Simplified vulnerable pattern (conceptual)
# plugin options written straight to the upload directory
open("/tmp/upload_files/plugin", "w").write(ATTACKER_OPTIONS)
# the daemon later loads the plugin -> attacker code runs

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)

  1. The attacker holds a high-privilege account able to reach the device's PPPoE WAN settings.
  2. They submit crafted plugin options through the settings handler.
  3. The handler stores the options as a plugin file without validation.
  4. The daemon loads the plugin, and the attacker's code runs as root.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely and offline: an uploader that stores any content (vulnerable) versus one that allowlists the file type and destination (fixed). No device, no network, no exploit.

docs.title: CVE-2026-15723 — GitLab: LDAP Account Takeover via OmniAuth SAML Identity Linking
docs.text: Field Value Severity High — CVSS 8.2 (v3.1) Product GitLab CE/EE with OmniAuth SAML + LDAP auto-linking enabled Type Improper input sanitization (CWE-90) in the LDAP email lookup during identity linking Vector Authenticated attacker signs in via SAML, links to a victim's LDAP-backed account through a poorly sanitized email lookup — no interaction from the victim required

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: All versions from 10.1 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1. Fixed in 19.3.6, 19.4.3, 19.5.1.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
When both OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking were enabled, GitLab tried to match the incoming SAML identity to an existing LDAP user by email. The email value taken from the SAML assertion was not properly sanitized before being used in the LDAP lookup path, so an attacker could shape it to match someone else's LDAP account. GitLab then linked the attacker's session to the victim's account:

# Simplified vulnerable pattern
def link_identity(saml_email):
    ldap_user = ldap_lookup(saml_email)   # BUG: unsanitized attacker input
    if ldap_user:
        link(current_session, ldap_user)  # victim's account linked to attacker

# Simplified fixed pattern
def link_identity_fixed(saml_email):
    email = strict_normalize(saml_email)  # canonicalize + validate first
    ldap_user = ldap_lookup_exact(email)
    if ldap_user and verified_owner(email, current_user):
        link(current_session, ldap_user)

Identity linking must never trust an unsanitized claim.

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
1. Target instance has OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking both enabled.
  2. Attacker authenticates with their own low-privilege SAML identity.
  3. During linking, the attacker supplies a crafted email value that the loose LDAP lookup resolves to the victim's LDAP-backed account.
  4. GitLab links the attacker's session to the victim's account — full takeover, zero victim interaction.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: loose vs. strict email matching when resolving an account for linking. Offline, no server, no exploit.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Upgrade: 19.3.6 / 19.4.3 / 19.5.1.
  • Review identity links: audit identities for unexpected SAML↔LDAP linkages, especially around privileged accounts.
  • Disable auto-linking if the SAML and LDAP user populations are not strictly aligned.
  • Enforce exact, verified email matching between identity providers before linking.

docs.title: CVE-2026-15748 — Forminator MIME Blocklist Bypass → Unauthenticated PHP Shell Upload
docs.text: Field Detail Severity Critical 9.8 (CVSS 3.1) Product Forminator Forms (WordPress), ≤ 1.56.1 Type Unrestricted file upload via blocklist bypass (CWE-434) Attack vector Network · unauthenticated form submission with forged upload field

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text: All versions up to and including 1.56.1. Fixed in 1.56.2.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: handle_file_upload validates uploads against a blocklist of dangerous MIME types using exact string-key matching. MIME types support pipe-separated alternatives, so declaring the file's type with a trailing pipe fails the exact match while the server still treats the payload as PHP. Separately, the upload field configuration is attacker-controlled through a forged Select field value, so the attacker dictates the allowed types for the submission.

The attacker submits a PHP shell declaring its MIME type with a trailing pipe character. 3. The blocklist's exact-match check misses → the file is accepted into the uploads directory. 4. The attacker requests the uploaded file → remote code execution, no login required.

The bundled poc.py demonstrates the exact-match versus normalized validation logic on synthetic inputs only — no server involved.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update Forminator to 1.56.2 immediately.
  • Scan wp-content/uploads/ for unexpected .php or other executable files.
  • Prefer allowlists of known-safe types over blocklists of bad ones; normalize and validate the real file extension server-side.

docs.title: CVE-2026-16460 — bootc + ostree: Two Holes in the OS Image Trust Chain (Signature Bypass)
docs.text:
Field Value Severity High — CVSS 7.4 (CVE-2026-16460), CVSS 8.1 (CVE-2026-16487) Product bootc + ostree — image-based Linux (RHEL image mode, Fedora Atomic) Type Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity (CWE-345) Vector Local (16460: staged deployments) / Network (16487: mutable-tag upgrades) → unsigned OS content becomes the host on reboot

This writeup covers two CVEs published together against the same product:

CVE Issue CVE-2026-16460 bootc and ostree finalize already-staged deployments without revalidating the container image against the current containers signature policy. Unsigned OS content staged under a prior permissive policy stays bootable after the policy is hardened to reject unsigned images. CVSS 7.4, AV:L/AC:H. CVE-2026-16487 bootc operating with the default containers signature policy: automatic or manual upgrades of a mutable image tag may apply unsigned content for registries that fall through to insecureAcceptAnything. An attacker who can update that tag gets arbitrary OS content executed as the host root filesystem on reboot. CVSS 8.1, AV:N/AC:H.

docs.title: Affected versions
docs.text:
• CVE-2026-16460: bootc/ostree builds predating the upstream fix — staged deployments are finalized without policy revalidation. Track the fix via the Red Hat CVE page.
  • CVE-2026-16487: bootc builds honoring the default containers signature policy with insecureAcceptAnything fallthrough. Track the fix via the Red Hat CVE page.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
A signature-policy decision is made once, at pull time, and then trusted forever. Two code paths skip the check at the moments that matter:

  1. Finalize path (CVE-2026-16460): the policy is consulted when content is staged, never when the staged deployment is finalized or booted. Hardening the policy afterwards changes the rules for new pulls, but the staged deployment keeps its old, unvalidated trust — and it is still the one queued to boot.
  2. Upgrade path (CVE-2026-16487): registries with no explicit rule in the policy fall through to insecureAcceptAnything, so for those registries the signature check silently never runs — on automatic and manual upgrades of mutable tags.
# Simplified vulnerable pattern (containers policy + bootc finalize)
policy:
  default: signedBy(trusted-key)   # checked ONLY at pull/stage time
  # no rule for attacker.registry  ->  insecureAcceptAnything fallthrough

finalize(staged_deployment):
    boot(staged.image)             # <-- no policy re-check here

docs.title: Proof of concept (conceptual)
docs.text:
Path A (CVE-2026-16460):

  1. With the containers signature policy still permissive, unsigned OS content is staged on the machine (attacker needs local access).
  2. The admin hardens the policy to reject unsigned images. The staged deployment is untouched and stays queued to boot.
  3. On reboot, bootc finalizes the staged deployment — no revalidation — and the machine boots attacker-controlled content as the host OS. Full compromise of confidentiality, integrity and availability.

Path B (CVE-2026-16487):

  1. The machine tracks a mutable tag (e.g. registry/app:latest) on a registry with no explicit policy rule, falling through to insecureAcceptAnything.
  2. An attacker who can update that tag (registry compromise, weak credentials) points it at unsigned, malicious OS content.
  3. The next automatic or manual upgrade pulls it with no signature check; on reboot it becomes the host root filesystem.

The accompanying poc.py demonstrates the pattern safely: a finalize step that skips revalidation versus one that re-checks the current policy, and a mutable tag that falls through to "accept anything" versus a pinned digest with an explicit signedBy rule. Fully offline, synthetic data — no exploit, no network calls.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Update bootc and ostree to the patched releases (see the Red Hat CVE pages above for errata).
  • Pin images to immutable digests, not mutable tags, wherever the fleet allows it.
  • Close the policy hole: remove any insecureAcceptAnything fallthrough from your containers signature policy; give every registry an explicit signedBy rule.
  • Audit every staged deployment on the fleet after any policy change — clear unvalidated staged content before it boots.
  • Rotate any credentials/tokens that could have been exposed on a compromised host and audit boot logs for unexpected staged content.
